data.prompt: Describe a person who has influenced you

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone very close to home. The person who has influenced me most is my father, who ran a small business in Sirajganj for over thirty years and has only recently retired. Obviously I have known him all my life, but I think I only really started to understand him as a teenager, when I began helping out in his shop after school. Growing up, I watched him deal with setbacks that would have [[discouraged]] most people, yet he always stayed calm and kept going. There were slow seasons, especially during the monsoon, when hardly anyone came in, but he never let his worries spill over into family life. What shaped me was not any single piece of advice, but the quiet example he set day after day. He treated every customer, however difficult, with the same [[integrity]], and he taught me that a good reputation is built slowly and lost quickly. When I was struggling to choose a career, he never pushed me in one direction; instead he encouraged me to be [[self-reliant]] and make my own decisions. Looking back, almost everything I value about hard work and honesty can be traced to him, and I try to bring the same patience to my job at the consultancy, especially with anxious students. His influence has been [[profound]], and I still catch myself asking what he would do in a tricky situation. In many ways he remains my quiet role model, even now that I am an adult, and I suspect he always will be.

followUps.q: Do you still ask your father for advice?
followUps.answer: Yes, quite often, especially about money or big decisions. Since he retired he has more time to talk, so we usually chat over tea in the evening, and his advice is still remarkably [[level-headed]].

followUps.q: Would you like to be like him in the future?
followUps.answer: In many ways, yes. I would love to have his patience and honesty, although I probably will not run a shop. I just hope people eventually see me as someone as trustworthy as he is.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is important for young people to have role models?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely vital for adolescents to have someone to look up to. Role models act as a kind of moral compass, offering guidance on how to navigate life. When a young person admires a professional, they are [[internalising]] the values of hard work and [[perseverance]] that led to that success. Without such figures, young people can feel a little [[unmoored]], lacking any real sense of direction.

part3Samples.q: How have the types of role models changed since your grandparents' time?
part3Samples.answer: There has been a rather dramatic shift, I would say. In my grandparents' era, role models tended to be figures within the immediate community, such as teachers or elders. Today, influence is increasingly [[dominated]] by celebrities and social media personalities, many of whom are famous for very little of substance. I find this shift somewhat concerning, because fame has become almost entirely [[disconnected]] from genuine [[merit]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people are more influenced by role models in real life or in the media?
part3Samples.answer: That is an interesting question. I would argue that media figures have a wider reach, but real-life role models, like a parent or mentor, have a far deeper and more [[lasting impact]]. The influence of a media personality is often [[superficial]] and [[fleeting]], whereas someone you interact with daily shapes your character in a much more meaningful way.

part3Samples.q: Why do some public figures fail to remain positive role models over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think the main reason is the immense pressure and [[scrutiny]] that come with public life. Constant attention can distort a person's judgement, and some become [[complacent]] once they achieve fame. There is also the temptation of wealth and power, which can gradually [[erode]] the very values that made them admirable in the first place. Sadly, staying grounded under that spotlight is genuinely difficult.

part3Samples.q: In the future, do you think AI or fictional characters could become role models?
part3Samples.answer: It is quite possible, and to some extent it is already happening. Virtual influencers are becoming increasingly [[prevalent]], and young people do form attachments to fictional heroes. However, I would be somewhat [[wary]] of this trend, because a fabricated character lacks the real struggles that make human role models relatable. I think something genuinely [[authentic]] would be lost in that shift.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

sample.answer: I would like to describe a lovely afternoon I spent with my nephew. Not long ago, during the winter, my elder sister paid us a surprise visit from Dhaka with her four-year-old son, and I ended up spending a whole afternoon with him. My sister had some errands to run in town with my mother, so I happily volunteered to keep him entertained. I had always found him endearing, but this was the first time we had really had a proper day together, just the two of us. He was remarkably [[inquisitive]] for his age, firing off questions about almost everything, some of which genuinely stumped me, like why the river never runs out of water. We built a fort out of cushions, drew a few clumsy animals, and I read him a couple of stories, putting on silly voices that he found hilarious. Later we walked down to the bank of the Jamuna to watch the boats, which he absolutely loved. What struck me most was how [[perceptive]] children are: he picked up on my mood instantly and kept trying to cheer me up. By evening I was exhausted, but it was the most [[rewarding]] kind of tiredness. It reminded me that spending time with a child forces you to slow down and be fully present, something adults rarely manage. Honestly, that afternoon was [[a welcome escape]] from my usual routine, and I have made a point of seeing him more often since, even if that means a long bus journey to Dhaka.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy spending time with children in general?
followUps.answer: Yes, I do, although I find it quite tiring. Children are so honest and [[unfiltered]] that you cannot pretend around them, and I think that is rather refreshing compared with the adult world.

followUps.q: Would you like to have children of your own one day?
followUps.answer: I think so, but not for a few years. I would like to be settled in my career first, and perhaps finish studying abroad, so that I can give them proper time and attention.

part3Samples.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?

sample.answer: When I think about someone with a lot on their plate, one person immediately stands out. The person who comes to mind is my mother, who somehow manages to juggle an enormous number of duties without ever seeming [[overwhelmed]]. Besides running the entire household, she helps look after my elderly grandparents in our ancestral village, which means travelling back and forth quite often, and she still finds time to help neighbours during any crisis. On top of that, she manages the household budget and keeps a close eye on my younger sister's studies. As for how she handles it all, what amazes me is how [[methodical]] she is; she plans her days carefully so nothing important slips through the cracks. She is usually up before everyone else, and by the time we sit down to breakfast half her list is already done. I have often seen her handle a sick relative, a household emergency and a family gathering all in the same week, yet she rarely complains. She has this quiet [[resilience]] that I deeply admire, and she genuinely believes that looking after others is a privilege rather than a burden. Whenever I feel stretched by my own comparatively minor workload, I think of her and feel slightly embarrassed. She has taught me that carrying responsibility gracefully is a skill in itself. Honestly, I consider her the most [[dependable]] person I know, and the whole family leans on her more than we probably realise. I really should tell her that more often.

followUps.q: Do you help your mother with her responsibilities?
followUps.answer: I try to, although not as much as I should. I do the shopping at the weekend and sometimes go with her to the village, but she still [[shoulders]] most of the work herself.

followUps.q: Do you think you will have more responsibilities in the future?
followUps.answer: Almost certainly. As my parents get older, I expect to take on more at home, and my career will bring its own pressures. I just hope I can cope with them as calmly as she does.

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

data.prompt: Describe a person you admire

sample.answer: Someone I genuinely admire is a former teacher of mine who went far beyond what his job required. I knew him through secondary school in Sirajganj, where he taught mathematics, but his real gift was noticing students who were quietly struggling. I was one of them for a while, because I found algebra completely baffling in my first year with him. In terms of his qualities, he was endlessly [[patient]], staying behind after class to help anyone who asked, and he never made you feel foolish for not understanding. What I admired most was his [[humility]]; despite being extremely knowledgeable, he always spoke to us as equals. He had a way of making difficult ideas feel [[accessible]], often using examples from the local market or cricket scores, and he clearly cared about the person, not just the grade. Years later, I still remember specific things he said that shaped how I think. As for why I admire him, I think what sets people like him apart is that they are motivated by a genuine desire to help rather than any reward. He was never well paid, and he could easily have earned more from private coaching, but he chose to help struggling students for free instead. He left a [[lasting impression]] on hundreds of students, and I count myself lucky to have been one of them. In fact, in my own job I often try to explain things to students the way he once explained things to me.

followUps.q: Are you still in touch with him?
followUps.answer: Not regularly, but I bump into him now and then in town. He is retired now, and he always asks about my work. It is quite touching that he still remembers me after all these years.

followUps.q: Would you ever like to become a teacher?
followUps.answer: Perhaps in some form. My job already involves a lot of guiding and explaining, and I find that side of it deeply [[fulfilling]], but I am not sure I have the patience for a classroom of teenagers.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the main purpose of education?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, education serves a dual purpose. On a practical level, it equips people with the knowledge and skills needed for employment. But more importantly, I believe its deeper purpose is to [[cultivate]] critical thinking and produce well-rounded, responsible citizens. Education should teach people how to think, not merely what to think. Sadly, many systems overemphasise [[rote learning]] at the expense of this broader [[enrichment]].

part3Samples.q: How is education today different from education in the past?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are considerable. In the past, education was largely teacher-centred, based on memorisation and strict discipline. Today, there is a much greater emphasis on interactive, student-centred learning, and technology has [[revolutionised]] access to information. Learning is now more [[collaborative]] and creative. However, I would argue that academic pressure and competition have also intensified, which is a rather [[double-edged]] development.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think exam results are given so much importance?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems from the need for a seemingly objective way to measure ability and allocate opportunities. Exams provide a convenient, [[quantifiable]] benchmark for universities and employers. However, this [[overreliance]] on results can be [[counterproductive]], as it encourages students to memorise for tests rather than truly understand. It also fails to capture vital qualities like creativity, which are far harder to quantify.

part3Samples.q: How do you think education will change in the next 20 years?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate dramatic changes, largely driven by technology. Personalised, AI-assisted learning could [[tailor]] lessons to each student's pace, and online education will make quality teaching far more accessible globally. The traditional classroom may become less central. There will likely also be a stronger focus on [[adaptable]] skills, given that people will need to [[reskill]] repeatedly throughout their careers.

part3Samples.q: How could education systems be improved?
part3Samples.answer: There are several improvements I would suggest. Firstly, systems should place less emphasis on high-stakes exams and more on continuous, practical assessment. Secondly, curricula should be [[modernised]] to include life skills such as financial literacy and emotional intelligence. Finally, investing in teacher training and reducing class sizes would allow for more [[personalised]] learning. The goal should be a more [[holistic]] and flexible model.

part3Samples.q: Some people say governments should promote positive role models. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree. Governments can certainly [[showcase]] admirable citizens, such as scientists or humanitarians, to counterbalance shallow celebrity culture. However, I am slightly cautious, because state-endorsed role models can easily become [[propaganda]] if handled poorly. So while the intention is commendable, it needs to be done [[transparently]] and without any political agenda.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a friend whose mind I have always found slightly intimidating. One of the most intelligent people I know is a close friend from university who studied physics, while I was doing business administration. We met because we lived in the same student hostel, and we have stayed close ever since, even though he now lives in Rajshahi. What sets him apart is not just how much he knows, but how quickly he grasps complicated ideas that leave the rest of us bewildered. He has this [[analytical]] mind that breaks any problem into neat, logical steps. I remember him explaining a statistics concept I had struggled with for weeks in about five minutes, and suddenly it made perfect sense. Yet he is never arrogant about it, which makes his intelligence all the more [[impressive]]. He is also [[intellectually curious]], always reading about subjects far outside his field, from history to economics. I think real intelligence is exactly this combination of sharpness and open-mindedness, rather than simply getting top marks. As for how I feel about him, talking to him is genuinely [[stimulating]], because he challenges your assumptions without ever making you feel small. I will admit that I sometimes feel a little slow beside him, but mostly I just feel grateful. Honestly, I always come away from our conversations having learned something, and that is rare. I suspect he will end up doing research abroad one day, and I will be very proud of him when he does.

followUps.q: Do you think intelligence is something people are born with?
followUps.answer: Partly, but I think curiosity and effort matter just as much. My friend was clearly gifted, but he also read constantly, so his intelligence was [[nurtured]] as much as it was inherited.

followUps.q: Do you often ask him for help?
followUps.answer: Now and then, mostly when I need to make sense of numbers at work. He is always happy to help, although he usually ends up teaching me far more than I actually asked for.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

sample.answer: If I could meet any famous person, it would probably be a well-known entrepreneur whose story I find genuinely inspiring. He is famous for building a huge technology company from almost nothing, starting out with a handful of friends and very little money. What fascinates me, though, is not the wealth but the [[perseverance]] behind it. I have read a great deal about him, in interviews and in a biography I borrowed from a friend, and I know how many times he failed before succeeding, which I find strangely reassuring. Several of his early ventures went bankrupt, and at one point even people close to him thought he should give up. What draws me to him is his reputation for thinking in genuinely [[unconventional]] ways, seeing opportunities others dismiss. As for why I would like to meet him, I would love to ask how he stayed motivated during the years when everything seemed to be collapsing. I imagine he would be surprisingly [[down-to-earth]], because people who have struggled tend to be. Since I studied business administration, I would also be curious to hear what he thinks young people in a country like Bangladesh should focus on. I think a single conversation with someone like that could be more [[enlightening]] than any book. Realistically it will never happen, but if it did, I would come prepared with a long list of questions and simply listen. Even a few minutes with him would give me a story to tell my family for years.

followUps.q: Would you like to be famous yourself?
followUps.answer: Not really. I think fame brings a lot of pressure and very little privacy. I would much rather be respected by the people around me than recognised by strangers in the street.

followUps.q: Do you think famous people are good role models?
followUps.answer: Some are, especially those who worked hard and stayed humble. But many are admired for the wrong reasons, so young people need to be quite [[discerning]] about whose example they follow.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think so many young people want to be famous?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely driven by social media, which has made fame appear both [[glamorous]] and easily attainable. Young people see influencers achieving wealth and adoration seemingly overnight, which is highly [[seductive]]. There is also a deeper human desire for validation and significance. Unfortunately, this often means chasing fame as an end in itself rather than as a [[by-product]] of genuine achievement.

part3Samples.q: How is fame today different from fame in the past?
part3Samples.answer: The nature of fame has changed completely. In the past, fame was usually earned through exceptional talent or accomplishment, and famous people were relatively few. Today, anyone can become famous overnight through a viral video, and fame is often [[fleeting]] and detached from any real skill. Modern celebrity is also far more [[invasive]], with stars under constant [[surveillance]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does celebrity culture have on young people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects are often [[detrimental]], in my view. Constant exposure to celebrities' curated, idealised lives can create unrealistic expectations and [[fuel insecurity]], especially about appearance. It can also promote materialism and a distorted sense of what matters. That said, positive celebrities who [[champion]] good causes can be a genuinely inspiring influence, so it is not entirely negative.

part3Samples.q: Do you think celebrity culture will become more or less influential in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I suspect it will become even more influential, but also more [[fragmented]]. Rather than a few global superstars, we are likely to see countless niche influencers, each commanding devoted audiences. Technology like virtual influencers may further blur the line between real and fabricated fame. Whether this influence is healthy will depend on whether audiences become more [[discerning]] and [[sceptical]].

He is the one person I can be completely [[candid]] with, without fear of judgement. What I value most is that our friendship has never felt like hard work; it is genuinely [[effortless]]. A middle-aged stranger, who turned out to be a local schoolteacher, noticed me looking anxious and stopped to ask if I needed help. What struck me was how genuinely [[considerate]] he was; not only did he give me directions, he actually walked me halfway there. He could easily have ignored me, as most people would have, so his kindness felt almost [[remarkable]]. Along the way we chatted, and he told me a little about the area, which turned a stressful moment into a pleasant one. He even recommended a small tea stall near my hotel, which I went back to every day that week. I was incredibly [[grateful]], and I remember trying to offer him something in return, which he politely refused. That small act of kindness has genuinely stayed with me, and it made me more willing to help strangers myself, especially students who come into our office looking lost and nervous. It was a reminder that a little [[compassion]] costs nothing but can mean a great deal. I never even learned his name, but I still think of him fondly.

followUps.answer: In big cities, perhaps a little, because everyone is in a hurry and slightly suspicious. But in smaller towns like mine, people still stop to help, and I find that very reassuring.

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though I would add a small [[caveat]]. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?

We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?

In my view, healthy relationships are not conflict-free; they simply handle disagreement [[maturely]] and constructively.

In terms of her qualities, she was genuinely [[approachable]], so people felt comfortable bringing problems to her before they escalated. Rather than taking credit, she was quick to [[acknowledge]] everyone's contribution, which made the whole team want to work harder. She also had a talent for staying calm under pressure, which was [[reassuring]] during stressful periods, such as the frantic weeks before university application deadlines. What I admired most was her fairness; she treated everyone equally, regardless of seniority. As for why I think she was a good leader, too many leaders confuse authority with respect, but she understood that respect has to be earned. Under her, the team was noticeably more [[motivated]] and loyal, and hardly anyone left, which is unusual in our industry. Honestly, she set a standard for how I would want to lead people myself one day, and whenever I help a new colleague settle in, I try to remember how she treated me as a nervous beginner.

part3Samples.q: What qualities make someone a good leader?

They need the ability to inspire and motivate others towards a common goal, but also the humility to listen. Crucially, effective leaders lead by example and take responsibility for failures rather than shifting blame. I think this [[accountability]], paired with genuine [[empathy]], is what earns lasting respect.

part3Samples.q: Is it better for a leader to be respected or feared?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe respect is far more effective than fear. A leader who rules through fear may achieve short-term [[compliance]], but this breeds resentment and stifles honest communication. A respected leader, by contrast, inspires genuine loyalty and willing effort. People follow such a leader out of [[conviction]] rather than intimidation, which produces far better and more [[sustainable]] results.

part3Samples.q: What happens to an organisation when it has poor leadership?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Poor leadership often results in low morale, as employees feel [[directionless]] and undervalued. This typically leads to reduced productivity and high staff turnover. Without a clear vision, an organisation can quickly [[stagnate]] or lose its way entirely. In short, weak leadership tends to [[permeate]] every level and undermine the whole enterprise.

part3Samples.q: How do you think leadership styles will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I believe we are moving away from the traditional top-down, authoritarian model towards something more [[collaborative]]. Future leaders will likely need to be more emotionally intelligent and adaptable, given how quickly the world changes. There will also be greater emphasis on [[transparency]] and inclusivity. In short, leadership is becoming less about command and more about [[facilitation]].

part3Samples.q: How can society develop better leaders?
part3Samples.answer: I think it starts with education that [[nurtures]] not just intelligence but character and empathy. Providing young people with genuine opportunities to take responsibility, through mentorship or community projects, helps [[cultivate]] leadership skills early. We should also reward ethical leadership rather than [[mere ambition]]. Essentially, good leaders are developed over time, not simply born.

part3Samples.q: Some say people today change jobs too often. Do you agree?

In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say schools focus too much on academics and not enough on emotional skills. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree with this criticism. Traditional education has long [[prioritised]] exam results above all else, often neglecting the emotional and social skills that are equally vital for a fulfilling life. Skills like managing stress, empathising and collaborating are rarely taught explicitly. I think a more [[holistic]] education, one that develops the whole person, would produce far more [[well-rounded]] and capable adults.

He runs a small practice near our home in Sirajganj and has looked after my family since I was a child. Beyond his obvious medical knowledge, what makes him stand out is how he treats patients as people rather than cases. He is incredibly [[thorough]], always taking the time to explain things clearly instead of rushing you out of the door. I have noticed that he has a calming presence, which is [[invaluable]] when you are worried about your health. He also keeps himself up to date, so his advice always feels current and trustworthy. What impresses me most is his [[dedication]]; he clearly sees medicine as a vocation, not just a job. I remember him coming to our flat late one night during the monsoon when my father had a high fever, which he certainly did not have to do. Because of this, the entire community trusts him completely, and appointments are always fully booked. I think being good at a job like his requires both skill and genuine [[empathy]], and he has both in abundance. As for how I feel about him, I have enormous respect for him. Honestly, he has set my expectations of what a good professional should be, and I try to bring some of his patience to my own work.

followUps.q: Would you like to have a job like his?
followUps.answer: Not really. I admire doctors enormously, but I do not think I could cope with the pressure or the sight of blood. I am much happier helping people in a less [[high-stakes]] way.

followUps.q: Do you think doctors are well respected in your country?
followUps.answer: Generally yes, especially good ones like him. Doctors are highly regarded in Bangladesh, and many parents dream of their children becoming one, although the profession is extremely demanding.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people happy at work?
part3Samples.answer: In my opinion, job satisfaction [[stems from]] more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is [[paramount]]. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of [[autonomy]] all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.

part3Samples.q: Is money or a sense of purpose more important for job satisfaction?
part3Samples.answer: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not [[compensate]] for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a [[threshold]], but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even [[burnout]], which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher [[staff turnover]]. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is [[detrimental]] to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be more or less satisfied with their jobs in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over [[tedious]], repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant [[connectivity]] could [[undermine]] satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

part3Samples.q: What can employers do to make their staff happier?
part3Samples.answer: Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine [[recognition]] for good work is [[fundamental]]. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. Simply listening to employees and giving them a degree of autonomy over their work is powerful. Investing in staff wellbeing is not just ethical; it is genuinely [[profitable]] in the long run.

part3Samples.q: Some say job security is more important than job satisfaction. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends heavily on a person's circumstances. For someone supporting a family, security is understandably the priority, as it provides essential [[peace of mind]]. However, I personally lean towards satisfaction, because a secure but miserable job can [[take a serious toll]] on one's mental health over time. Ideally, one should not have to sacrifice one for the other, though reality often forces a [[compromise]].

He worked the family land for most of his life, and he lived through some genuinely difficult times, and yet he has never become bitter or cynical about life. In terms of what he is like, he is gentle and quick-witted, and he still wakes up at dawn to walk around the fields. He is also incredibly [[humble]] about his own achievements, rarely talking about the hardships he overcame. I love listening to his stories, because each one seems to carry a subtle lesson without ever being preachy. Despite his age, he remains genuinely [[open-minded]], curious about new technology and interested in what young people think. He even asks me to show him cricket highlights on my phone, and he has strong opinions about every player. What I respect most is his [[wisdom]]; whenever the family faces a problem, he has this quiet way of putting things in perspective. I also think there is something we can all learn from his [[contentment]]; he seems at peace with his life in a way that is rare. Honestly, I hope I can grow old with even half of his grace and good humour.

followUps.q: Do you think older people are respected enough in your country?

part3Samples.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite [[pronounced]], largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to [[tension]], though it also brings a healthy [[diversity]] of perspectives.

part3Samples.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are quite [[stark]]. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

part3Samples.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
part3Samples.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to [[empathise]], with each side viewing the other's values as [[alien]]. A lack of open, patient communication only [[widens that gulf]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
part3Samples.answer: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now [[evolves]]. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could [[amplify]] the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help [[bridge]] it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?
part3Samples.answer: [[Fostering]] genuine dialogue is essential. Creating opportunities for generations to interact meaningfully, whether in families or communities, builds mutual understanding. Both sides need to approach differences with [[humility]] rather than judgement. I also think education plays a role in teaching young people to respect their elders while encouraging older people to remain [[receptive]] to new ideas.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

A businessperson I really admire is the founder of a local company that started as a tiny shop and grew into a respected national brand. The business makes food products, things like biscuits and snacks that you can find in almost every corner shop in Bangladesh. What I find inspiring is not just the commercial success, but the way he treated his employees like family throughout. He was known for reinvesting profits into his staff and community rather than simply [[maximising]] his own wealth. In terms of what he achieved, I have read that he took real risks in the early years, when the venture could easily have [[collapsed]]. Over time, though, he turned a single shop into several factories, providing jobs for a great many people, including in rural areas where work is scarce. That kind of courage, combined with a clear [[vision]], is what separates genuine entrepreneurs from the rest. He also stayed grounded despite his success, which earned him enormous loyalty. As for why I admire him, it is partly personal, because my father ran a small business for over thirty years, so I know how hard it is simply to survive. What I admire most is that he proved you can build something profitable while remaining [[ethical]]. Honestly, in an age when many businesses cut corners, his example is refreshing, and it has shaped how I think about running a company myself one day.

followUps.q: Would you like to start your own business?
followUps.answer: Possibly, one day. With my background in business administration, it is tempting, but I would want some experience abroad first. Starting a company without proper preparation seems far too [[precarious]] to me.

followUps.q: Do you think successful businesspeople should give back to society?
followUps.answer: Yes, I do. Businesses depend on their communities, so it seems fair that they share some of their success, whether through charity, fair wages or supporting local education.

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say money cannot buy happiness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though with a [[nuance]]. It is certainly true that beyond meeting our basic needs, more money does not reliably increase happiness, and the richest people are not necessarily the happiest. Lasting happiness comes from relationships and purpose. However, I would add that a lack of money, and the poverty and stress it brings, can definitely cause unhappiness. So money cannot buy happiness, but [[financial security]] can certainly remove a major source of [[misery]] and anxiety.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a teacher who, in a way, is part of the reason I can speak English today. The teacher who influenced me most was my secondary school English teacher, who genuinely changed how I saw the subject. Before her class, I found English dull and mechanical, just grammar rules to memorise for exams. She taught us English language and literature for two years, and she had this gift for making lessons feel [[engaging]], often using stories, songs and debates instead of dry exercises. Sometimes she would ask us to act out scenes from short stories, which felt terrifying at first but was great fun, and it made the language feel alive for the first time. What set her apart was her genuine belief in her students; she could spot potential we could not see in ourselves. She was also endlessly [[encouraging]], praising effort rather than just results, which built my confidence enormously. As for how she influenced me, I still remember how she pushed me to enter a writing competition I would never have attempted alone. I did not win, but I was shortlisted, and that small success meant the world to me. That single act of [[faith]] in me changed my relationship with the language completely. Honestly, a large part of why I am comfortable using English today is [[attributable]] to her, including in my job, where I use it every single day. I think great teachers do exactly this: they light a spark that keeps burning long after the classroom.

followUps.q: Are you still in touch with her?
followUps.answer: Sadly not directly, as she moved to another district some years ago. But I heard through a friend that she is still teaching, and I like to think she is still [[igniting]] that same spark in her students.

followUps.q: Do you think teachers are more important than textbooks?
followUps.answer: Definitely. A textbook gives you information, but a good teacher gives you the motivation to use it. I think most people remember a great teacher far longer than any book they studied.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a conversation that genuinely changed the direction of my life. It was just after I had finished my studies, and I was [[paralysed]] by the number of choices in front of me. Some friends were preparing for government jobs, others were going abroad, and I had no idea which way to turn. He sat me down one evening after dinner and told me something simple but profound: that it is better to try and fail than to spend your life wondering. What made his advice so valuable was that he spoke from experience, having left a safe job himself to try something new in his thirties. He encouraged me to stop overthinking and [[take the plunge]], even if the first step was a small one. That conversation was genuinely [[pivotal]], because it shifted me from fear to action. I ended up making a decision I had been putting off for months, and it turned out well: the following week I applied for a position at an education consultancy, and I have been working there ever since. Looking back, his words were exactly what I needed at that [[crucial]] moment. Honestly, I still repeat that advice to friends who find themselves stuck, and to nervous students too, because I have seen for myself how much difference it can make.

followUps.q: Do you usually take advice from other people?
followUps.answer: Yes, but I try to be selective. I listen to people who have real experience of the situation, and then I [[weigh up]] their views before deciding. In the end, the decision has to be mine.

followUps.q: Have you ever given someone advice that helped them?
followUps.answer: I hope so. In my job I advise students every day about universities and courses, and a few have come back to thank me, which is one of the most satisfying parts of the work.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?

part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more [[volatile]] than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to [[pursue]] fulfilment. Additionally, rapid technological change means some jobs disappear while new ones emerge, which [[compels]] people to adapt and retrain.

part3Samples.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?

part3Samples.q: How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?

He started as a child on a cheap second-hand guitar and was so [[dedicated]] that he would play for hours until his fingers were sore. He never had formal lessons; he learned by listening to recordings and copying older musicians, sometimes slowing the songs down so he could catch every note. Watching him perform is genuinely [[mesmerising]]; he can shift from a gentle melody to something powerful in seconds. What I respect most is that despite his obvious gift, he remains humble and is always eager to learn from others. I think raw talent only gets you so far, and his discipline is what turned potential into real [[mastery]]. Honestly, seeing someone so devoted to their craft is inspiring, and it reminds me that excellence is rarely accidental.

followUps.q: Have you ever tried to learn the guitar?
followUps.answer: Once, briefly. He gave me a few lessons, but I gave up after about a month because my fingers hurt and I clearly had no [[aptitude]] for it. I am much better at listening.

followUps.q: Do you think he could become a professional musician?
followUps.answer: I think he easily could, if he wanted to. The problem is that music is a risky career here, so he treats it as a passion alongside his regular job, at least for now.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

She is a retired schoolteacher, and she has lived in our building for as long as we have. Whether it is checking on the elderly residents, collecting parcels, or cooking for a family going through a hard time, she is always the first to step in. She also helps younger children in the building with their homework for free. As for how she helps, what strikes me is that her generosity is completely [[selfless]]; she never expects anything in return. She has this natural [[warmth]] that makes people feel comfortable asking her for help, which many are too proud to do. During a difficult period in our own family, when my mother had to stay in the village for weeks to look after my grandparents, she quietly supported us in ways we did not even ask for, sending over meals almost every evening and checking whether my sister needed anything. As for why she does it, I genuinely think some people are simply wired to be [[altruistic]], and she is one of them. I also suspect it gives her a sense of purpose since she retired. Her kindness has a way of bringing the whole neighbourhood closer together. Honestly, she is a living reminder that small, consistent acts of [[generosity]] matter far more than grand gestures.

followUps.q: Do you help your neighbours too?
followUps.answer: I try to. I carry heavy shopping up the stairs for older neighbours and help with anything technical, like setting up phones. It is a small contribution compared with hers, but it all [[adds up]].

followUps.q: Do you think people help each other less than in the past?
followUps.answer: Somewhat, especially in cities where people barely know their neighbours. In smaller towns like mine, though, that community spirit is still quite strong, and I really hope it lasts.

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but I think it is too simplistic to blame technology alone. It is true that excessive screen time can replace real interaction and [[foster]] unhealthy comparison. However, technology can also connect isolated people, such as those far from family. So the technology itself is [[neutral]]; the real issue is how we use it. The deeper causes lie in broader [[societal]] changes.

Despite the age gap, we have always got on remarkably well. He is the sort of neighbour everyone wishes they had: friendly, respectful and never [[intrusive]]. He is a retired government officer who lives alone now that his children have moved abroad, so he enjoys a bit of company. He keeps an eye on our flat when we visit my grandparents in the village, and in return we help him with anything that requires climbing a ladder or heavy lifting, like carrying his shopping up the stairs. What I like most is his endless supply of fascinating stories from his younger years, which are genuinely [[captivating]]. He is also incredibly [[considerate]], always mindful of noise and careful never to overstep. On Friday evenings he sometimes invites me in for tea, and we end up discussing cricket and politics for hours. I think good neighbours are a kind of quiet blessing that people underestimate until they lose them. Over the years he has become almost like extended family, and the building would feel noticeably [[emptier]] without him. Honestly, his presence is a big part of what makes our neighbourhood feel like home.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important to have good neighbours?
followUps.answer: Absolutely. Neighbours are often the first people who can help in an emergency, long before family arrives. Living near people you trust also gives you real [[peace of mind]] every day.

followUps.q: Do you know most of your neighbours well?
followUps.answer: Most of the ones in our building, yes. We greet each other on the stairs and exchange food during Eid, although I know the newer families less well than those who have been here for years.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is a paradox of modern life. Despite being more digitally connected than ever, many people feel increasingly isolated. Urbanisation has weakened traditional community bonds, and busy, individualistic lifestyles leave little time for genuine connection. Ironically, social media can [[exacerbate]] the problem by replacing deep relationships with [[superficial]] online interaction, leaving a real emotional [[void]].

part3Samples.q: Is loneliness worse in cities or in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: This is quite counterintuitive. You might assume the countryside, being less populated, would be lonelier, but often the opposite is true. Rural communities tend to be tight-knit, where everyone knows each other. Cities, by contrast, can be profoundly [[alienating]]; you can be surrounded by millions yet feel completely [[anonymous]]. So urban loneliness, born of that anonymity, is arguably the more [[acute]] problem.

part3Samples.q: What effects can long-term loneliness have on a person?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be genuinely serious. Prolonged loneliness is strongly linked to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. It can also have physical consequences, as chronic isolation is thought to weaken the immune system and even affect [[longevity]]. Beyond that, it can trap people in a negative cycle, where low mood makes them [[withdraw]] further, deepening the isolation and their sense of [[despair]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I fear it might, if current trends continue. As societies become more individualistic and people increasingly work and socialise remotely, opportunities for spontaneous human contact may [[diminish]]. An ageing population in many countries could also worsen the situation. However, I remain hopeful that growing awareness of the issue will [[prompt]] communities and governments to take [[preventive]] action.

part3Samples.q: What can communities do to reduce loneliness?
part3Samples.answer: Communities can play a powerful role. Creating accessible public spaces and organising local events, from community gardens to social clubs, gives people natural opportunities to connect. Initiatives that specifically reach out to isolated individuals, like [[befriending schemes]] for the elderly, are especially valuable. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a culture where people look out for their neighbours can rebuild the [[social fabric]] that has frayed.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].

As for how she learned it, what amazes me is that she taught herself largely through films, music and online conversation, which shows extraordinary discipline. She practised every single day for years, even writing short diary entries in Japanese script. Her pronunciation is so [[authentic]] that native speakers are often surprised she is not from Japan. I think what makes her so good is that she was never afraid of making mistakes, which is where most learners get stuck. She immersed herself completely, treating the language as a passion rather than a chore. Watching her switch effortlessly between Bengali and Japanese is genuinely [[admirable]], and it makes me slightly envious. She often says that learning a language opens a window into a whole culture, and I think she is right. Honestly, her [[commitment]] is inspiring, and it has motivated me to be more serious about improving my own English, especially since I hope to study abroad myself one day.

followUps.q: Would you like to learn another foreign language?

followUps.q: Is learning English important in your country?
followUps.answer: Very important. English opens doors to higher education and better jobs, and in my work I see every day how much students' futures [[hinge on]] their English test scores.
