part3Samples.q: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?
part3Samples.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

part3Samples.q: How has globalisation changed local cultures?
part3Samples.answer: The changes are significant. Local cultures have been enriched by exposure to global ideas, technologies and cuisines. However, they have also been challenged, as global brands, media and the English language spread, sometimes [[eclipsing]] local traditions and languages. The result is often a hybrid culture, blending the local and the global. So globalisation has made cultures more [[interconnected]] and diverse in some ways, yet more [[uniform]] in others.

part3Samples.q: What effect does the spread of English have on other languages?
part3Samples.answer: The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.

part3Samples.q: Do you think all cultures will eventually become the same?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think so, though they will certainly grow more similar in some respects. While globalisation is a powerful homogenising force, human beings have a deep-seated need for distinct identity and belonging, which tends to make cultures [[resilient]]. We are also seeing movements to actively preserve and revive local traditions. So rather than becoming identical, I expect cultures to blend and influence one another while retaining their [[distinctive]] [[essence]].

part3Samples.q: How can countries protect their cultural identity in a globalised world?
part3Samples.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

As for how he shows it, what impresses me is that he never seems to cut corners, no matter how [[exhausted]] he is. He handles everything himself in these early stages, from serving customers to doing the accounts, and he does it all with a smile. I think what drives him is a deep sense of [[determination]] to build something of his own rather than work for someone else. There have been moments when I worried he was pushing himself too hard, especially when he stopped seeing friends for months, but his energy is remarkable. Watching his effort slowly pay off has been genuinely [[inspiring]] to witness, and the café is now busy most evenings. As for how I feel about him, I am enormously proud of him. Honestly, he has completely changed my idea of what commitment looks like, and he reminds me that success is usually far less glamorous than people imagine.

followUps.q: Do you think hard work always leads to success?

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

data.title: Describe a sportsperson you admire
data.prompt: Describe a sportsperson you admire

sample.answer: As a big cricket fan, I did not have to think very long about this one. A sportsperson I genuinely admire is a famous cricketer from my country, who is something of a national hero. He has played for Bangladesh for many years, and he has been part of some of the team's most memorable victories against much bigger cricketing nations. Beyond his obvious talent, what I admire is the [[humility]] he shows despite enormous fame. He came from a modest background and worked his way up through sheer [[perseverance]], which makes his story relatable to ordinary people. On the field he is famous for staying calm under pressure, a quality that separates good players from truly great ones. What impresses me most is his [[consistency]]; he performs at a high level year after year, which requires incredible discipline. Off the field, he is known for his charity work, which shows real character. I think athletes like him are role models precisely because of how they carry themselves, not just their statistics. His [[dignity]] in both victory and defeat is something young people can genuinely learn from. I still remember watching one of his match-winning innings with my father and younger sister, all of us shouting at the television and my mother rushing in from the kitchen to see what had happened. Honestly, he makes the whole nation proud, and rightly so, and whenever he walks out to bat, the entire country seems to hold its breath.

followUps.q: Have you ever watched him play live?
followUps.answer: Not yet, unfortunately. Tickets for big matches in Dhaka sell out quickly, and it is a long journey from Sirajganj. But watching him in a stadium is definitely on my [[bucket list]].

followUps.q: Do you play cricket yourself?
followUps.answer: Only casually these days. I played a lot as a child with friends in the neighbourhood, but now I mostly watch it, usually with my father, who is an even bigger fan than I am.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is important for young people to have role models?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely vital for adolescents to have someone to look up to. Role models act as a kind of moral compass, offering guidance on how to navigate life. When a young person admires a professional, they are [[internalising]] the values of hard work and [[perseverance]] that led to that success. Without such figures, young people can feel a little [[unmoored]], lacking any real sense of direction.

part3Samples.q: How have the types of role models changed since your grandparents' time?
part3Samples.answer: There has been a rather dramatic shift, I would say. In my grandparents' era, role models tended to be figures within the immediate community, such as teachers or elders. Today, influence is increasingly [[dominated]] by celebrities and social media personalities, many of whom are famous for very little of substance. I find this shift somewhat concerning, because fame has become almost entirely [[disconnected]] from genuine [[merit]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people are more influenced by role models in real life or in the media?
part3Samples.answer: That is an interesting question. I would argue that media figures have a wider reach, but real-life role models, like a parent or mentor, have a far deeper and more [[lasting impact]]. The influence of a media personality is often [[superficial]] and [[fleeting]], whereas someone you interact with daily shapes your character in a much more meaningful way.

part3Samples.q: Why do some public figures fail to remain positive role models over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think the main reason is the immense pressure and [[scrutiny]] that come with public life. Constant attention can distort a person's judgement, and some become [[complacent]] once they achieve fame. There is also the temptation of wealth and power, which can gradually [[erode]] the very values that made them admirable in the first place. Sadly, staying grounded under that spotlight is genuinely difficult.

part3Samples.q: In the future, do you think AI or fictional characters could become role models?
part3Samples.answer: It is quite possible, and to some extent it is already happening. Virtual influencers are becoming increasingly [[prevalent]], and young people do form attachments to fictional heroes. However, I would be somewhat [[wary]] of this trend, because a fabricated character lacks the real struggles that make human role models relatable. I think something genuinely [[authentic]] would be lost in that shift.

part3Samples.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone who taught me a great deal in a very short time. A person I would love to work with is a former mentor of mine who now runs a successful consultancy in Dhaka, advising small businesses on strategy. I got to know him during an internship in my final year of business administration, and even in those three months I learned an enormous amount. What makes him an ideal colleague is that he is both brilliant and genuinely [[collaborative]]; he treats junior people as partners rather than subordinates. He has a way of bringing out the best in a team by giving people real [[ownership]] of their work. I remember him letting me present part of a report to a client, which was terrifying but hugely valuable. As for why I would like to work with him, I think working alongside him again would be incredibly [[stimulating]], because he constantly pushes those around him to think bigger. He is also refreshingly honest, offering feedback that is direct but never harsh. As for how I feel about the idea, it excites me, although I know I would need more experience before I could keep up with him. Honestly, I believe the people you work with shape your career more than the job itself, and he is exactly the kind of person who makes you better. Being part of a team he leads would be a genuine [[privilege]], and perhaps one day, after studying abroad, I will get that chance.

followUps.q: Do you prefer working alone or in a team?
followUps.answer: It depends on the task, but generally I prefer teamwork. Other people spot mistakes I miss and bring ideas I would never think of. Working alone can feel quite [[isolating]] after a while.

followUps.q: Are you in touch with him now?
followUps.answer: Yes, occasionally. We connected on a professional networking site, and he sometimes comments on my posts. Last year he even offered to write me a reference if I apply for a master's abroad.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people happy at work?
part3Samples.answer: In my opinion, job satisfaction [[stems from]] more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is [[paramount]]. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of [[autonomy]] all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.

part3Samples.q: Is money or a sense of purpose more important for job satisfaction?
part3Samples.answer: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not [[compensate]] for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a [[threshold]], but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even [[burnout]], which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher [[staff turnover]]. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is [[detrimental]] to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be more or less satisfied with their jobs in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over [[tedious]], repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant [[connectivity]] could [[undermine]] satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

part3Samples.q: What can employers do to make their staff happier?
part3Samples.answer: Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine [[recognition]] for good work is [[fundamental]]. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. Simply listening to employees and giving them a degree of autonomy over their work is powerful. Investing in staff wellbeing is not just ethical; it is genuinely [[profitable]] in the long run.

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone whose confidence I have always slightly envied. A strikingly confident person I know is a former classmate who now works in sales for a mobile phone company. We studied business administration together, and we were often in the same group for presentations, so I had plenty of chances to watch her in action. From the day I met her, she had this natural [[self-assurance]] that drew people to her. What I find interesting is that her confidence never tips over into arrogance; she is genuinely comfortable in her own skin. As for how she shows it, she can walk into a room full of strangers and start a conversation without the slightest [[hesitation]], which I have always envied. In class presentations, while the rest of us were shaking, she spoke clearly and even enjoyed the difficult questions. I think a lot of her confidence comes from thorough preparation, so she rarely feels caught off guard. She is also unafraid of failure, treating setbacks as [[short-lived]] rather than devastating. Watching her handle difficult situations calmly has taught me a great deal. As for how I feel about her, I admire her enormously. Honestly, I think confidence like hers is partly a personality trait and partly a skill you can build. Being around her is genuinely [[empowering]], because her belief in herself somehow rubs off on the people nearby. I certainly became a better presenter just by watching her, and I still borrow some of her techniques at work.

followUps.q: Are you a confident person?
followUps.answer: More than I used to be. I was quite shy at university, but my job forces me to speak to students and parents every day, and that has gradually helped me [[come out of my shell]].

followUps.q: Do you think confidence can be learned?
followUps.answer: Yes, I believe so. Practice and preparation make a huge difference. The more often you face something that frightens you, like public speaking, the less frightening it becomes over time.

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree, though it never disappears entirely. As people mature, they generally develop a firmer sense of identity and care less about others' approval, making them more [[resilient]] to pressure. However, the pressure simply takes on a more [[subtle]] form in adulthood, such as keeping up with colleagues' lifestyles. So it lessens, but it certainly does not [[vanish]].

data.title: Describe a person who apologised to you
data.prompt: Describe a person who apologised to you

sample.answer: I would like to talk about an apology that actually made a friendship stronger. I remember an occasion when a close friend apologised to me after a misunderstanding that had strained our friendship for weeks. It happened about two years ago, and the friend was someone I had known since school. We had fallen out over something fairly trivial, a comment he made about me in a group chat, which both of us had blown out of proportion. For a few weeks we barely spoke, and it felt strange not having him around, because we used to talk almost every day. Then one evening he turned up at our flat unannounced and asked if we could go for a walk by the river. What made his apology memorable was how [[sincere]] it was; he did not make excuses or try to shift the blame. He admitted openly that he had been in the wrong, which takes real [[humility]]. I think apologising properly is genuinely difficult, because it requires swallowing your pride. His honesty completely [[disarmed]] me, and any lingering resentment melted away almost instantly. In the end I apologised too, for my own stubbornness. We ended up talking for hours and our friendship actually became stronger than before. Honestly, that experience taught me how powerful a genuine apology can be in [[repairing]] a relationship. It also reminded me that admitting fault is a sign of strength, not weakness, something many people never seem to learn.

followUps.q: Do you find it easy to apologise?
followUps.answer: Not always, to be honest. Like most people, I can be a bit proud, but I have learned that a quick, genuine apology usually [[defuses]] a situation far better than defending myself.

followUps.q: Do you think people apologise less nowadays?
followUps.answer: Perhaps a little. People often send a quick sorry by message instead of saying it in person, which feels less meaningful. A face-to-face apology still carries much more weight, I think.

part3: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?

part3Samples.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
part3Samples.answer: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be [[constructive]] if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. There is growing awareness of the importance of emotional intelligence and communication skills, which are increasingly taught in schools and workplaces. If this trend continues, future generations may be better [[equipped]] to handle disagreements. On the other hand, online communication can sometimes make people more [[polarised]] and less willing to [[compromise]], so it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What is the best way to resolve a serious disagreement?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective approach usually involves calm, honest dialogue where both sides genuinely listen to one another. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a [[neutral third party]] as a [[mediator]] can be [[invaluable]]. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

part3Samples.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though I would add a small [[caveat]]. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a colleague whose sense of style everyone in our office notices. A person whose style I genuinely admire is a colleague of mine who always manages to look effortlessly elegant. She joined our consultancy about a year ago as a senior counsellor, and we often work together on university applications, so I see her almost every day. She never seems to be trying too hard, yet every outfit looks carefully considered. What I find impressive is how [[versatile]] her wardrobe is; she can look professional at work and stylish at a social event with equal ease. At the office she usually wears a simple salwar kameez or a sari in muted colours, and at weddings she looks even more graceful, without ever seeming overdressed. She favours simple, classic pieces over loud trends, which gives her a timeless, [[sophisticated]] look. I think what makes her stand out is her attention to small details, like how well things fit and the way colours [[complement]] one another. She once told me that dressing well is less about money and more about knowing what suits you, which struck me as genuinely wise. As for how I feel about her style, I find it quietly inspiring. Honestly, being around her has made me a little more thoughtful about my own appearance, and I now iron my shirts rather more carefully. I think the way you present yourself quietly shapes how others perceive you, and she understands that [[instinctively]].

followUps.q: Do you care much about fashion?
followUps.answer: Not a great deal. I like to look neat and presentable, especially for work, but I rarely follow trends. I prefer [[understated]] clothes that are comfortable and will not go out of style quickly.

followUps.q: What do people in your country usually wear on special occasions?
followUps.answer: Traditional clothes, mostly. Men wear a panjabi, especially at Eid, and women often wear colourful saris. Weddings are the most formal occasions, and people dress very elaborately for them.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fashion is important to some people?
part3Samples.answer: For many people, fashion is a genuine form of [[self-expression]], allowing them to communicate their personality, mood and identity without words. It can boost confidence and create a sense of belonging to a particular group. For some, it is also an art form and a source of creativity. While I personally value comfort over trends, I completely understand why fashion [[holds such significance]]; it is a powerful, [[visual language]] of identity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people care more about fashion now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some ways, yes. The rise of social media has made appearance more visible and, arguably, more important, with influencers constantly showcasing new trends. [[Fast fashion]] has also made trendy clothing cheap and accessible, [[fuelling]] constant consumption. However, past eras had their own strong fashion cultures too. So perhaps it is not that people care more, but that fashion has become more fast-paced, [[disposable]] and publicly displayed than ever before.

part3Samples.q: What effect does the fashion industry have on the environment?
part3Samples.answer: The environmental impact is unfortunately severe, particularly from fast fashion. The industry is a major consumer of water and a significant source of pollution and carbon emissions. The culture of buying cheap, disposable clothing generates enormous [[textile waste]], much of which ends up in landfill. So while fashion brings joy and self-expression, its current [[unsustainable]] model [[exacts a heavy toll]] on the planet that urgently needs addressing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think fashion will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate sustainability will become a [[driving force]]. As awareness of fast fashion's harm grows, I expect a shift towards more durable, ethical and recycled clothing, and a move away from [[throwaway culture]]. Technology may also personalise fashion, and digital or virtual clothing could even emerge. So I am hopeful the future of fashion will be more sustainable, more conscious, and perhaps less [[wasteful]] than the current model.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to make fashion more sustainable?
part3Samples.answer: Several changes are needed. On the industry side, brands should adopt ethical, eco-friendly production and be more transparent. Consumers can play a huge role by buying less, choosing quality over quantity, and embracing [[second-hand]] or recycled clothing. Repairing and reusing garments rather than discarding them also helps. Ultimately, moving away from a throwaway mindset towards more [[durable]], [[considered consumption]] is the most impactful solution.

data.prompt: Describe a person who encouraged you to achieve a goal

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone who, quite honestly, stopped me from giving up. A person who encouraged me to achieve an important goal was my elder cousin, at a time when I was preparing for a major exam and had almost lost faith in myself. The goal was to get into a good public university to study business administration, and the admission test was extremely competitive. After a disappointing mock test, I had convinced myself that I was not capable, and I was ready to give up. She refused to let me quit, and her belief in me was genuinely [[unwavering]]. Rather than just offering empty words, she sat with me, helped me plan, and kept me [[accountable]] week after week. She made me a detailed timetable and called every Friday to check my progress. What I appreciated most was that her support was practical, not just emotional. Whenever I felt [[demoralised]], she would remind me how far I had already come. Thanks largely to her, I stayed disciplined and eventually achieved a result I am still proud of, and I got a place on the course I wanted. As for how I felt, I was overjoyed and hugely relieved, but above all grateful. Honestly, I am not sure I would have managed it without her constant encouragement. That experience taught me how much difference one supportive person can make, and I try to be that [[encouraging]] presence for others now, especially the nervous students I work with.

followUps.q: Do you still set goals for yourself?
followUps.answer: Yes, although they are different now. At the moment my main goal is to strengthen my profile so I can study abroad. I find that breaking a goal into small steps makes it feel [[within reach]].

followUps.q: Do you think encouragement is more important than talent?
followUps.answer: In many cases, yes. Plenty of talented people give up because nobody believes in them, while ordinary people achieve a lot with the right support. Ideally, of course, you need both.

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

sample.answer: When I think back to my childhood, one face always comes to mind. I would like to talk about my best friend from childhood, who lived just a few houses down from us in Sirajganj. We met when we were barely five years old, on the very first day of primary school, and quickly became [[inseparable]]. Almost every afternoon was spent playing cricket in the lane, exploring the neighbourhood or getting into harmless mischief. During the monsoon we used to race paper boats in the flooded streets, and in the dry season we flew kites from the rooftops until our mothers called us in for dinner. Those years were wonderfully [[carefree]], with none of the responsibilities that come later. What made our friendship special was how easily we understood each other, without any of the awkwardness that adults sometimes have. As for whether we are still in touch, sadly his family moved to Rajshahi when we were teenagers, and we gradually drifted apart, which I still find a little [[melancholy]]. We do reconnect occasionally, usually by phone around Eid, and it is lovely how quickly the old bond resurfaces. The last time we met, we spent the whole evening laughing about the things we had done as boys. Honestly, childhood friendships have a special kind of [[innocence]] that is hard to recreate later in life. I look back on those days with enormous fondness, and I feel grateful to have had such a good companion growing up.

followUps.q: Would you like to spend more time with him?
followUps.answer: Definitely. I have been meaning to visit him in Rajshahi for ages, but work always gets in the way. This year I am determined to finally make the trip and spend a proper weekend together.

followUps.q: Do children today have as much freedom as you did?
followUps.answer: Probably not. Many parents worry more about safety now, and children spend more time indoors on screens. I think they miss out on the kind of outdoor adventures we [[took for granted]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some people think children are given too much freedom today. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree. Modern parenting rightly encourages children's independence, but in some cases [[the pendulum has swung]] too far, and children lack clear boundaries. A total absence of limits can leave children feeling [[insecure]] rather than free. That said, the opposite extreme is equally harmful, so the goal should be freedom within a [[framework]] of sensible, loving guidance.

As for why I want to know her better, it is because she has a rare combination of intelligence and warmth. Too often first meetings feel superficial, but this one felt genuinely meaningful. We exchanged contacts, so I am hopeful we will meet again the next time I am in Dhaka. Honestly, it is quite unusual to feel [[an instant rapport]] with someone, and I do not want to let it fade.

followUps.q: How do you usually make new friends?
followUps.answer: Mostly through people I already know, like friends of friends or colleagues. I have made a few friends through work as well, since I meet so many different people at the consultancy.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone in my own family whose parenting I genuinely admire. A person I consider an excellent parent is my elder sister, and watching her raise her two children has been a real education. She lives in Dhaka with her husband and children, including a lively four-year-old son, and we see them whenever they visit Sirajganj or I go to stay with them. As for how she raises them, what impresses me is how she balances warmth with [[discipline]]; she is affectionate but never lets her children become spoiled. She listens to them genuinely, treating even their small worries as important, which I think builds real trust. Rather than simply giving orders, she explains the reasons behind rules, so her children grow up thinking for themselves. She limits their screen time, reads to them every night and makes sure they spend plenty of time with their grandparents, which I think matters enormously. She is also remarkably [[patient]], even on the difficult days when most people would lose their temper. As for why I think she is a good parent, what I admire most is that she leads by example, modelling the values she wants them to [[absorb]]. I think parenting is one of the hardest jobs in the world, and she makes it look almost effortless. Honestly, her children are turning out kind and confident, which is the clearest possible proof of her [[nurturing]] approach. I suspect our mother taught her more than she realises.

followUps.q: Do you think you would be a good parent?
followUps.answer: I hope so. I think I would be patient and fair, like my sister, but I would probably struggle with discipline because I tend to give in too easily. I would definitely ask her for [[guidance]].

followUps.q: Do parents today have an easier job than in the past?
followUps.answer: In some ways yes, with more information and support available. But they also face new pressures, like managing screen time and intense competition in education, which makes parenting quite demanding.

part3Samples.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is robbing children of a real childhood. Do you agree?

There is a legitimate concern that excessive screen time is replacing the outdoor play, imagination and face-to-face friendships that define a healthy childhood. However, technology also offers genuine benefits and is simply the reality of the modern world. So rather than [[demonising]] it, I believe the answer lies in [[moderation]], ensuring children still enjoy a rich, balanced upbringing.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a man whose kindness is known throughout our neighbourhood. The most generous person I know is an old family friend who seems to find genuine joy in giving. For many years he ran a shop next to my father's in the market, so I have known him since I was a small boy, and he still calls me by my childhood nickname. His generosity is not just about money, though he is quietly charitable; it is more about his time and attention. Whenever anyone is in trouble, he is the first to offer help, often before being asked. What makes his kindness so [[genuine]] is that he never seeks recognition for it; in fact, he prefers to help [[discreetly]]. I remember him supporting a struggling family in our neighbourhood for months without anyone knowing, paying their children's school fees until the father found work again. I only found out years later, through my father. During Ramadan, he also quietly sends food to families who cannot afford much for iftar. I think true generosity like his is increasingly [[uncommon]] in a world that often prizes self-interest. As for how I feel about him, I have enormous respect for him, and being around him is a gentle reminder to be more giving myself. He genuinely believes that we are all better off when we look after one another, and he lives by that principle. Honestly, his [[benevolence]] has left a lasting impression on everyone who knows him.

followUps.q: Do you think people in your country are generous?
followUps.answer: Generally, yes. Charity is an important part of our culture and religion, especially during Ramadan and Eid, when people make a real effort to share food and money with those who are [[less fortunate]].

followUps.q: Is it better to give money or time?
followUps.answer: Both matter, but I think time is often more valuable. Money solves immediate problems, whereas giving someone your time and attention shows that you genuinely care about them as a person.

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say money cannot buy happiness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though with a [[nuance]]. It is certainly true that beyond meeting our basic needs, more money does not reliably increase happiness, and the richest people are not necessarily the happiest. Lasting happiness comes from relationships and purpose. However, I would add that a lack of money, and the poverty and stress it brings, can definitely cause unhappiness. So money cannot buy happiness, but [[financial security]] can certainly remove a major source of [[misery]] and anxiety.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a friend whose job I find almost unbelievably exciting. A person with a genuinely interesting job is a friend of mine who works as a wildlife photographer. We met through a mutual friend a few years ago, and he now works freelance for magazines and conservation groups. His work takes him to remote corners of the world, capturing animals in their natural habitats, although his favourite place is still the Sundarbans, closer to home. What makes his job so [[fascinating]] is the unpredictability; no two days are ever the same, and patience is everything. He once spent nearly a week waiting quietly to photograph a single rare bird, which shows extraordinary [[dedication]]. He has also told me about spending nights on a boat in the mangrove forest, hoping for a glimpse of a tiger, which he finally saw on his third trip. I find the combination of adventure, artistry and science in his work genuinely [[enviable]]. Of course, he is quick to point out that it is far less glamorous than it looks, involving long hours in [[harsh]] conditions, from heat and mosquitoes to heavy rain. Still, I think there is something wonderful about a job that keeps you so connected to nature. As for how I feel about it, listening to his stories always makes my own routine feel a little dull. Honestly, he has one of the few careers that I think I could happily do myself, provided someone else carried the heavy equipment.

followUps.q: Would you like to try wildlife photography yourself?
followUps.answer: I would love to try it once, perhaps on a short trip to the Sundarbans with him. But I suspect I lack the patience to sit still for days, so it would probably remain a hobby at best.

followUps.q: Do you think interesting jobs are more important than well-paid jobs?
followUps.answer: For me, balance matters. A fascinating job that barely pays is hard to sustain, but a well-paid job you find [[soul-destroying]] is worse. Ideally, you find work that offers both.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people happy at work?
part3Samples.answer: In my opinion, job satisfaction [[stems from]] more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is [[paramount]]. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of [[autonomy]] all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.

part3Samples.q: Is money or a sense of purpose more important for job satisfaction?
part3Samples.answer: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not [[compensate]] for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a [[threshold]], but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even [[burnout]], which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher [[staff turnover]]. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is [[detrimental]] to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be more or less satisfied with their jobs in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over [[tedious]], repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant [[connectivity]] could [[undermine]] satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

part3Samples.q: What can employers do to make their staff happier?
part3Samples.answer: Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine [[recognition]] for good work is [[fundamental]]. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. Simply listening to employees and giving them a degree of autonomy over their work is powerful. Investing in staff wellbeing is not just ethical; it is genuinely [[profitable]] in the long run.

part3Samples.q: Some say humans have no right to interfere with nature. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: This is a nuanced issue. I agree we should minimise harmful interference, such as destroying habitats or exploiting species, as we have caused enormous damage. However, I would argue we now have a responsibility to [[intervene]] positively, through conservation, to repair the damage we have already done. Given our impact, complete non-interference is neither possible nor helpful. So rather than not interfering at all, we should act as responsible [[stewards]], protecting rather than [[plundering]].

She came to our university in Bangladesh for a year as an exchange student, and we were in several of the same classes. Her home town is Izmir, on the Aegean coast, and she has shown me so many photos that I feel I almost know it. Getting to know her has been genuinely [[eye-opening]], because our backgrounds are quite different in some ways yet surprisingly similar in others. She has taught me a great deal about her country's food, festivals and customs, which I find fascinating. What I appreciate most is how her perspective has broadened my own; she often challenges assumptions I did not even realise I held. Our conversations are always [[enriching]], and we enjoy comparing how our two cultures approach things like family and hospitality. We even discovered that our families celebrate Eid in quite similar ways. As for how I feel about the friendship, I think friendships across cultures are especially valuable, because they quietly [[break down stereotypes]]. She is warm, curious and completely without prejudice, which makes her wonderful company, and we still video call every couple of months. Honestly, knowing her has made me more [[open-minded]], and it has confirmed my belief that people everywhere have far more in common than we tend to assume.

followUps.q: Is it easy to make friends with people from other cultures?
followUps.answer: It can take a little more effort at first, because of language and different customs. But once you get past that initial [[awkwardness]], I think those friendships are often especially close and rewarding.

part3Samples.q: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?
part3Samples.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

part3Samples.q: How has globalisation changed local cultures?
part3Samples.answer: The changes are significant. Local cultures have been enriched by exposure to global ideas, technologies and cuisines. However, they have also been challenged, as global brands, media and the English language spread, sometimes [[eclipsing]] local traditions and languages. The result is often a hybrid culture, blending the local and the global. So globalisation has made cultures more [[interconnected]] and diverse in some ways, yet more [[uniform]] in others.

part3Samples.q: What effect does the spread of English have on other languages?
part3Samples.answer: The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.

part3Samples.q: Do you think all cultures will eventually become the same?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think so, though they will certainly grow more similar in some respects. While globalisation is a powerful homogenising force, human beings have a deep-seated need for distinct identity and belonging, which tends to make cultures [[resilient]]. We are also seeing movements to actively preserve and revive local traditions. So rather than becoming identical, I expect cultures to blend and influence one another while retaining their [[distinctive]] [[essence]].

part3Samples.q: How can countries protect their cultural identity in a globalised world?
part3Samples.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about the person our whole family turns to in difficult times. The wisest person in my family is undoubtedly my grandmother, who despite having little formal education has an extraordinary understanding of people and life. She lives with my grandfather in our ancestral village home not far from Sirajganj, and we visit them often, especially during Eid, when the whole family gathers in the old house. What makes her so wise is not book knowledge but decades of hard-won experience, raising a large family through floods and lean years. She has this [[uncanny]] ability to sense when something is wrong, often before anyone says a word. Whenever the family faces a difficult decision, we instinctively turn to her, because her judgement is remarkably [[sound]]. She rarely tells you what to do; instead she asks the right questions and lets you reach your own conclusion. I think that is the mark of genuine wisdom, and it means you actually learn something. Her advice is always [[grounded]] in common sense rather than emotion, which is why it is so reliable. As for how she has helped me, over the years she has helped me through several tough moments simply by putting things in perspective. When I was nervous about starting my first job, she reminded me that everyone is a beginner once, and that honesty matters more than cleverness. Honestly, I treasure my conversations with her, and I know I will miss her [[counsel]] enormously one day.

followUps.q: Do you visit her often?
followUps.answer: Fairly often, usually once or twice a month with my parents. The village is not far, so we can go for the day. Sitting with her on the veranda is one of the most [[tranquil]] parts of my month.

followUps.q: Do you think older people are wiser than younger people?
followUps.answer: Often, but not always. Age gives people experience, but wisdom depends on whether they reflect on it. Some young people are remarkably wise, and some older people never seem to learn.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite [[pronounced]], largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to [[tension]], though it also brings a healthy [[diversity]] of perspectives.

part3Samples.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?

The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

part3Samples.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
part3Samples.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to [[empathise]], with each side viewing the other's values as [[alien]]. A lack of open, patient communication only [[widens that gulf]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
part3Samples.answer: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now [[evolves]]. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could [[amplify]] the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help [[bridge]] it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?

sample.answer: I would like to describe a former colleague who once solved a tricky problem at work in a genuinely clever way. He worked with me at the education consultancy until last year, when he left to do a master's degree in Australia. Our team was stuck on a project because of a scheduling conflict that seemed impossible to resolve. We had organised a university fair, but two of the most popular universities could only send representatives at exactly the same time, and we had only one hall big enough for the crowds we were expecting. While the rest of us were arguing, he calmly suggested a completely different approach that none of us had considered. He proposed dividing the hall with screens and running both sessions side by side. What impressed me was how [[resourceful]] he was; he found a simple solution hidden in plain sight. His thinking was refreshingly [[lateral]], approaching the problem from an angle nobody else had tried. Within an hour, something that had frustrated us for days was neatly sorted out, and the fair went smoothly. As for how I felt, I was relieved but also slightly embarrassed that I had not thought of it myself. I think his real strength is staying calm and [[rational]] when everyone else is panicking. That episode taught me that the best solutions are often surprisingly simple, once someone [[ingenious]] points them out. Honestly, I still think about his approach whenever I feel stuck on a difficult problem myself.

followUps.q: Are you good at solving problems?
followUps.answer: Reasonably good, I think, especially practical ones. I tend to be methodical rather than creative, so I break problems into steps. I have learned, though, that stepping away for a while often brings a [[breakthrough]].

followUps.q: Do you think problem-solving skills can be taught?
followUps.answer: Yes, to some extent. Schools can encourage it by giving students open-ended tasks instead of memorisation. But experience is the best teacher, because real problems rarely come with clear instructions.

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

Last week, for instance, we started talking about a cricket match and somehow ended up debating whether ambition really makes people happy. He is also wonderfully [[open-minded]], so I can share half-formed thoughts without fear of being judged. I think good conversation is a bit of an art, and he is a master of it, although he would never admit that. He knows when to be serious and when to be [[playful]], which keeps things from ever feeling heavy. Honestly, I always come away from our chats feeling energised and having learned something new. In a world where so much communication happens through screens, having someone you can talk to for hours is genuinely [[precious]]. I never take those conversations for granted, and I think they have made me a far better listener and a slightly more thoughtful person as well.

followUps.q: Are you a talkative person?
followUps.answer: It depends on who I am with. With close friends and family I can talk for hours, but in large groups of strangers I tend to be quieter and listen more than I speak.

However, it lacks the richness of face-to-face interaction, where tone, body language and physical presence convey so much. For deep, emotional conversations, nothing beats being together in person. So digital tools are a wonderful [[supplement]], but not a full [[substitute]] for genuine human contact.

part3Samples.q: How is the way young people communicate different from older generations?

Young people have grown up as [[digital natives]], so they favour instant messaging, voice notes and social media over phone calls, which many find [[intrusive]]. Older generations often prefer calls or in-person conversation. Young people also communicate more through images, emojis and memes, a kind of [[visual shorthand]]. This can lead to occasional misunderstanding between the generations, though both are simply adapting to their era.

Instant messaging has spawned a whole new informal language of abbreviations, emojis and slang, which allows for quick, expressive communication. Some worry this is [[eroding]] traditional writing skills and grammar, especially among the young. However, I take a more relaxed view; language has always [[evolved]], and people generally understand when to switch between casual and formal [[registers]]. So it is evolution, not decay.

We may increasingly communicate through augmented reality overlays too. part3Samples.q: How can people avoid becoming too dependent on digital communication?

Consciously choosing to call or meet someone rather than always texting preserves deeper connection. Turning off unnecessary notifications reduces the [[constant pull]] of our devices.
