sample.answer: I'd like to describe a train journey I took a couple of years ago, because my friends and I still talk about it. A journey that stands out vividly in my memory was a long train ride I took through the countryside with a group of close friends. We were travelling from Dhaka to Sylhet to see the tea gardens, but honestly the journey itself turned out to be the highlight. There were four of us, all old university friends, and we had managed to get seats together in the same carriage. We set off early in the morning with bags of snacks and far too much luggage. The train wound slowly through [[picturesque]] landscapes of green paddy fields, rivers and small villages, and later past gentle hills covered in tea. We spent hours chatting, playing cards and simply watching the ever-changing scenery, which was wonderfully [[soothing]]. At almost every station, vendors came on board selling tea and snacks, which only added to the fun. What made it so memorable was not the destination but the shared experience and the sense of freedom. There was something almost [[nostalgic]] about the slow rhythm of train travel, so different from the rush of flying. We laughed until our sides ached and made memories I still treasure. Honestly, that journey taught me that travel is often about the moments in between rather than just arriving. It remains one of my most [[cherished]] trips, precisely because it was so [[unhurried]] and full of good company. By the time we arrived, we were tired, but none of us wanted it to end.

followUps.q: Would you like to make that journey again?
followUps.answer: Definitely. I'd love to do it again, maybe with my younger sister this time, since she has never been to Sylhet. Though I suspect it would not feel quite the same without my friends.

followUps.q: Do you prefer travelling by train or by bus?
followUps.answer: By train, without a doubt. Buses in Bangladesh can be quite cramped and the roads are often jammed, whereas on a train you can stretch your legs and actually enjoy the view.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree with this, at least for private cars in the busiest central areas. Many cities that have [[pedestrianised]] their centres seem to have seen reduced pollution, safer streets and more vibrant public life, which is very appealing. However, it must be done carefully, ensuring excellent public transport alternatives and access for deliveries and those with disabilities. So rather than a [[blanket ban]], I support significantly restricting cars to create more [[liveable]], people-friendly centres.

data.prompt: Describe a time you were late for something
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a morning I would honestly rather forget. A time I was embarrassingly late was for an important job interview a few years ago, just after I had finished university. The interview was in Dhaka, so I stayed the night before at my elder sister's flat, thinking that would give me plenty of time. I had planned everything carefully, but on the day, the traffic was absolutely [[horrendous]] due to an unexpected road closure. I sat helplessly in a CNG auto-rickshaw, watching the minutes tick away, growing more [[jittery]] by the second. I kept checking my watch every thirty seconds, as if that would somehow make the traffic move. I called ahead to apologise, which was [[mortifying]], and eventually arrived nearly half an hour late, [[flustered]] and sweating. To my relief, the interviewers were surprisingly understanding, and the interview went reasonably well despite my terrible start. One of them even joked that being stuck in Dhaka traffic was practically a local tradition, which helped me relax a little. As for how I felt, I was ashamed at first and then hugely relieved. However, the whole experience taught me a valuable lesson about leaving a proper buffer for the unexpected. Since then I have become almost [[obsessive]] about arriving early for anything important. Honestly, the stress of that day was enough to change my habits for good. I now always plan for delays, because I never want to feel that particular kind of panic again. It was a bad day, but I am oddly grateful for it now.

followUps.q: Did you get the job in the end?
followUps.answer: No, I didn't, though I don't think it was only because I was late. Luckily, a few weeks later I was offered my current job at the consultancy, which suits me much better anyway.

followUps.q: Are people in your country usually on time?
followUps.answer: Honestly, not always. Traffic in the cities is so unpredictable that people tend to be quite relaxed about being a little late. For formal things like interviews, though, punctuality really matters.

part3Samples.q: Do you think public transport should be free?
part3Samples.answer: I find the idea appealing, though it is complex. Making public transport free could reduce traffic, cut pollution and help [[lower-income]] people enormously, which are [[compelling]] social benefits. However, it would be extremely expensive to fund and might lead to overcrowding or reduced service quality without careful management. So while I support [[heavily subsidising]] it to keep it affordable, whether it should be entirely free depends on a country's priorities and budget.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
part3Samples.answer: Each has its merits, but from a societal viewpoint, public transport is clearly [[preferable]]. It is far more environmentally friendly, reduces congestion, and is cheaper for the user. Private cars, however, offer [[unmatched]] convenience, comfort and flexibility, especially where public transport is poor. So while I personally value the freedom of a car, I believe well-developed public transport is the more sustainable and [[equitable]] option for society as a whole.

part3Samples.q: What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
part3Samples.answer: Traffic congestion has serious and costly effects. It wastes an enormous amount of people's time, reducing productivity and quality of life. It significantly worsens air pollution, harming public health and the environment. It also causes frustration and stress for commuters and can [[hamper]] emergency services. Economically, the lost hours and fuel represent a huge [[drain]]. So congestion is far more than an inconvenience; it [[undermines]] a city's efficiency and wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think transport will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant transformation. Electric vehicles will likely become the norm, drastically cutting emissions, and [[autonomous]], self-driving cars may reshape how we travel. Cities will probably invest more in cycling, walking and clean public transport. Concepts like [[shared mobility]] could reduce car ownership. So the future of transport is likely to be cleaner, smarter and more [[integrated]], hopefully making our cities less polluted and more liveable.

part3Samples.q: How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
part3Samples.answer: A combination of measures is most effective. Investing heavily in reliable, affordable public transport gives people a genuine alternative to driving. Encouraging cycling and walking through better [[infrastructure]] helps too. Some cities use [[congestion charging]] to [[discourage]] car use in busy areas. Better urban planning that reduces the need to travel far is also valuable. Essentially, the solution lies in making sustainable options more attractive than driving, rather than simply widening roads.

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

data.prompt: Describe a time you solved a difficult problem
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a problem at work that had nothing to do with paperwork and everything to do with people. A difficult problem I once solved involved a serious misunderstanding between two members of a team I was working with at the consultancy. One of them handled students' documents and the other handled visa files, and each felt the other was causing delays. Their disagreement had escalated to the point where it was affecting everyone's work. At first I was reluctant to get involved, because it was not really my responsibility, but I could see the whole office was suffering. Rather than taking sides, I decided to sit down with each of them separately to understand their perspectives. It quickly became clear that the whole conflict stemmed from poor communication rather than any real [[malice]]. I then arranged a calm conversation between them over tea, acting as a neutral [[mediator]]. It was a delicate situation that required a lot of [[tact]], but eventually they [[cleared the air]]. We also agreed on a simple shared checklist, so nobody would be left guessing about who was doing what. What I found most rewarding was seeing them work together productively again afterwards. Honestly, resolving that tension felt like a genuine achievement, and it taught me the value of listening carefully before [[jumping to conclusions]]. It made me realise that many difficult problems are really just communication failures in disguise, and patience is often the best tool. I still feel quite proud of how that turned out.

followUps.q: Do the two colleagues get on well now?
followUps.answer: Surprisingly well, yes. They still tease each other now and then, but it is friendly. They even sit together at lunch, which nobody in the office would have predicted a year ago.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy solving problems like this?
followUps.answer: I do, as long as they don't happen too often. I find it satisfying to untangle a situation and see people relax again, although it can be quite draining while it is going on.

part3Samples.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
part3Samples.answer: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be [[constructive]] if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. There is growing awareness of the importance of emotional intelligence and communication skills, which are increasingly taught in schools and workplaces. If this trend continues, future generations may be better [[equipped]] to handle disagreements. On the other hand, online communication can sometimes make people more [[polarised]] and less willing to [[compromise]], so it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What is the best way to resolve a serious disagreement?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective approach usually involves calm, honest dialogue where both sides genuinely listen to one another. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a [[neutral third party]] as a [[mediator]] can be [[invaluable]]. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

sample.answer: There are a few things I am proud of, but one stands out above the rest. An achievement I am genuinely proud of was completing a challenging professional qualification while working full time. It was a certificate course in international student counselling, which I finished last year to become better at my job. Balancing study with a demanding job was far harder than I had anticipated. For nearly a year, I sacrificed most of my evenings and weekends, which required real [[discipline]]. I would come home from the office, have dinner with my family and then [[burn the midnight oil]] at my desk, often with a cup of tea going cold beside me. There were moments when I felt like giving up, especially when the material seemed impossibly difficult. On those nights, a quick walk by the river usually helped me clear my head and start again. What kept me going was a stubborn [[determination]] to finish what I had started. When I finally passed the final exam, the sense of relief and pride was overwhelming. My father was so delighted that he bought sweets for half the neighbourhood. What made it so meaningful was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and [[persistence]]. Honestly, that accomplishment gave me a huge confidence boost and proved to myself that I could handle serious challenges. It remains one of my proudest moments, not because of the qualification itself, but because of the [[resilience]] it took to get there. It taught me I am capable of far more than I thought.

followUps.q: Has the qualification helped you in your job?
followUps.answer: Yes, quite a lot. I feel more confident advising students now, especially about choosing courses and preparing for interviews, and my manager has started giving me some of the more complicated cases.

followUps.q: How did your family support you during that time?
followUps.answer: They were very patient. My mother kept bringing me tea late at night, and my younger sister, who is a serious student herself, often studied beside me, which kept both of us motivated.

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the first time I spoke in front of a large audience, because it was a genuine milestone for me. A memorable first for me was trying public speaking at a fairly large event, something I had always dreaded. It happened about a year ago, when our consultancy organised a study abroad seminar for students and parents in a hall in Sirajganj. My manager asked me to give a short presentation, and my instinct was to refuse, but I forced myself to accept, partly because I knew I could not avoid it forever. In the days leading up to it, I was genuinely [[terrified]], rehearsing constantly and imagining every possible disaster. I even practised in front of my younger sister, who turned out to be a surprisingly tough audience. When the moment came, my heart was pounding and my mouth was dry. But once I started speaking, something surprising happened; I gradually became more [[composed]], and the words began to flow. By the end, I actually felt a rush of [[exhilaration]]. It was far from perfect, but I had done it, and the sense of achievement was immense. A few parents even came up afterwards with questions, which told me I had made sense. I was still shaking a little, but I was smiling from ear to ear. Honestly, pushing through that fear was genuinely [[liberating]], and it taught me that we are often far more capable than our anxiety suggests. Since then I have been much more willing to [[step outside my comfort zone]].

followUps.q: Have you given any presentations since then?
followUps.answer: Yes, several. We now hold seminars every few months, and I usually present the section on applications. I still get a few butterflies beforehand, but nothing like that first time.

followUps.q: Would you like to try any other new things in the future?
followUps.answer: I'd really like to study abroad myself one day. After helping so many students do it, I think experiencing it first-hand would be both challenging and incredibly worthwhile.

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly disagree with this narrow view. While money is a tangible and convenient measure, and financial security certainly matters, equating it with success ignores far more important dimensions of a good life. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. True success, in my view, is measured by fulfilment, relationships and character, not currency.

data.title: Describe a time you felt nervous
data.prompt: Describe a time you felt nervous

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my first day at the education consultancy where I still work. A time I felt intensely nervous was on my first day at a new job, walking into an office full of complete strangers. It was only a few months after I had finished my BBA, and it was my first proper full-time job. I had really wanted the role, which somehow made me even more [[apprehensive]] about making a bad impression. The night before, I barely slept, and I think I ironed my shirt at least twice. I even left home forty minutes early, just in case the rickshaw got stuck in traffic. My mind was racing with worries about whether I would fit in or make some embarrassing mistake. I remember my hands were slightly shaking as I introduced myself. To my relief, my new colleagues were warm and [[welcoming]], which gradually [[put me at ease]]. One senior colleague took me out for tea and explained how everything worked, which made a huge difference. By lunchtime, most of my nerves had [[melted away]], and I began to feel genuinely [[optimistic]] about the job. Looking back, I realise that my anxiety had been almost entirely in my head. What I learned was that nervousness before something important is completely natural, and it usually fades once you actually begin. That experience taught me to trust that things generally turn out far better than my worried mind predicts. When I got home that evening, my family were waiting to hear every detail over dinner.

followUps.q: Do you still feel nervous at work sometimes?
followUps.answer: Occasionally, mostly before meeting parents who are very worried about sending their child abroad. But it is a useful kind of nervousness now, because it makes me prepare properly.

followUps.q: What do you usually do to calm your nerves?
followUps.answer: I take a few slow breaths and remind myself that I have prepared. If I have time, a short walk and a cup of tea usually help me feel settled again.

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say people today change jobs too often. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not entirely agree that it is a problem. Changing jobs frequently is often a sensible way to gain diverse experience, increase pay and find a better fit, especially in a fast-changing economy. The old model of [[lifelong loyalty]] is somewhat [[outdated]]. That said, changing too often can look unstable to employers and prevent one from developing deep [[expertise]], so a degree of balance is wise.

data.prompt: Describe a time you gave advice to someone

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about some advice I gave to one of my oldest friends from university. A time I gave advice that actually made a difference was when this close friend was agonising over whether to change careers. He had been working in a bank for two years and was deeply unhappy in his job, because what he really wanted was to teach, but he was terrified of the [[uncertainty]] of starting over. He came to me feeling completely stuck, and I could see he just needed someone to help him think clearly. We met at our usual tea stall by the river and talked for hours. Rather than telling him what to do, I encouraged him to [[weigh up]] what he truly valued in the long term. I shared my own experience of taking a similar risk when I chose my current job, which seemed to [[reassure]] him. I also suggested he speak to a few teachers first, to see what the job was really like day to day. My main advice was that regret over never trying is usually worse than the fear of failing. It was a genuinely [[delicate]] conversation, because I did not want to push him into anything. In the end, he made the change and is now far happier teaching at a college. He told me recently that our conversation was the push he needed. Honestly, seeing him thrive was incredibly [[gratifying]], and it reminded me that sometimes the best help is simply helping someone find their own answer.

followUps.q: Do people often come to you for advice?
followUps.answer: Quite often, actually, probably because of my job. Students and their parents ask me about studying abroad every day, and friends seem to assume I am good with big decisions too.

followUps.q: Is there anyone whose advice you always trust?
followUps.answer: My grandfather. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp, and he has a way of cutting through a problem with one simple question. I always come away seeing things more clearly.

part3Samples.q: What factors do you think are most important when choosing a career?
part3Samples.answer: I think the most important factor is genuine interest, because you will spend a huge portion of your life working. A job you are passionate about is far more sustainable than a purely [[lucrative]] one. That said, practical considerations like financial security, job stability and growth opportunities cannot be ignored. Ideally, people should seek a career that [[strikes a healthy balance]] between passion and [[pragmatism]].

part3Samples.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?
part3Samples.answer: This is the classic dilemma. In an ideal world, you would have both. If forced to choose, I lean towards a job you love, because passion tends to lead to better performance and long-term fulfilment, and money alone rarely brings lasting [[contentment]]. However, this is somewhat a [[privilege]]; those with financial pressures may reasonably [[prioritise]] a stable income first.

part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more [[volatile]] than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to [[pursue]] fulfilment. Additionally, rapid technological change means some jobs disappear while new ones emerge, which [[compels]] people to adapt and retrain.

part3Samples.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I believe jobs involving skills that machines cannot easily replicate will be most valuable. This includes creative fields, healthcare, and roles requiring emotional intelligence and complex problem-solving. Careers related to technology, such as AI and data science, will obviously be in high demand, as will jobs focused on [[sustainability]] and renewable energy. Essentially, roles that are [[adaptable]] and distinctly human will [[thrive]].

part3Samples.q: How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?
part3Samples.answer: Better career guidance in schools would make an enormous difference. Too often, students choose paths with little real understanding of what the jobs actually involve. Providing internships and work experience gives them valuable [[exposure]] to different fields. Mentorship from professionals can also offer honest, [[first-hand]] insight. Essentially, we need to help young people make [[informed]] choices rather than blind ones.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

data.prompt: Describe a time you worked as part of a team

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a group project from my BBA, because it taught me a lot about working with other people. A memorable experience of teamwork was a group project during my university years, where we had to deliver a major presentation in just two weeks. The task was to design a complete marketing plan for a small local business and then present it to our lecturers. Our team was made up of five people with very different personalities and strengths. One was brilliant with numbers, another was a confident speaker, and one was very creative with design. At first, coordinating everyone was genuinely challenging, and there were a few [[clashes]] over how to approach things. My role naturally became that of the organiser, keeping track of deadlines and making sure everyone stayed [[on the same page]]. What made it work in the end was our willingness to [[compromise]] and play to each other's strengths. We met almost every evening in the library, often staying until it closed. As we got closer, the atmosphere became genuinely [[collaborative]], and the project came together beautifully. On the day itself, everyone played their part, and it felt like a genuine team effort. We ended up receiving one of the highest marks in the class. Honestly, the experience taught me more about cooperation than any lecture could, and I felt really proud of what we had built together. It showed me that a good team is far more than the sum of its parts, provided everyone is [[committed]] to the same goal.

followUps.q: Are you still in touch with the people from that team?
followUps.answer: With most of them, yes. We have a group chat that is still surprisingly active, and whenever a couple of us are in Dhaka at the same time, we try to meet up for dinner.

followUps.q: Do you prefer working alone or in a team?
followUps.answer: It depends on the task. For detailed paperwork I like to work alone and concentrate, but for planning or solving problems, I think a team usually comes up with far better ideas.

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say great leaders are born, not made. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely disagree with that idea. While some people may have a natural [[charisma]] or confidence, I firmly believe leadership is a set of skills that can be learned and refined through experience. History is full of leaders who [[grew into the role]]. To claim leaders are simply born [[undermines]] the value of hard work and personal development.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a complaint I made last year, which turned out much better than I expected. A time I had to make a complaint was over a faulty product I had bought online, which stopped working within days. It was a pair of wireless headphones that I used for listening to music on my evening walks by the river. I was quite frustrated, as it had been fairly expensive and I felt genuinely [[let down]]. I contacted the company's customer service, determined to stay calm and polite rather than [[lose my temper]], which I find rarely helps. I explained the situation clearly and provided all the necessary evidence, including photos and my order details. When I had heard nothing after two days, I phoned their helpline and patiently explained it all again. To my surprise, the representative was genuinely [[apologetic]] and handled the matter far better than I expected. They arranged a full refund and even offered a discount on a future purchase, which I thought was a [[gracious]] gesture. The whole thing was sorted out in less than a week. What I learned from the experience was that complaining effectively is really about being clear and reasonable rather than angry. Honestly, the whole thing was resolved far more [[amicably]] than I had feared, and I felt quite satisfied afterwards. It also made me realise that most companies genuinely want to keep their customers happy. It reminded me that a firm but respectful approach usually gets the best results, and I have used the same approach several times since.

followUps.q: Do you often complain when something goes wrong?
followUps.answer: Not very often. I only complain when it really matters, like when I have paid good money for something. For small things, I usually decide it is not worth the time and energy.

followUps.q: Do you still shop online after that experience?
followUps.answer: Yes, I do, but I am more careful now. I read the reviews properly and check the return policy before buying anything expensive, which I never used to bother with.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a small moment of kindness that happened in the main market in Sirajganj a few months ago. A time I helped a stranger was when I came across an elderly man who had stumbled and dropped his shopping on a busy street. There were vegetables and a bag of rice spread across the road, and rickshaws were [[weaving around]] him. Most people simply walked past, which I found rather [[disheartening]]. I stopped to help him gather his things and made sure he was not hurt. Luckily, apart from a small scrape on his hand, he was fine. He seemed a little shaken, so I stayed with him for a few minutes and offered to walk him to a nearby bench outside a tea stall. He was incredibly grateful, and we ended up having a lovely short chat; it turned out he was a retired schoolteacher who now lived alone, since his children had moved to Dhaka for work. What struck me was how such a small gesture clearly meant a great deal to him. Honestly, it took only a couple of minutes of my time, yet it felt genuinely meaningful. It reminded me that we often overlook small chances to be kind because we are so [[caught up in]] our own lives. That brief encounter left me feeling [[heartened]] for the rest of the day, and it made me more [[attentive]] to people around me who might need help. I still see him in the market sometimes, and he always waves.

followUps.q: Do you think people help strangers less than in the past?
followUps.answer: In big cities, perhaps. Everyone is in a hurry and slightly wary of strangers. In smaller towns like mine, people still tend to stop, although even here I notice it happening less.

followUps.q: Has anyone ever helped you when you were a stranger somewhere?
followUps.answer: Yes, when I got lost in Chattogram once, a shopkeeper drew me a little map and pointed me in the right direction. I have never forgotten how kind he was.

part3: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
Are moral values the same across all cultures?

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but I think it is too simplistic to blame technology alone. It is true that excessive screen time can replace real interaction and [[foster]] unhealthy comparison. However, technology can also connect isolated people, such as those far from family. So the technology itself is [[neutral]]; the real issue is how we use it. The deeper causes lie in broader [[societal]] changes.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a trip that did not go to plan at all, but still turned out well. A time I had to change my plans quite suddenly was when a long-awaited trip with friends fell through at the last minute due to bad weather. The original plan was to spend three days in Cox's Bazar, but a cyclone warning was issued the day before we were due to leave, and our bus was cancelled. I had been looking forward to it for weeks, so the cancellation was initially a [[crushing disappointment]]. Rather than sulking about it, though, we decided to be flexible and [[make the best of]] the situation. We ended up organising a day trip to a char, one of the sandy river islands in the Jamuna, something none of us had planned. We hired a small boat, packed a picnic and spent the afternoon walking on the sandbanks and watching the fishermen bring in their nets. To our surprise, it turned out to be a wonderful day, arguably better than the original plan. What I took from it was that rigidity often leads to frustration, whereas being [[adaptable]] opens up unexpected opportunities. It was a good reminder that plans [[falling apart]] is not always a bad thing. Honestly, some of my best experiences have come from [[spontaneous]] changes like that, and I remember feeling surprisingly content on the boat home as the sun went down. I now try to hold my plans a little more loosely and stay open to whatever comes.

followUps.q: Did you manage to go to Cox's Bazar later?
followUps.answer: Yes, about three months later, once the weather had settled. It was lovely, but funnily enough, when we talk about that year, it is usually the day on the char that we remember.

followUps.q: Do you usually plan your trips carefully?
followUps.answer: I plan the essentials, like transport and where to stay, but I leave the rest fairly open. Too much planning makes a trip feel like work, and the unexpected moments are often the best.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the time I got lost in Chattogram, a city I had never visited before. It was about three years ago, when I went there with some university friends on a short study tour. A time I got hopelessly lost was during that trip, when I wandered off from my group one afternoon to explore the older part of the city near the port. Before long I realised I had no idea where I was, and to make matters worse, my phone battery had died. I felt a growing sense of [[panic]] as the narrow lanes all started to look the same, and I was completely [[disoriented]]. Rather than making it worse by rushing, I forced myself to [[keep a level head]] and think logically. I asked a friendly shopkeeper for directions, and although his local dialect was quite hard for me to follow, he was very patient and even drew me a little map on a scrap of paper. Eventually I found my way back to a landmark I recognised and reunited with my relieved group, who had been searching for me for nearly an hour. I felt rather [[sheepish]], and my friends teased me about it for the rest of the trip. Looking back, although it was stressful at the time, it turned into a strangely memorable [[escapade]]. It taught me to pay more attention to my surroundings and always memorise a few key landmarks. Honestly, getting lost made me a more careful traveller.

followUps.q: Do you usually rely on your phone for directions?
followUps.answer: Yes, far too much, if I am honest. Since that day, though, I always make sure my phone is charged, and I try to notice a couple of landmarks wherever I go.

followUps.q: Have you been back to Chattogram since then?
followUps.answer: Once, for work, to attend an education fair. This time I stayed close to the venue, but I did recognise the lane where the kind shopkeeper had helped me, which made me smile.

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a celebration that my whole family still talks about. A special occasion I celebrated with real joy was my parents' wedding anniversary, which my sisters and I organised as a surprise last year. We had been planning it secretly for weeks, which made the anticipation even more exciting, and keeping it from my mother was not easy, because she notices everything. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and their two children, and my grandparents travelled in from the village. We decorated the house, invited close relatives and arranged all their favourite food, including the biryani my father loves. My younger sister was in charge of the cake, and I handled the guest list. The look of genuine surprise and delight on my parents' faces was absolutely [[priceless]]. It was a wonderfully [[heartwarming]] evening, full of laughter, old stories and a few happy tears. My grandmother even told us how my parents first met, which none of us had heard before. What made it so special was seeing the whole family come together to honour them. In our increasingly busy lives, these gatherings feel [[few and far between]], and so all the more precious. My four-year-old nephew kept trying to blow out the candles before anyone else, which had everyone in fits of laughter. I remember feeling an overwhelming sense of gratitude and love that evening. Honestly, occasions like this remind me of what truly matters. The whole event was thoroughly [[unforgettable]], and I think it meant just as much to us as it did to my parents. It is a night I will always [[treasure]].

followUps.q: Do you often celebrate special occasions with your family?
followUps.answer: Yes, especially Eid, when everyone tries to be together. We are a close-knit family, so even smaller occasions like birthdays usually end with a big dinner at home.

followUps.q: What did your parents say about the surprise?
followUps.answer: My father was lost for words, which is rare for him. My mother cried a little and then immediately started worrying whether there was enough food for everyone, which made us all laugh.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think festivals are important?
part3Samples.answer: Festivals serve several important purposes. They provide a much-needed break from routine and an occasion for joy and celebration. More deeply, they reinforce cultural identity and bring communities and families together in shared rituals. They also pass traditions from one generation to the next. In my view, this sense of [[collective]] celebration and [[belonging]] is something people fundamentally need, which is why festivals remain so [[cherished]] across cultures.

part3Samples.q: How are festivals celebrated differently now compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: The essence remains, but the style has changed. In the past, celebrations were often simpler and more community-focused, with everyone participating directly. Today, festivals have become more [[commercialised]], with an emphasis on spending and consumption. Technology has also changed things; people now share their celebrations on social media. So while festivals are still meaningful, some argue they have lost a degree of [[authenticity]], becoming more about [[consumerism]] than genuine tradition.

part3Samples.q: What effect does commercialisation have on traditional festivals?
part3Samples.answer: The effect is [[double-edged]]. On one hand, commercialisation can boost the economy and [[raise a festival's profile]], making it more widely known. On the other, it can [[dilute]] the festival's original spiritual or cultural meaning, reducing it to a shopping opportunity. The genuine sentiment behind the celebration can get lost amid the advertising and pressure to spend. So it brings visibility, but often at the cost of authenticity and true significance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional festivals will remain popular in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they will, though they will continue to evolve. While the way we celebrate may change, the fundamental human need for community, joy and shared meaning will ensure festivals [[endure]]. There may even be a [[resurgence]] of interest as people seek authenticity in an increasingly digital world. So while some may become more modernised or commercial, I think the core appeal of festivals will [[persist]] and remain relevant for generations.

part3Samples.q: How can the true spirit of festivals be preserved?
part3Samples.answer: Preserving the spirit requires conscious effort. Emphasising the values behind the festival, such as togetherness, gratitude or reflection, rather than just the material aspects, is important. Involving young people in traditional practices and explaining their meaning helps too. Communities can prioritise participation over consumption. Essentially, if we consciously focus on the [[essence]] of a festival rather than its [[commercial trappings]], its true spirit can [[thrive]].

I remember trying to prepare myself mentally for both possible outcomes, which was difficult. On the day they were published online, my whole family crowded round the computer with me. When the results finally came and turned out to be positive, the relief was [[immense]], and my mother immediately handed out sweets to the neighbours. What that experience taught me was how to cope with uncertainty, which is a genuinely useful skill. Honestly, learning to [[sit with that discomfort]] rather than let it consume me was invaluable. Education should teach people how to think, not merely what to think. Sadly, many systems overemphasise [[rote learning]] at the expense of this broader [[enrichment]].

part3Samples.q: How is education today different from education in the past?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are considerable. In the past, education was largely teacher-centred, based on memorisation and strict discipline. Today, there is a much greater emphasis on interactive, student-centred learning, and technology has [[revolutionised]] access to information. Learning is now more [[collaborative]] and creative. However, I would argue that academic pressure and competition have also intensified, which is a rather [[double-edged]] development.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think exam results are given so much importance?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems from the need for a seemingly objective way to measure ability and allocate opportunities. Exams provide a convenient, [[quantifiable]] benchmark for universities and employers. However, this [[overreliance]] on results can be [[counterproductive]], as it encourages students to memorise for tests rather than truly understand. It also fails to capture vital qualities like creativity, which are far harder to quantify.

part3Samples.q: How do you think education will change in the next 20 years?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate dramatic changes, largely driven by technology. Personalised, AI-assisted learning could [[tailor]] lessons to each student's pace, and online education will make quality teaching far more accessible globally. The traditional classroom may become less central. There will likely also be a stronger focus on [[adaptable]] skills, given that people will need to [[reskill]] repeatedly throughout their careers.

part3Samples.q: How could education systems be improved?

Secondly, curricula should be [[modernised]] to include life skills such as financial literacy and emotional intelligence. Finally, investing in teacher training and reducing class sizes would allow for more [[personalised]] learning. The goal should be a more [[holistic]] and flexible model.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. As the weeks went on, keeping that promise became genuinely [[demanding]], because my own workload kept [[piling up]]. There were evenings when I was exhausted and tempted to cancel, but I felt a strong sense of [[obligation]] not to let her down. My mother kept us going with endless cups of tea. When she eventually did well, the pride I felt was [[immense]], and our bond grew even stronger. Keeping that promise meant missing a few cricket matches with friends, but I never regretted it for a moment. part3Samples.q: Do you think it will be harder to trust information in the future?

What I learned was the importance of listening rather than simply trying to win the argument. Honestly, resolving it [[amicably]] actually strengthened our friendship rather than damaging it. It taught me that disagreements are a normal part of any close relationship, and how you handle them matters far more than the disagreement itself. part3Samples.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
part3Samples.answer: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be [[constructive]] if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?

That experience left me feeling small in the best possible way, and it sparked a lasting fascination with astronomy. part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?

The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say factories should be moved away from residential areas. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this as a sensible measure. Locating polluting factories away from where people live can significantly reduce residents' [[direct exposure]] to harmful air and water pollution, protecting public health. However, it is not a complete solution, as pollution still spreads, and it may simply [[shift the burden]] to another community. So while separating industry from homes is beneficial, it must be combined with actually reducing the pollution [[at its source]].

It was my first proper trip abroad, so I was already slightly on edge. We had just arrived in Kathmandu late in the evening, and I found myself unable to communicate with a taxi driver, which was becoming quite [[nerve-racking]]. He spoke almost no English, and our few words of Nepali were not enough to explain where our guesthouse was. Then I remembered a translation app on my phone, which turned out to be a [[lifesaver]]. I simply typed what I wanted to say, and it translated it instantly, allowing us to understand each other. It even read the sentence out loud, and the driver laughed and nodded. It felt almost [[miraculous]] that a small device could bridge such a gap so easily. What impressed me most was how [[seamless]] and quick the whole process was. Without it, I honestly do not know how I would have managed. The experience really opened my eyes to how [[indispensable]] technology has become in daily life. While I sometimes worry that we rely on it too heavily, moments like that remind me of its genuine value. It turned a potentially frustrating situation into a smooth one, and I was extremely grateful for it. In the end we reached the guesthouse safely, and the driver even recommended a good place for breakfast. We ended up using that app for the rest of the trip.

followUps.q: Do you use translation apps in your daily life?
followUps.answer: Occasionally at work, when a student sends me a document in a language I don't know. But for English I prefer to rely on myself, because I want to keep improving my own skills.

followUps.q: Do you think technology makes travelling easier?
followUps.answer: Definitely. Maps, booking apps and translation tools remove a lot of the stress. The only downside is that people sometimes stare at their screens instead of enjoying where they are.

part3: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
How was life different before smartphones?
What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
Some fear AI will one day become smarter than humans. Do you share this concern?

part3Samples.q: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: On the whole, I think they have, though not without significant drawbacks. Smartphones have put a world of information, communication and services in our pockets, which is genuinely empowering and convenient. However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of [[dependence]] that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them [[consciously]] rather than [[compulsively]].

part3Samples.q: How was life different before smartphones?
part3Samples.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.

part3Samples.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely [[impair]] both our mental and physical wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more [[anticipatory]] and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to [[blur]] further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

part3Samples.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
part3Samples.answer: There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. [[Designating]] device-free times and zones, such as during meals or in the bedroom, helps re-establish boundaries. Using apps that track and limit screen time can raise awareness of usage. Ultimately, consciously replacing [[mindless scrolling]] with more rewarding activities is the most sustainable way to [[loosen the phone's grip]].

part3Samples.q: Some fear AI will one day become smarter than humans. Do you share this concern?
part3Samples.answer: I have measured concern rather than alarm. AI already surpasses us in narrow tasks like calculation, and it will keep improving. The idea of a general intelligence exceeding humans is more [[speculative]], but not impossible in the long term. My concern is less about a science-fiction takeover and more about the immediate risks of misuse and lack of control. So I think a degree of [[vigilance]] is wise, but [[hysteria]] is unhelpful.
