data.prompt: Describe a time you spent in nature
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a few days I spent deep in the Sundarbans, the huge mangrove forest in the south of Bangladesh. A time I spent immersed in nature that I remember fondly was a three-day boat trip there with a few friends, about two winters ago. We had grown tired of busy streets and craved a proper escape into the wild. From the moment we arrived, the change was [[striking]]; the air was fresh, and the only sounds were birdsong, rustling leaves and the water lapping against the boat. We spent the days gliding along narrow channels, spotting deer, monkeys and even crocodiles on the muddy banks, although sadly no tigers. We slept in small cabins on the boat, and the crew cooked fresh fish for us every evening. Early one morning we walked along a wooden trail through the forest, and the silence was almost eerie. In the evenings we sat on the deck under a sky full of stars. Being so completely disconnected from screens was genuinely [[refreshing]], almost like a reset for my mind, because there was hardly any phone signal. What I found most [[rejuvenating]] was the simple, slow pace of it all. There is something deeply [[grounding]] about being surrounded by nature with none of the usual distractions. Honestly, I returned home feeling calmer and more clear-headed than I had in months. The experience made me realise how much modern life disconnects us from the natural world, and how [[restorative]] it is to reconnect. I would love to go back one day and take my younger sister with me.

followUps.q: Do you often spend time in nature?
followUps.answer: Not as much as I'd like, but I do walk by the Jamuna most evenings. It is not a forest, of course, but watching the river and the open sky helps me unwind after work.

followUps.q: Were you worried about seeing a tiger?
followUps.answer: A little, to be honest, although the guides were very experienced and we mostly stayed on the boat. Part of me was actually disappointed not to catch even a glimpse of one.

part3: Why is it important to protect wildlife?
Should we prioritise protecting animals or supporting human development?
What are the main reasons some animal species are becoming extinct?
Are you hopeful about the future of wildlife conservation?
What can be done to protect endangered species?
Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why is it important to protect wildlife?
part3Samples.answer: Protecting wildlife is important for several profound reasons. Ecologically, every species plays a role in maintaining the [[delicate balance]] of ecosystems that humans ultimately depend on for clean air, water and food. There is also a strong ethical argument that we have a duty to protect other living creatures. Furthermore, [[biodiversity]] has immense scientific and economic value. So conservation is not merely sentimental; it is essential for [[ecological stability]] and our own survival.

part3Samples.q: Should we prioritise protecting animals or supporting human development?
part3Samples.answer: I reject the idea that these are truly in opposition, though tensions certainly arise. In the short term, development sometimes conflicts with conservation, and people's immediate needs are understandably a priority. However, in the long run, human development depends entirely on a healthy natural world. Destroying nature for short-term gain is ultimately [[self-defeating]]. So rather than choosing one over the other, I believe we must pursue sustainable development that [[reconciles]] both [[imperatives]].

part3Samples.q: What are the main reasons some animal species are becoming extinct?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is human activity. Habitat destruction, as forests and wild areas are cleared for agriculture and development, is the biggest threat, leaving animals nowhere to live. Poaching and overfishing directly deplete populations, while pollution and, increasingly, climate change disrupt ecosystems. So extinction is largely a tragic consequence of human [[encroachment]], [[exploitation]] and environmental [[degradation]], rather than natural causes.

part3Samples.q: Are you hopeful about the future of wildlife conservation?
part3Samples.answer: I hold a cautious hope. The threats are severe, and we are losing species at an [[alarming rate]], which is deeply concerning. However, there are genuine success stories where dedicated conservation efforts have brought species [[back from the brink]]. Growing public awareness, international cooperation and new technologies for monitoring wildlife are encouraging. So while the challenge is immense, I believe that with sufficient commitment, we can still preserve much of our [[natural heritage]].

part3Samples.q: What can be done to protect endangered species?
part3Samples.answer: A range of measures is required. Establishing and properly funding protected areas and national parks safeguards vital [[habitats]]. Enforcing strict anti-poaching laws and [[cracking down on]] illegal wildlife trade is crucial. International cooperation and treaties help protect [[migratory]] species. Supporting local communities so they benefit from conservation rather than exploitation is also key. Ultimately, addressing the root causes, like habitat loss and climate change, is essential for lasting protection and recovery.

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about an event I still feel a little sad about missing. A time I sadly missed an important event was a close friend's wedding, which I had genuinely been looking forward to. He was one of my best friends from university, and the wedding was in Rajshahi about two years ago. Unfortunately, I [[came down with]] a high fever just a day before and was simply too unwell to travel. It was supposed to be the first time our whole university group had been together in years. I was absolutely [[devastated]], because I had promised to be there and had even helped with some of the preparations. Lying at home while the celebration went on without me was deeply [[frustrating]], especially when photos and videos kept arriving on my phone. I remember feeling guilty, even though the situation was entirely out of my control. My mother insisted I stay in bed, and of course she was right. My friend was incredibly understanding, which only made me feel worse about missing it. To make up for it, I visited them as soon as I recovered and gave them a [[heartfelt]] gift, a framed photo of our old university group. Honestly, the experience taught me how unpredictable life can be and how we cannot always control our circumstances. It also showed me the value of a [[forgiving]] friend. Although I still regret missing it, I have [[made peace with]] the fact that some things are simply beyond our control. My friend and his wife still joke that I owe them a dance.

followUps.q: Do you often go to weddings?
followUps.answer: Quite often, actually. Weddings in Bangladesh are big occasions, and between relatives, neighbours and friends, there always seems to be one coming up, especially in the winter season.

followUps.q: How did your friend react when you told him you couldn't come?
followUps.answer: He was very kind about it. He told me to rest and not to worry, and he even called me during the reception so I could say a few words to everyone.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some say festivals have become too commercial. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this observation. Many festivals now seem dominated by advertising, sales and pressure to spend, which can [[overshadow]] their original cultural or spiritual meaning. The focus has shifted, in some cases, from [[togetherness]] to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an [[irreversible]] one.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my younger sister, who is probably the most hard-working person I know. A time I felt enormously proud of a family member was when she finished at the top of her year in her HSC exams and received an award at her college's prize-giving ceremony last year. I had watched her study relentlessly for two years, often sacrificing her social life, so her success felt thoroughly [[well-deserved]]. The whole family went to the ceremony, and my parents were dressed in their best clothes. In our family, education has always been treated as something precious, so this meant a great deal to my parents. Sitting in the audience, I felt [[a lump in my throat]] as her name was called out for the special award. It was a genuinely [[emotional]] moment for the whole family, and my mother could not stop wiping her eyes. What made me so proud was not just the achievement itself, but the [[perseverance]] and discipline she had shown to get there. I remembered all the times she had doubted herself and kept going anyway, sometimes studying until two in the morning. Honestly, seeing her hard work pay off so publicly was one of the most [[uplifting]] experiences I have had. Afterwards, we went out for sweets and tea, and she could not stop smiling. I told her how proud I was, and I meant every word. It was a powerful reminder that dedication truly does pay off in the end, and it made me want to push myself harder too.

followUps.q: Do you and your sister get on well?
followUps.answer: Very well. We tease each other constantly, as siblings do, but she is also the person I talk to when something is bothering me. She gives surprisingly wise advice for her age.

followUps.q: How did your family celebrate her success?
followUps.answer: We had a special dinner at home, and my mother cooked all her favourite dishes. My father also phoned my grandparents in the village, who were absolutely delighted to hear the news.

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the first really expensive thing I ever bought for myself. A time I spent money on something genuinely special was when I bought my first proper laptop with money I had saved myself. It was during my second year at university, and I paid for it with the money I earned from private tuition, teaching two schoolchildren in the evenings. It took me months of careful budgeting, as it was a significant amount for me at the time. I had to be quite [[frugal]], cutting back on unnecessary spending to reach my goal. I kept a small notebook where I wrote down every taka I saved. I stopped eating out, walked instead of taking rickshaws, and said no to a few trips with friends. When I finally had enough and walked into the shop to buy it, the feeling was incredibly [[satisfying]]. It was a mid-range model, nothing fancy, but to me it felt like the most valuable thing in the world. What made it so special was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and patience, without asking my father for anything. It was not just a purchase; it felt like a genuine [[accomplishment]]. The laptop went on to become essential for my studies and work, so it turned out to be a wise investment too. Honestly, buying something you have saved hard for feels far more rewarding than a casual, [[impulsive]] purchase. That experience taught me the value of patience and [[delayed gratification]], a lesson I still carry with me.

followUps.q: Do you still have that laptop?
followUps.answer: I do, although it is quite slow now. My younger sister used it for her studies for a while, and these days it mostly sits on my desk at home for watching cricket highlights.

followUps.q: Are you good at saving money now?
followUps.answer: Reasonably good, yes. I put a little aside every month, partly because I would like to study abroad one day, and that goal makes it much easier to resist unnecessary spending.

part3Samples.q: How important is money in life?
part3Samples.answer: Money is [[undeniably]] important, but its importance has limits. It is essential for meeting our basic needs, providing security, and giving us freedom and opportunities, so I would never dismiss it. However, beyond a certain point of comfort, its ability to improve our happiness [[diminishes sharply]]. Health, relationships and purpose matter far more. So I see money as a vital tool and [[enabler]], but a poor ultimate goal in itself.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to save money or spend it?
part3Samples.answer: A healthy balance between the two is ideal. Saving is [[prudent]], providing security, peace of mind and the means to achieve future goals or weather emergencies. However, being excessively frugal can mean missing out on valuable experiences and enjoyment in the present. Spending wisely, particularly on experiences and things that genuinely enrich life, is worthwhile. So I favour disciplined saving combined with mindful spending, avoiding both reckless [[extravagance]] and joyless [[hoarding]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does the pursuit of wealth have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The pursuit of wealth has mixed effects. Positively, it can motivate hard work, innovation and achievement, driving both personal and economic progress. However, an excessive obsession with wealth can be corrosive, leading people to become greedy, materialistic, and to neglect relationships, ethics and their own wellbeing. It can foster perpetual dissatisfaction too. So while a healthy desire to prosper is fine, an [[all-consuming]] [[fixation]] on money can genuinely [[distort]] a person's values.

part3Samples.q: Do you think the gap between rich and poor will grow in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am concerned that it might, without deliberate intervention. Trends like automation, which may concentrate wealth among those who own the technology, and globalisation could widen the gap further. However, there is also growing awareness of inequality and political pressure to address it through [[progressive taxation]] and social policy. So the outcome is not [[predetermined]]; whether the gap widens or narrows will depend on the political choices societies make to [[redistribute]] opportunity.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce poverty?
part3Samples.answer: Reducing poverty requires a comprehensive approach. Access to quality education and healthcare is fundamental, as it enables social mobility. Creating decent, well-paid jobs and ensuring fair wages tackles the [[root causes]]. Social [[safety nets]], like unemployment support, protect the most vulnerable. Progressive taxation can fund these efforts. Ultimately, empowering people with opportunities and skills, rather than mere [[handouts]], offers the most sustainable path out of poverty.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a fear that followed me for most of my life. A significant fear I managed to overcome was my long-standing fear of water, which had followed me since childhood, when I slipped into a pond and swallowed a lot of water before someone pulled me out. Growing up beside the Jamuna, not being able to swim was both limiting and slightly embarrassing. For years I avoided swimming entirely, and I would always find an excuse when my friends went to the river. Eventually, about two years ago, I decided enough was enough, and my cousin in the village, who is a strong swimmer, offered to teach me in the pond behind my grandparents' house. The first few sessions were genuinely [[terrifying]], and I nearly gave up several times. My cousin, however, was incredibly patient and encouraging, which made all the difference. Every weekend we travelled to the village, and he would stand beside me in the water, holding me up until I found my balance. Slowly but surely, my confidence began to grow, and I became less [[petrified]] of deep water. The moment I finally swam from one side of the pond to the other unaided was absolutely [[exhilarating]], and my grandfather clapped from the bank. Overcoming that fear gave me a huge sense of achievement that went far beyond swimming itself. Honestly, it taught me that most fears shrink once you [[confront them head-on]] rather than avoiding them. It was a genuinely [[empowering]] experience, and it made me braver about tackling other things I had been putting off out of fear.

followUps.q: Do you swim regularly now?
followUps.answer: Not regularly, but whenever we visit my grandparents in summer, I go into the pond with my cousins. I am still not a strong swimmer, but I am no longer afraid, which is what matters.

followUps.q: Do you think children should learn to swim?
followUps.answer: Absolutely, especially in a country with so many rivers and ponds like Bangladesh. It is a basic safety skill, and it is much easier to learn as a child than as an adult.

part3Samples.q: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?
part3Samples.answer: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely [[outdated]], especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn [[keeps the mind sharp]], opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a [[lifelong pursuit]], not a phase.

part3Samples.q: Is it easier to learn when you are young or when you are older?
part3Samples.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

part3Samples.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
part3Samples.answer: It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?

The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. sample.answer: I'd like to describe a day that made me happier than I had felt in a long time. A moment that filled me with genuine happiness was a spontaneous reunion with old friends I had not seen in years. We had all drifted apart after finishing our BBA, scattered by work and life, some in Dhaka, some in Chattogram and a couple abroad. Then, quite unexpectedly, one of them organised a get-together last winter, and almost everyone managed to come. I was so excited that I took the early morning bus from Sirajganj and arrived far too early. We met at a small restaurant near our old university campus in Dhaka. The moment we all saw each other again was absolutely [[heartwarming]]; it felt as though no time had passed at all. We spent hours [[reminiscing]], laughing about old memories and catching up on each other's lives. We even walked past our old classrooms and the tea stall where we used to spend far too much time. What made it so special was the [[effortless]], genuine warmth between us. In our busy adult lives, such [[carefree]] gatherings have become increasingly rare. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by people who knew the real me. Honestly, that day reminded me how important old friendships are, and how easily we let them slip away. The whole reunion was thoroughly [[joyful]], and it left me determined to make more effort to stay in touch. We stayed so long that the restaurant staff eventually had to ask us, very politely, to leave. Since then, we have tried to meet at least once a year.

followUps.q: Do you find it hard to stay in touch with old friends?
followUps.answer: Sometimes, yes. Everyone is busy with work and family now. But a quick message or a phone call now and then keeps the connection alive, even if we can't meet often.

followUps.q: What else usually makes you happy?
followUps.answer: Simple things, mostly. A good dinner with my family, a cricket match on television, or a quiet walk by the river in the evening. I don't think happiness needs to be complicated.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a moment when I surprised myself by staying calm. A time I managed to stay calm under real pressure was during a minor emergency at a family gathering, when my grandfather suddenly felt faint. It happened last Eid at my grandparents' village home, where the whole family had gathered for lunch. It was a very hot afternoon, and he had been busy greeting guests all morning. There was an immediate sense of alarm among everyone, and the atmosphere quickly became [[chaotic]], with people shouting advice from every direction. For some reason, I felt a strange sense of clarity and knew someone had to [[take charge]]. I calmly helped him sit down in the shade, brought water, and reassured everyone while we decided whether to call the local doctor. I also asked the children to step back and give him some air. My younger sister ran to fetch a hand fan, which helped a lot. Staying [[composed]] was not easy, because I love him dearly, but I knew that adding to the panic would only make things worse. Thankfully, he recovered within a few minutes, and it turned out he was simply tired and dehydrated. Afterwards, several relatives told me how [[reassuring]] my calmness had been, which surprised me. Honestly, I had not known I was capable of keeping such a level head. That experience taught me that staying [[rational]] in a crisis is a genuinely valuable ability, and it gave me more confidence in myself. My grandmother still mentions it whenever the family gets together.

followUps.q: Is your grandfather well now?
followUps.answer: Yes, thankfully. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp and active. Since that day, though, we make sure he rests more and drinks plenty of water, especially during the hot months.

followUps.q: Do you think staying calm can be learned?
followUps.answer: I think so, at least partly. Some people are naturally calmer, but practice and experience help a lot. The more difficult situations you face, the less likely you are to panic.

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say great leaders are born, not made. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely disagree with that idea. While some people may have a natural [[charisma]] or confidence, I firmly believe leadership is a set of skills that can be learned and refined through experience. History is full of leaders who [[grew into the role]]. To claim leaders are simply born [[undermines]] the value of hard work and personal development.

A senior student from my hometown, who was already in his third year, went out of his way to help me settle in. My father had got his number from a family friend, and he met me at the bus station on my very first day. He helped me find accommodation, showed me around, and introduced me to people, which was incredibly [[generous]] of him. He even taught me which buses to take and where to find cheap but decent food near campus. Without his support, those first few weeks would have been far more [[daunting]] and lonely. What struck me was that he expected absolutely nothing in return; his kindness was completely [[selfless]]. I remember feeling deeply [[indebted]] to him, especially since we had barely known each other before. His help made an enormous difference to how quickly I adjusted. Honestly, the experience reminded me how much a small act of kindness can mean to someone in a vulnerable situation. It also inspired me to be equally [[supportive]] when I later saw first-year students struggling to settle in. I still remember his generosity fondly.

part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

A time I taught something to someone was when I helped her learn the basics about two years ago, because she had always found smartphones intimidating. She was keen to stay in touch with my elder sister in Dhaka and see her grandchildren more often, but felt hopelessly lost with the technology. I decided to teach her step by step, and I quickly realised how much [[patience]] it required. I had to slow right down and explain things I [[take for granted]], like swiping, typing a message or finding the camera. I wrote the steps in Bengali on a small card, which she kept beside her phone for months. There were moments of frustration on both sides, but she kept pressing the wrong buttons and then apologising, which made us both laugh. We persevered, usually with a cup of tea in the evenings. What made it so [[rewarding]] was watching her confidence grow, until she could video-call her grandchildren all by herself. Her delight was genuinely [[touching]], and it made every patient hour worthwhile. Honestly, the experience taught me as much as it taught her; it made me far more [[empathetic]] towards people who struggle with technology. It reminded me that teaching is really about seeing things through someone else's eyes. Seeing how much it improved her daily life was deeply satisfying. Now she sends me more messages than anyone else I know.

followUps.answer: I do, as long as the person is keen to learn. In my job I explain application processes to students every day, so I suppose teaching has become a natural part of my life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite [[pronounced]], largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to [[tension]], though it also brings a healthy [[diversity]] of perspectives.

part3Samples.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are quite [[stark]]. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

part3Samples.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
part3Samples.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to [[empathise]], with each side viewing the other's values as [[alien]]. A lack of open, patient communication only [[widens that gulf]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
part3Samples.answer: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now [[evolves]]. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could [[amplify]] the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help [[bridge]] it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?
part3Samples.answer: [[Fostering]] genuine dialogue is essential. Creating opportunities for generations to interact meaningfully, whether in families or communities, builds mutual understanding. Both sides need to approach differences with [[humility]] rather than judgement. I also think education plays a role in teaching young people to respect their elders while encouraging older people to remain [[receptive]] to new ideas.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the biggest professional risk I have taken so far. A significant risk I once took was leaving a secure position to join a small, unproven education consultancy that had only just opened. I had been working in the accounts office of a large company for a few months after my BBA, which was safe but, honestly, quite dull. It was a genuinely [[daunting]] decision, because the new company had no guarantee of success and I was giving up stability. Everyone around me thought I was being [[reckless]], which made me doubt myself at times. My mother kept asking whether I was sure, almost every evening at dinner. However, I felt a strong pull towards the opportunity, because I genuinely wanted to help students study abroad, and I decided to trust my instincts. The early months were certainly [[turbulent]]; we had very few clients, and there were moments when I feared I had made a terrible mistake. Gradually, though, the company [[found its feet]], and the experience turned out to be one of the most rewarding of my career so far. What I gained in skills and confidence was [[immeasurable]]. Honestly, taking that leap taught me that calculated risks are sometimes necessary for real growth. It reinforced my belief that playing it safe is not always the wisest choice. Looking back, I am genuinely glad I was bold enough to follow my instincts, and I feel a quiet pride whenever I see how far the company has come. Today it is a busy office with a steady stream of students.

followUps.q: Are you generally someone who likes taking risks?
followUps.answer: Not really. I am quite careful by nature, and I like to think things through. But I have learned that a well-considered risk can be worth taking, especially when you are young.

followUps.q: How did your parents feel about the risk?
followUps.answer: They were worried at first, naturally. My father, having run his own business for over thirty years, understood the idea of starting small, and his support gave me a lot of confidence.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?

part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a morning when I got up far earlier than I ever normally would. A time I got up unusually early was to watch the sunrise from a hilltop during a short trip to Bandarban with friends, about two years ago. We had to wake at around four in the morning, which was genuinely [[brutal]], especially as none of us are naturally early risers. The reason was simple: people had told us that the sunrise over the hills, with clouds drifting below you, was something you had to see at least once. Half asleep, we made the climb in the dark, questioning why we had agreed to it, with only our phone torches to guide us. Our guesthouse owner had kindly woken us with hot tea before we set off. It was surprisingly cold, and I remember wishing I had brought a thicker jacket. But the moment the sun began to rise over the horizon, all the tiredness [[melted away]]. The view was absolutely [[breathtaking]], with the sky shifting through shades of orange and pink, and a sea of clouds stretching out beneath us. It was a genuinely [[serene]] moment, and we stood there in near silence, simply taking it in. What made it so worthwhile was that we had earned that view through real effort. Honestly, that early start turned out to be the [[crowning moment]] of the whole trip. It taught me that sometimes the best moments require sacrificing a bit of comfort, and I would happily do it again.

followUps.q: Are you usually an early riser?
followUps.answer: Not naturally. On working days I get up around seven, which is early enough for me. At the weekend I try to sleep in a little, although the call to prayer usually wakes me anyway.

followUps.q: Do you think getting up early is good for people?
followUps.answer: For many people, yes. The morning is quiet and you can get a lot done before the day becomes busy. But I think it depends on the person, since some people genuinely work better at night.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?

Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?

Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?

A failure that ultimately taught me a great deal was when I performed poorly in an important exam early in my studies. It was a financial accounting exam in the first year of my BBA, and I came very close to failing it. I had been [[overconfident]] and had not prepared nearly as thoroughly as I should have. I had done well at college, so I assumed university would be just as easy, and I spent far too much time with friends. My classmates were surprised, because I had always seemed so relaxed about studying. When the results came out, I was genuinely [[crestfallen]], and it was a humbling experience. I remember phoning my father and struggling to tell him. At first I felt quite [[demoralised]], but after some reflection I realised the failure was entirely my own doing. Rather than dwelling on it, I decided to treat it as a [[wake-up call]]. I completely changed my study habits, becoming far more [[disciplined]] and organised, and I started reviewing my notes every evening instead of cramming at the last minute. The next time around, my results improved dramatically, which proved the lesson had sunk in. Honestly, that early failure was one of the most [[instructive]] experiences of my life. It taught me that setbacks are not the end of the world but valuable opportunities to grow. I now genuinely believe that how you respond to failure matters far more than the failure itself.

followUps.answer: Much more calmly than I expected. He told me that his business had failed more than once in the early years, and that what matters is getting back up. That conversation really helped.

followUps.answer: Yes, in small doses. Failing early, when the stakes are low, teaches you humility and resilience. People who never fail can struggle badly when something finally goes wrong later in life.

I spent hours researching places to visit and imagining what it would be like to see the Himalayas with my own eyes. Helping students travel abroad is my job, but this time it was finally my turn, which made it even more special. The night before departure I was so [[restless]] that I barely slept, and I checked my passport at least five times. My younger sister made me promise to bring her back a souvenir. When the day finally arrived and the plane took off, I felt a rush of pure [[exhilaration]]. The trip itself lived up to every expectation, filled with new sights, foods and experiences, especially the view of snow-capped mountains from Pokhara. What made the excitement so special was that it was building towards something I had dreamed about for years. Honestly, the joy of looking forward to it was almost as good as the trip itself. That experience taught me that anticipation is a wonderful part of any adventure. It remains one of the most [[unforgettable]] and genuinely [[thrilling]] experiences of my life.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy planning trips?
followUps.answer: Very much. Reading about a place, choosing where to stay and making a rough plan is half the fun for me. My friends usually leave the planning to me, which I don't mind at all.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a meal that, for me, sums up what Eid is really about. A special meal that stands out in my memory was a large family feast during Eid last year, prepared mostly by my mother and grandmother. We celebrated at my grandparents' home in our ancestral village, and the whole extended family gathered there, which is increasingly rare these days. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and children, and my uncles and cousins came too. My job was to help my grandfather greet the guests and make sure everyone had a seat. The table was [[laden with]] traditional dishes, like beef curry, chicken roast, polao and several kinds of sweets, and the aromas alone were [[mouthwatering]]. What made the meal so special was not just the food, though it was absolutely delicious, but the sense of togetherness. We spent hours eating, talking and laughing, with several generations gathered around one table, from my grandfather in his eighties to my four-year-old nephew. There is something deeply [[comforting]] about a home-cooked meal shared with people you love. In our busy lives, such [[unhurried]] gatherings feel genuinely precious. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by family and good food. After lunch, the older men sat in the courtyard drinking tea while the children played. Honestly, meals like that are about far more than eating; they are about connection and belonging. It is a [[treasured]] memory, and it reminds me that the best meals are the ones shared with the people who matter most. I am already looking forward to the next Eid.

followUps.q: Can you cook any of those dishes yourself?
followUps.answer: Only a simple chicken curry, I am afraid. The Eid dishes take real skill and a lot of time, so I leave them to my mother and grandmother and happily do the washing up instead.

followUps.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
followUps.answer: At home, definitely. Restaurants are nice for a change, but nothing compares to my mother's cooking, and eating together at home feels far more relaxed and personal.

part3Samples.q: How important is food to a country's culture?
part3Samples.answer: Food is absolutely central to culture, in my view. It is far more than mere [[sustenance]]; it reflects a nation's history, geography, values and social customs. Sharing a meal is a universal expression of hospitality and community. Traditional dishes carry deep [[sentimental]] and cultural significance, passed down through generations. So I would say cuisine is one of the most [[tangible]] and beloved expressions of a country's identity.

part3Samples.q: How have people's eating habits changed over the years?
part3Samples.answer: Eating habits have changed considerably. In the past, people mostly ate home-cooked, seasonal and local food, often together as a family. Today, busy lifestyles have led to more processed food, takeaways and eating [[on the go]], often alone. [[Portion sizes]] have grown, and international cuisine is now widely available. While this offers more variety and convenience, I think it has come at some cost to health and the [[communal]] nature of dining.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fast food has become so popular?
part3Samples.answer: Its popularity comes down to a few key factors. Firstly, it is convenient and quick, which suits our increasingly busy, time-poor lifestyles. Secondly, it is relatively cheap and consistently tasty, engineered to appeal to our [[cravings]]. Aggressive marketing has also made it [[ubiquitous]] and aspirational. Unfortunately, this convenience comes at a cost, as many argue its popularity has contributed to rising rates of [[obesity]] and related health problems.

part3Samples.q: How do you think the way we eat will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant changes driven by health and sustainability concerns. Plant-based diets and [[alternative proteins]], like lab-grown meat, are likely to become far more [[mainstream]] as we address the environmental impact of food. Technology may also personalise nutrition. Hopefully, there will be a renewed appreciation for healthy, [[sustainable]] eating. So our diets may become more conscious and innovative, balancing convenience with health and the planet.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to encourage people to eat more healthily?
part3Samples.answer: A range of measures could help. Education about nutrition from a young age is fundamental, so people can make informed choices. Making healthy food more affordable and accessible, while perhaps [[taxing unhealthy options]], can shift behaviour. Clear [[food labelling]] and restrictions on junk food advertising, especially to children, would also help. Ultimately, creating an environment where the healthy choice is the easy, [[appealing]] choice is the most effective approach.

part3Samples.q: Some say festivals have become too commercial. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this observation. Many festivals now seem dominated by advertising, sales and pressure to spend, which can [[overshadow]] their original cultural or spiritual meaning. The focus has shifted, in some cases, from [[togetherness]] to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an [[irreversible]] one.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my first visit to Dhaka, which made a lasting impression on me. A first visit that I still remember vividly was my trip to the capital when I was about seventeen, which was surprising since it is only a few hours from Sirajganj by road. I went there with my father for a short admission coaching course, and everything about it felt new and slightly [[overwhelming]] at first. The city was enormous, fast-paced and far busier than my quiet hometown, with endless traffic, crowds and noise. We stayed with a relative in Mirpur, and I remember standing on the roof at night, amazed by how many lights there were. Once I got my bearings, though, I found it genuinely [[exhilarating]]. I spent my free time exploring historical sites, markets and museums, soaking it all in, often with a cousin who lived there as my guide. I especially loved the old part of the city, with its narrow lanes, rickshaws and centuries-old buildings. What struck me most was the sheer diversity of people and experiences packed into one place. I found the whole experience thoroughly [[eye-opening]], and it [[broadened my horizons]] considerably. Honestly, visiting somewhere completely unfamiliar reminded me how much there is to discover beyond your own small world. Although it was a little daunting at times, I came away feeling more [[self-assured]] and independent. It made me eager to explore even more new places, and a couple of years later I went back there to study.

followUps.q: How often do you go to Dhaka now?
followUps.answer: Fairly often, maybe once every month or two. My elder sister lives there with her family, and I also go for work sometimes, to attend education fairs or meet university representatives.

followUps.q: Would you prefer to live in Dhaka or in your hometown?
followUps.answer: My hometown, at least for now. Dhaka has more opportunities, but it is exhausting and crowded. In Sirajganj life is calmer, and I can walk by the river whenever I like.

part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I did for my father, who has always put his family first. A time I went out of my way to make someone happy was when I organised a small surprise for him on his retirement last year. He had run a small business for over thirty years, often putting the family's needs before his own, so I wanted to do something meaningful. He is quite a modest man, and I knew he would never ask for any kind of celebration himself. With help from my mother and sisters, I secretly gathered old friends, relatives and a few of his long-time customers, and arranged a modest gathering at home to honour him. My mother cooked his favourite dishes, and my younger sister made a small album of old photos from his shop. The look of genuine surprise and joy on his face was absolutely [[priceless]]. He was clearly [[touched]] that so many people had come to celebrate him, and at one point his voice broke as he thanked everyone. What made it so special was seeing someone who rarely asks for anything finally being appreciated. Honestly, the whole thing was as rewarding for me as it was for him. There is a unique kind of happiness that comes from making someone else feel [[valued]]. It reminded me that thoughtful gestures often mean far more than expensive gifts. Seeing him so [[at peace]] that evening is a memory I will always [[treasure]], and it deepened our bond.

followUps.q: How does your father spend his time now that he has retired?
followUps.answer: He reads the newspaper for hours, visits his friends at the local tea stall and spends a lot of time in the village with my grandparents. He seems more relaxed than I have ever seen him.

followUps.q: Do you often do things to make your family happy?
followUps.answer: I try to. Usually it is small things, like bringing home sweets or taking my mother to visit her parents. I think those little gestures matter more than big occasions.

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a disagreement during my BBA that ended far better than I expected. A time I reached a hard-won agreement was during a group project when a classmate and I had fundamentally different visions for the final result. We were designing a business plan for a small café, and I wanted to focus on low prices for students, while he wanted a more upmarket place with a stylish design. Initially, neither of us was willing to [[budge]], and the disagreement threatened to [[derail]] the entire project. The tension was uncomfortable, and progress [[ground to a halt]], which was frustrating for the rest of the group. Eventually I suggested we step back and actually listen to each other's reasoning properly, so we met one evening over tea to talk it through. The rest of the group were clearly relieved to see us talking calmly again. Once we did, I realised his idea had genuine merit that I had dismissed too quickly. Through calm discussion, we managed to blend both approaches into something better than either original plan: affordable food in a comfortable, attractive setting. Reaching that [[compromise]] required real humility on both sides, but it was worth it. What I learned was that being stubborn rarely helps, whereas being flexible often leads to a superior outcome. Honestly, the final result was far stronger for having combined our ideas, and I felt relieved and quite proud. It taught me that the best solutions often emerge from disagreement, provided both people are willing to be [[level-headed]] and open-minded.

followUps.q: Are you still friends with that classmate?
followUps.answer: Yes, we actually became good friends after that project. He now works for a bank in Dhaka, and we still joke about our imaginary café whenever we meet up.

followUps.q: Do you find it easy to change your mind?
followUps.answer: Easier than I used to. When someone gives me a good reason, I am happy to change my view. What I find harder is admitting it straight away, but I am working on that.

part3Samples.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
part3Samples.answer: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be [[constructive]] if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. There is growing awareness of the importance of emotional intelligence and communication skills, which are increasingly taught in schools and workplaces. If this trend continues, future generations may be better [[equipped]] to handle disagreements. On the other hand, online communication can sometimes make people more [[polarised]] and less willing to [[compromise]], so it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What is the best way to resolve a serious disagreement?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective approach usually involves calm, honest dialogue where both sides genuinely listen to one another. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a [[neutral third party]] as a [[mediator]] can be [[invaluable]]. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a performance that completely changed how I think about music. A time I was genuinely impressed was when I went to a large classical music festival in Dhaka with my elder sister and her husband a few years ago. I had always enjoyed music, but I had never experienced anything on that scale in person. The festival ran through the night in a huge open-air venue, with thousands of people sitting on the ground and listening in near silence. We had brought a thin mat and a flask of tea, like most of the people around us. From the moment the performance began, I was completely [[captivated]]. The sheer skill of the musicians, a sitar player and a tabla player responding to each other in perfect harmony, was absolutely [[remarkable]]. What impressed me most was the emotion they managed to convey purely through their instruments, with no words at all. The sound was so rich and powerful that I felt it [[resonate]] in my chest. It was a genuinely [[mesmerising]] experience, quite unlike listening to a recording on my phone. I came away with a whole new appreciation for the years of discipline behind such a performance, since musicians like that often train from childhood. Honestly, it left me feeling deeply [[moved]], and it reminded me of the extraordinary things humans can achieve through dedication. By the time we left, the sun was coming up, and I was tired but completely inspired. I have been eager to attend more live performances ever since.

followUps.q: What kind of music do you usually listen to?
followUps.answer: Mostly Bengali songs, both old classics and some modern bands, and a bit of English pop. I listen while walking by the river in the evening, which is probably my favourite time for music.

followUps.q: Have you ever wanted to learn a musical instrument?
followUps.answer: Yes, the tabla, after that festival. I never actually started, though, because I didn't have the time. Perhaps one day, when life is a little less busy, I will finally give it a try.
