part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the most adventurous thing I have ever done, which was a trek in the hills of Bandarban. An adventurous thing I did that pushed me well outside my comfort zone was going on a fairly challenging trek to Keokradong, one of the highest peaks in Bangladesh, with a group of four friends from university. It was about two years ago, in the dry season, when the paths are safer. I am not the most outdoorsy person, so agreeing to it was already a stretch for me. The trail was steep and [[gruelling]] in places, and at several points I genuinely wondered whether I could make it. My legs ached and my lungs burned, but my friends kept [[egging me on]]. We stopped in small villages along the way, where local people offered us water and bananas, which was incredibly kind. We spent the night in a simple guesthouse beside a lake on the way. Reaching the summit after hours of effort was absolutely [[exhilarating]], and the [[panoramic]] view of endless green hills was more than worth it. What made it so rewarding was proving to myself that I was tougher than I had believed. Honestly, I surprised myself with how much I enjoyed the challenge, despite the discomfort. That experience gave me a real taste for adventure and a newfound confidence in my own [[resilience]]. It taught me that stepping outside your comfort zone, while difficult, is often where the most memorable experiences are found. My mother, of course, was relieved to see me home in one piece.

followUps.q: Would you do something like that again?
followUps.answer: Yes, I think so, although I would train a bit beforehand this time. My friends have been talking about a trek in Nepal, and I would love to join them if work allows.

followUps.q: Do you think young people today are adventurous enough?
followUps.answer: Some are very adventurous, but many spend most of their free time on screens. I think a little adventure, even something small, builds confidence in a way that nothing online can.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about learning to drive, which tested my patience more than almost anything else. A time I had to keep pushing through real difficulty was while learning to drive about two years ago, which I found far harder than I had expected. I wanted to learn because my father had recently retired and was no longer comfortable driving long distances, so someone in the family needed to take the car to the village. The roads here are full of rickshaws, buses and people crossing without warning, so even a short drive felt stressful. I struggled with confidence behind the wheel and failed my first test, which was genuinely [[disheartening]]. Part of me was tempted to give up entirely and rely on buses and rickshaws instead. However, I knew driving would be a valuable skill, so I forced myself to [[persevere]]. I booked more lessons, practised early in the mornings when the roads were quiet and slowly [[chipped away at]] my nervousness. Progress was frustratingly slow at times, and it required a lot of [[patience]]. When I finally passed on my second attempt, the sense of accomplishment was immense, precisely because it had not come easily. Honestly, that experience taught me the value of [[persistence]] more than almost anything else. It proved that giving up at the first setback would have cost me a skill I now use regularly. My grandparents are always delighted when I drive my parents to visit them, and I have carried that lesson into other challenges ever since.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy driving now?
followUps.answer: On quiet roads, yes, especially the drive to my grandparents' village, which passes through lovely green fields. In busy town traffic, though, I still find it more tiring than enjoyable.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important for young people to learn to drive?
followUps.answer: It is useful, but not essential for everyone. In big cities, public transport or ride-sharing can be easier. In smaller towns, though, being able to drive gives you a lot more independence.

part3Samples.q: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?
part3Samples.answer: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely [[outdated]], especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn [[keeps the mind sharp]], opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a [[lifelong pursuit]], not a phase.

part3Samples.q: Is it easier to learn when you are young or when you are older?
part3Samples.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

part3Samples.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
part3Samples.answer: It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer [[subsidies]] or learning accounts. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

part3Samples.q: Some say cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree with this, at least for private cars in the busiest central areas. Many cities that have [[pedestrianised]] their centres seem to have seen reduced pollution, safer streets and more vibrant public life, which is very appealing. However, it must be done carefully, ensuring excellent public transport alternatives and access for deliveries and those with disabilities. So rather than a [[blanket ban]], I support significantly restricting cars to create more [[liveable]], people-friendly centres.

That was when I completed my BBA, just before I started my job at an education consultancy. It is not particularly expensive, but its [[sentimental]] value is enormous. It has a dark blue body with a thin silver clip, and it writes beautifully. He handed it to me with a short note saying he hoped I would use it to sign many important documents in my career. I remember reading the note twice with a [[lump in my throat]]. What made it so special was the [[thoughtfulness]] behind it, rather than the object itself. My father ran a small business for over thirty years, and I think he knew better than anyone how much a signature can carry. My father is not a man of many words, so this gesture was genuinely [[touching]]. I keep it safely on my desk and use it only on special occasions. In fact, I used it to sign my first employment contract, which felt like keeping a small promise to him. Every time I hold it, I am reminded of his quiet faith in me. Honestly, it is the kind of gift that grows more [[precious]] with time. I think the best presents are those that carry meaning and memory, not just a high price tag. This pen is something I intend to keep for the rest of my life and perhaps pass on one day.

followUps.q: Do you still use the pen?
followUps.answer: Yes, but only for important things, like signing contracts or writing Eid cards. I'm quite careful with it, because refilling a fountain pen and cleaning it properly takes a bit of patience.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think everyone has the right to affordable housing?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe that access to decent, affordable housing is a [[fundamental human right]], not a privilege. Shelter is a basic need, and stable housing is the foundation upon which people build healthy, productive lives. When housing becomes unaffordable, it drives inequality, homelessness and [[hardship]]. So I think governments have a clear responsibility to ensure that housing is available and affordable to all, treating it as an essential rather than a mere [[commodity]].

part3Samples.q: Is it better to rent or to own a home?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their advantages, depending on circumstances. Owning a home offers stability, security and the chance to build wealth over time, which is why many [[aspire to]] it. Renting, however, offers greater flexibility and freedom from the burdens of maintenance and large [[mortgages]], which suits those who value mobility. So there is no universal answer; it depends on one's financial situation, life stage and how much stability versus flexibility one [[prioritises]].

part3Samples.q: Why is housing so expensive in many cities?
part3Samples.answer: The high cost is driven by a fundamental imbalance between supply and demand. As people [[flock to]] cities for work, demand for housing soars, while the supply of new homes often fails to keep pace due to limited land and slow construction. Property speculation and foreign investment can also inflate prices. So it is largely a matter of high demand meeting [[constrained]] supply, made worse by [[speculation]], pushing prices beyond ordinary people's reach.

part3Samples.q: How do you think housing will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate several developments. To address shortages and sustainability, we may see more compact, [[high-density]] and eco-friendly housing, along with innovative solutions like modular or [[prefabricated]] homes. Smart-home technology will likely become standard. There may also be a shift towards [[co-living]] arrangements, especially in expensive cities. So future housing may become smaller and denser, but hopefully smarter, greener and more affordable, adapting to modern needs.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to make housing more affordable?
part3Samples.answer: Increasing the supply of housing is fundamental, particularly affordable and social housing built by governments. Reforming planning regulations to allow more construction can help. Measures to [[curb]] speculation, such as taxes on empty properties, may also [[cool prices]]. Rent controls and support for first-time buyers are other options. Essentially, treating housing as a basic need rather than a pure [[investment vehicle]] is key to keeping it accessible and fair.

part3Samples.q: Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly disagree with this narrow view. While money is a tangible and convenient measure, and financial security certainly matters, equating it with success ignores far more important dimensions of a good life. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. True success, in my view, is measured by fulfilment, relationships and character, not currency.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something small that I keep in a drawer beside my bed. An object with deep sentimental value to me is an old wristwatch that belonged to my grandfather. He wore it for decades, and a few years ago, when the small dial became hard for him to read, he took it off his wrist and gave it to me. He lives in our ancestral village not far from Sirajganj, and I still remember him pressing it into my hand during one of our visits and telling me to look after it better than he had. So I've had it for about four years now. The watch itself is fairly worn and no longer even keeps perfect time, yet I would not trade it for anything. The leather strap is cracked and the glass has a tiny scratch across it, but I've deliberately never had it polished. What makes it so [[precious]] is the memories it carries; I remember him glancing at it constantly throughout my childhood. Holding it now brings back a flood of warm, [[nostalgic]] feelings. It is a [[tangible connection]] to a man I love and admire deeply. He is in his eighties now but still remarkably sharp, and he always asks whether I'm taking care of it. I keep it safely stored and only take it out occasionally, almost like a [[relic]]. Honestly, its emotional worth is completely disconnected from its monetary value. I think objects like this become [[irreplaceable]] precisely because of the people and memories attached to them. One day I hope to pass it on to my own children, along with the stories of the wonderful man who gave it to me.

followUps.q: Do you ever wear the watch?
followUps.answer: Only occasionally, usually when I visit my grandfather. He always notices straight away and smiles, which makes it feel like a small, shared ritual between the two of us.

followUps.answer: Perhaps not always. Many young people prefer new things, but I think we [[come to appreciate]] old objects later in life, once we understand the memories and stories behind them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite [[pronounced]], largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to [[tension]], though it also brings a healthy [[diversity]] of perspectives.

part3Samples.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are quite [[stark]]. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

part3Samples.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
part3Samples.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I lost a couple of years ago, which still bothers me a little when I think about it. Something important I once lost was a small notebook in which I had jotted down ideas and personal reflections for over a year. It was a plain brown notebook, but it held everything from favourite quotations to plans for my career and thoughts about studying abroad. I must have left it somewhere while travelling, and by the time I realised, it was gone. I was coming back from Dhaka on a crowded bus after visiting my sister, and I think it slipped out of my bag when I [[dozed off]]. I was genuinely [[distraught]], because its contents were irreplaceable and deeply personal. I retraced my steps and asked around, but sadly it never turned up. I even phoned the bus company and went back to the ticket counter the next day, but nobody had handed anything in. For days I felt a real [[sense of loss]], almost as though I had lost a part of myself. What upset me most was that no amount of money could recover what was written inside. Eventually I had to [[come to terms with]] the fact that it was gone and try to move on. The experience taught me a valuable lesson about backing things up and being more careful with things that matter. These days I keep my notes on my laptop as well as on paper. Honestly, it still stings a little when I think about it. It made me realise how [[attached]] we can become to seemingly ordinary objects, simply because of what they represent to us.

followUps.answer: Much more careful now than I used to be. After losing that notebook, I always double-check my bag before getting off a bus, and I keep important things in one zipped pocket.

part3Samples.q: Why is honesty important in relationships?
part3Samples.answer: Honesty is really the [[bedrock]] of any healthy relationship. Without it, trust cannot exist, and trust is what allows people to feel safe and secure with one another. Even small lies, once discovered, can [[erode]] that foundation and breed suspicion. In my view, being truthful, even when it is difficult, is what gives a relationship genuine depth and [[resilience]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people are more or less honest than they were in the past?
part3Samples.answer: That is a difficult question. I do not think human nature has fundamentally changed, but the opportunities for [[deception]] have multiplied with technology, from online scams to fake identities. At the same time, the internet has made it much harder to hide dishonesty, since [[misdeeds]] are quickly exposed. So perhaps we are no less honest, just more [[transparent]].

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when trust in institutions breaks down?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences are deeply damaging. When people lose faith in institutions like government or the media, it breeds [[cynicism]] and division. I know progress would be slow at first, requiring real [[perseverance]]. Still, the thought of one day being able to play a piece I love is genuinely exciting. I think playing an instrument would also be a wonderful way to relax and express myself. I can even imagine playing simple tunes for my little nephew when my elder sister visits from Dhaka. Honestly, I believe it would be a hugely [[fulfilling]] hobby that I could enjoy for the rest of my life. It is definitely something I intend to make time for once my schedule allows.

followUps.q: Did you learn any music at school?
followUps.answer: Very little, apart from singing the national anthem and a few songs for cultural programmes. Music wasn't really treated as a serious subject, which I think was a [[missed opportunity]].

followUps.q: Is there any other instrument you'd like to learn?
followUps.answer: Perhaps the harmonium, because it's so central to traditional Bengali music. My grandmother loves old songs played on it, so learning it would let me play for her in the village.

part3: Why do you think music is important to people?
How has the way people listen to music changed?
What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?

Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

The sky was painted in layers of orange and gold, and the water reflected every shade of it. Honestly, it reminded me of the quiet countryside around my grandparents' village, and of evening walks along the Jamuna, which made it feel personal. followUps.q: Have you ever tried painting yourself?
followUps.answer: Only at school, and the results were quite [[underwhelming]]. I enjoy looking at art far more than creating it, although I'd like to try sketching one day, just to relax.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I pick up every single morning before I leave home. An object I genuinely use every single day is my backpack, which has become an essential part of my routine. It's a plain black one made of tough, water-resistant material, which is very handy during the monsoon. It carries everything I need for the day, from my laptop and documents to my water bottle and other essentials. What makes it so useful is how practical and well-organised it is, with plenty of compartments. I keep students' files in the main section, my laptop in a padded sleeve, and small things like keys, pens and a charger in the front pocket, so I never waste time searching for anything. It is comfortable to carry even when heavily loaded, which is genuinely [[invaluable]] during long commutes. I have had it for several years now, and it has proved remarkably [[durable]] despite constant use. My elder sister gave it to me when I started my final year at university, so it has been with me through exams, job interviews and my first years at the consultancy. Honestly, I rely on it so much that I would feel completely lost without it. It might seem like an ordinary object, but it plays a surprisingly important role in keeping my day organised. Over the years it has become a bit worn, but I have grown quite [[attached]] to it. I think it is a perfect example of how the most [[mundane]] objects often turn out to be the most useful ones in daily life.

followUps.q: Would you buy a new backpack soon?
followUps.answer: Not unless it breaks. One of the zips is starting to stick, but I'd rather get it repaired, because it still does its job perfectly and I know exactly where everything goes.

followUps.q: Do you usually carry a lot with you?
followUps.answer: Probably more than I need. Between my laptop, student files, a charger and my water bottle, it gets quite heavy, so I'm trying to [[travel lighter]] and keep more documents digitally.

How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say sustainable products are too expensive for ordinary people. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is some truth to this currently, though it is changing. It is true that some sustainable products, like organic food or electric cars, carry a higher [[price tag]], which can put them [[out of reach]] for those on tight budgets. This is a real barrier to [[widespread adoption]]. However, as demand grows and technology improves, prices are steadily falling. So while cost is a genuine obstacle today, I believe sustainability is becoming increasingly affordable and accessible.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I hope to own in the next few years. A vehicle I would love to own one day is a reliable, fuel-efficient car, ideally something practical rather than flashy. I'm thinking of a small family car with enough room for my parents and my younger sister. Even in a modest town like Sirajganj, having my own car would make daily life significantly more [[convenient]]. The main reason I want one is the freedom it offers; I would no longer depend on crowded public transport or unreliable schedules. At the moment, getting anywhere means haggling with rickshaw drivers or squeezing onto packed buses, especially on the long journey to Dhaka. I imagine using it for my daily commute and for weekend trips out of town, which I rarely manage now. Above all, I'd use it to drive my parents to my grandparents' village home, which we visit often, and to see my elder sister and her children in Dhaka whenever we like. What appeals to me most is the sense of [[independence]] it would bring. I would probably choose something environmentally friendly, since fuel efficiency matters to me. Owning a car would feel like a real [[milestone]], a sign of stability and progress. I think my father, who worked so hard for so many years, would be especially proud to sit in the passenger seat. Honestly, though it is a considerable expense, I think it would genuinely improve my quality of life. It is a goal I am steadily working towards, and I know the sense of freedom would make it thoroughly [[worthwhile]].

followUps.q: Can you drive at the moment?
followUps.answer: Not very well, honestly. I've had a few lessons from a cousin, but I'd need proper training before driving on our roads, because traffic can be quite [[unpredictable]], especially on the highways.

followUps.q: Would you prefer an electric car?
followUps.answer: Ideally, yes, because it would be better for the environment. But charging points are still rare outside the big cities here, so for now a fuel-efficient car seems far more realistic.

part3Samples.q: Do you think public transport should be free?
part3Samples.answer: I find the idea appealing, though it is complex. Making public transport free could reduce traffic, cut pollution and help [[lower-income]] people enormously, which are [[compelling]] social benefits. However, it would be extremely expensive to fund and might lead to overcrowding or reduced service quality without careful management. So while I support [[heavily subsidising]] it to keep it affordable, whether it should be entirely free depends on a country's priorities and budget.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
part3Samples.answer: Each has its merits, but from a societal viewpoint, public transport is clearly [[preferable]]. It is far more environmentally friendly, reduces congestion, and is cheaper for the user. Private cars, however, offer [[unmatched]] convenience, comfort and flexibility, especially where public transport is poor. So while I personally value the freedom of a car, I believe well-developed public transport is the more sustainable and [[equitable]] option for society as a whole.

part3Samples.q: What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
part3Samples.answer: Traffic congestion has serious and costly effects. It wastes an enormous amount of people's time, reducing productivity and quality of life. It significantly worsens air pollution, harming public health and the environment. It also causes frustration and stress for commuters and can [[hamper]] emergency services. Economically, the lost hours and fuel represent a huge [[drain]]. So congestion is far more than an inconvenience; it [[undermines]] a city's efficiency and wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think transport will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant transformation. Electric vehicles will likely become the norm, drastically cutting emissions, and [[autonomous]], self-driving cars may reshape how we travel. Cities will probably invest more in cycling, walking and clean public transport. Concepts like [[shared mobility]] could reduce car ownership. So the future of transport is likely to be cleaner, smarter and more [[integrated]], hopefully making our cities less polluted and more liveable.

part3Samples.q: How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
part3Samples.answer: A combination of measures is most effective. Investing heavily in reliable, affordable public transport gives people a genuine alternative to driving. Encouraging cycling and walking through better [[infrastructure]] helps too. Some cities use [[congestion charging]] to [[discourage]] car use in busy areas. Better urban planning that reduces the need to travel far is also valuable. Essentially, the solution lies in making sustainable options more attractive than driving, rather than simply widening roads.

part3Samples.q: Some say factories should be moved away from residential areas. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this as a sensible measure. Locating polluting factories away from where people live can significantly reduce residents' [[direct exposure]] to harmful air and water pollution, protecting public health. However, it is not a complete solution, as pollution still spreads, and it may simply [[shift the burden]] to another community. So while separating industry from homes is beneficial, it must be combined with actually reducing the pollution [[at its source]].

Something I once borrowed that proved incredibly useful was a professional camera I borrowed from a close friend for a family event. The event was a small gathering we held at home when my father retired after running his business for over thirty years. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her family, and my grandparents travelled in from the village, so I knew it was a day worth remembering. I had wanted to capture the occasion properly but could not justify buying an expensive camera for a single day. My friend, who is a keen photographer, generously offered to lend me his, which was very [[considerate]] of him. I was slightly nervous about handling such a valuable and [[delicate]] piece of equipment. He kindly gave me a quick lesson on how to use it, which I really appreciated. The photos it produced were of a quality I could never have achieved with my phone, so I was genuinely [[grateful]]. My favourite is a shot of my father laughing with my grandfather, which now sits framed in our living room. I made sure to return it promptly and in perfect condition, as I did not want to [[betray his trust]]. I also printed a few of the best photos for him as a small thank-you. Honestly, the whole experience reminded me how valuable it is to have [[generous]] friends. It also made me consider eventually investing in a decent camera of my own.

followUps.answer: Not often. I don't like troubling people, so I only borrow when it's really necessary, and I always make sure I return things quickly and in the same condition.

followUps.q: Do you lend your own things to friends?
followUps.answer: Yes, usually books. I'm happy to lend them, although I've learnt to write my name inside the cover, because a few have [[mysteriously vanished]] over the years.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though I would add a small [[caveat]]. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

She gave it to me when I got my first job, during one of our visits to the village, and I have treasured it ever since. It is not particularly valuable in monetary terms, but its [[sentimental]] worth is immeasurable. The ring is quite plain and old-fashioned, yet that simplicity is part of its [[charm]]. I wear it on special occasions, such as Eid, weddings and family gatherings, and doing so makes me feel closely connected to her. My grandmother has very little formal education, but she is one of the wisest people I know, and when she gave it to me, she simply said that honest work deserved something honest to wear. Every time I put it on, it brings back warm memories of that afternoon on her veranda. What makes it so meaningful is that it is a [[tangible link]] to my family's past. Honestly, it is one of my most [[cherished]] possessions, precisely because of the memories attached to it rather than its appearance. I intend to look after it carefully and one day pass it on within the family. Items like this become genuinely [[irreplaceable]], carrying stories that no new purchase ever could.

followUps.answer: Not much, generally. A simple silver ring or a watch is quite common, but most men keep it modest. Women, on the other hand, often wear beautiful gold jewellery at weddings and festivals.

followUps.q: Would you ever sell it?
followUps.answer: Never, no matter how much someone offered. It's not about the money at all; selling it would feel like giving away a piece of my family's history, and my grandmother would be [[heartbroken]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. It also means my mother no longer has to carry heavy bags back from the bazaar in the heat. This frees up time I can then spend on work or relaxation, which matters enormously to me. Honestly, it has completely transformed how I manage my errands. I am aware there is a slight risk of becoming overly [[reliant]] on such conveniences, but used sensibly it is a genuine time-saver. I still enjoy going to the local market now and then, because there is something about [[haggling]] with the vegetable sellers that no app can replace. In a fast-paced world where time is arguably our most precious resource, tools like this are extremely welcome. part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

part3Samples.q: How important is it for people to follow the news?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is quite important for people to stay reasonably informed, as it is part of being an engaged citizen. Understanding current events helps us make sense of the world and participate in democracy. However, I would add a [[caveat]]; consuming too much news, especially negative or sensational content, can be [[overwhelming]] and [[anxiety-inducing]]. So the ideal is to stay informed through reliable sources without becoming obsessed.

part3Samples.q: How has the way people get news changed over the years?
part3Samples.answer: The change has been revolutionary. In the past, people relied on scheduled TV bulletins and printed newspapers, receiving curated news once or twice a day. Now, news is constant, instant and consumed largely through social media and online sources. This has made news more accessible, but also more [[fragmented]] and harder to verify. The rise of citizen journalism is a benefit, but so too is the spread of [[unverified]], [[sensational]] content.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fake news spreads so easily?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. Social media algorithms tend to prioritise engaging content, and false or sensational stories are often more [[provocative]] than the truth. People also share things impulsively without verifying them, especially if they confirm existing beliefs. The lack of traditional editorial gatekeepers online means misinformation can spread [[unchecked]]. Combined with a general decline in media literacy, this creates the perfect conditions for falsehoods to [[proliferate]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional newspapers will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: In their printed form, I think they will largely decline, as younger generations consume news almost entirely online. However, I do not believe quality journalism itself will disappear; rather, it will continue its shift to digital platforms and subscription models. The [[reputable]] news organisations behind the papers may well [[endure]], just in a different format. So the printed page may fade, but the institution of journalism should [[persist]].

part3Samples.q: What can be done to combat the spread of misinformation?
part3Samples.answer: Tackling this requires a combined effort. Improving media literacy so people can critically [[evaluate]] sources is perhaps the most important long-term solution. Social media platforms must also take greater responsibility, using fact-checking and adjusting algorithms that reward sensationalism. Supporting quality, independent journalism is equally vital. Ultimately, an informed, [[sceptical]] public is the best defence against the [[tide of misinformation]].

I have held onto it for well over a decade now, moving it carefully from one flat to another whenever my family moved. These days it lives in a drawer in my desk. It contains my youthful thoughts, dreams and daily events, which are often [[amusing]] to read back now. There's one entry where I announced very seriously that I would become a famous cricketer, and another describing an argument with my younger sister over the last piece of a mango. I have kept it because it is a genuine [[time capsule]] of who I once was. Whenever I flick through it, I feel a wave of [[nostalgia]] for a simpler time in my life. What makes it so precious is that no amount of money could recreate those honest, [[unfiltered]] memories. It is fascinating, and occasionally [[embarrassing]], to see how much my perspective has changed. Honestly, I think keeping such personal records is genuinely valuable. It reminds me of how far I have come and grounds me in my own history. I fully intend to keep it for the rest of my life; it is far too [[meaningful]] to ever throw away.

followUps.answer: Not a daily one, sadly. Life got busier, but I still jot down my thoughts in a notebook now and then, especially after important events, because I know I'll enjoy [[looking back on]] them later.

followUps.q: Would you let anyone read your old diary?
followUps.answer: Only my younger sister, and only certain pages. Some entries are far too embarrassing, although we had a good laugh when she found the one about our argument over the mango.

Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?

However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, [[job insecurity]] and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the [[hardships]] have shifted in nature.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?

People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

I'd probably go back to writing things down in a notebook, keeping important numbers on paper and visiting people in person more often, which might not be such a bad thing. part3Samples.q: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: On the whole, I think they have, though not without significant drawbacks. Smartphones have put a world of information, communication and services in our pockets, which is genuinely empowering and convenient. However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of [[dependence]] that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them [[consciously]] rather than [[compulsively]].

part3Samples.q: How was life different before smartphones?
part3Samples.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.

part3Samples.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely [[impair]] both our mental and physical wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more [[anticipatory]] and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to [[blur]] further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

part3Samples.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
part3Samples.answer: There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. part3Samples.q: Some say technology is making face-to-face conversation a dying skill. Do you agree?

It is certainly true that some young people, accustomed to texting, can feel awkward in direct conversation and may struggle to read social cues. However, humans are inherently social, and the need for real connection persists. So the skill may be underused and in need of [[nurturing]], but I do not believe it will ever become [[obsolete]].

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something you can see at almost every celebration in Bangladesh. An object of real cultural importance in my country is the traditional handloom sari, which carries deep significance. It is far more than a piece of clothing; it is a symbol of our heritage and identity. Woven by skilled artisans, each one is a genuine work of [[craftsmanship]], often taking days or even weeks to complete. The finest example is probably the jamdani, a delicate, almost transparent cotton sari whose weaving tradition has been recognised internationally. Women wear handloom saris at weddings, at Eid and especially at Pohela Boishakh, when the streets are full of red and white. They are also given as gifts at important family moments. I have known about it my whole life, having seen the women in my family wear them at every important occasion. My mother keeps a few folded carefully in her cupboard for special days, and since Sirajganj has a long tradition of handloom weaving, I've often seen weavers at work in nearby villages. What makes it so important is that it represents a centuries-old tradition that is sadly [[under threat]] from mass production. Wearing one on special days feels like honouring our [[ancestry]]. The intricate designs are genuinely [[exquisite]], and no two are ever identical. Honestly, I think it is vital that we protect such traditional crafts before they disappear. They connect us to our roots in a tangible way. I feel a real sense of pride whenever I see this beautiful item being worn and celebrated.

followUps.q: Have you ever bought a sari for someone?
followUps.answer: Yes, I bought a handloom sari for my mother last Eid. Choosing one was surprisingly difficult, because there were so many beautiful designs, but she loved the colour I picked.

followUps.q: Do young women in Bangladesh still wear saris?
followUps.answer: Yes, especially on special occasions like Pohela Boishakh and weddings. For everyday life, many prefer the salwar kameez, which is more practical, but the sari is still [[deeply cherished]].

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?

However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?

Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is considerable truth to this, though it is not the whole picture. It is often argued that wealthy nations and large corporations reap the greatest rewards, while poorer countries may suffer exploitation and cultural erosion. The benefits are undeniably [[unevenly]] distributed. However, globalisation has arguably also lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty in developing nations. So while the [[playing field]] is far from level, I would not say the benefits are exclusively for the [[privileged]].

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I brought back to life last year. Something I managed to repair myself was an old bicycle that had been sitting unused for years because of a series of faults. It was the bike I used to ride to school, and it had been gathering dust in a corner of our building's parking area ever since. The tyres were flat, the chain was rusted and the brakes barely worked. One of the pedals was also loose, so it made an awful clicking sound whenever anyone tried to ride it. Rather than throwing it away or paying for repairs, I decided to attempt to fix it myself, which was rather [[ambitious]] given my limited skills. I watched several tutorials, bought a few basic parts and set about it patiently over a weekend. I patched the inner tubes, scrubbed the rust off the chain and oiled it, then replaced the brake pads and tightened everything I could find. The bicycle mechanic near our local market kindly lent me a special tool when I got stuck. The process was more [[fiddly]] than I expected, and there were moments of real frustration. But gradually, piece by piece, the bicycle came back to life. When I finally took it for a ride along the river, the sense of [[accomplishment]] was genuinely satisfying. What pleased me most was that I had saved money and rescued something from the [[scrap heap]]. Honestly, repairing it myself was far more [[rewarding]] than simply buying a new one. It gave me a real appreciation for fixing things rather than discarding them.

followUps.q: Do you still ride the bicycle?
followUps.answer: Yes, mostly for short trips around town and for evening rides along the river. It's also a nice way to get some exercise without having to go to a gym.

followUps.q: Do you usually repair things or replace them?
followUps.answer: I try to repair them where possible. It's cheaper, less wasteful and more satisfying, although with modern electronics that's getting harder, because many simply aren't designed to be [[repairable]].

part3Samples.q: What does it mean to live sustainably?
part3Samples.answer: To me, living sustainably means meeting our own needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. In practice, it involves being mindful of our consumption, reducing waste, and using resources efficiently and responsibly. It is about living within the planet's ecological limits rather than [[depleting]] them. Essentially, it is a shift from a throwaway, [[exploitative]] mindset to one of [[stewardship]] and long-term responsibility.

part3Samples.q: Are people more environmentally conscious now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, considerably so. Environmental awareness has grown enormously over recent decades, driven by scientific evidence, media coverage and visible impacts like extreme weather. Concepts like recycling, carbon footprints and sustainability are now part of everyday conversation, which was not the case a generation ago. However, I would add that awareness does not always [[translate into action]]. So people are certainly more [[conscious]], even if their behaviour has not fully [[caught up]].

part3Samples.q: Why is it hard for people to change to a more sustainable lifestyle?
part3Samples.answer: Several barriers make it difficult. Sustainable options are sometimes more expensive or less convenient than the alternatives, so cost and habit get in the way. Many people also feel their individual actions are [[insignificant]] against such a vast problem. Additionally, our entire economic system is built around consumption, making unsustainable choices the default. So it is a combination of practical obstacles, [[ingrained habits]] and a sense of [[powerlessness]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think future generations will live more sustainably?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful they will, partly [[out of necessity]]. As the impacts of unsustainable living become more severe, future generations will likely be forced to adapt. [[Encouragingly]], young people today already show strong environmental values and are pushing for change. Advances in green technology should also make sustainable living easier and cheaper. So I believe sustainability will increasingly become the norm rather than the exception, driven by both necessity and [[shifting values]].

part3Samples.q: How can governments encourage sustainable behaviour?
part3Samples.answer: Governments have powerful tools [[at their disposal]]. They can use financial incentives, like subsidies for renewable energy or electric cars, and taxes on pollution and waste to [[steer behaviour]]. Investing in sustainable infrastructure, such as public transport and recycling, makes green choices easier. Regulation and clear information, like [[carbon labelling]], also help. Essentially, by making the sustainable choice the easy, affordable and default option, governments can drive widespread change.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

I still remember my father bringing home Bengali adventure stories from the market, and I would read them again and again until the pages were falling out. These days I read almost every evening before bed, mostly non-fiction and the occasional novel, and on Fridays I sometimes manage a couple of hours with a cup of tea. What I love about it is how it allows me to escape into different worlds and [[broaden]] my knowledge at the same time. Reading is also wonderfully [[therapeutic]]; after a stressful day, losing myself in a good book helps me unwind completely. I tend to switch between history, biographies and books about psychology, so there is always something new to look forward to. Beyond entertainment, it has noticeably improved my vocabulary and the way I express myself, which really helps in my job, since I spend a lot of time writing to students and universities. Honestly, in an age dominated by screens, I think reading is an increasingly [[underrated]] pleasure. It costs very little yet offers enormous rewards. I always keep a book on my bedside table, and I feel slightly restless if I go too long without one. Looking back, those simple story books were a truly [[formative]] influence on me, and reading is a hobby I hope to keep for the rest of my life.

followUps.q: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
followUps.answer: Printed books, without a doubt. I like the feel of the paper and being able to scribble notes in the margins. I do read on my phone when travelling, but it never feels quite the same.

followUps.q: Would you like your family to read more?
followUps.answer: My younger sister already reads a lot, so she doesn't need encouragement. I'd love my nephew in Dhaka to develop the habit, though, so I always bring him a colourful picture book when I visit.
