part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

sample.answer: A skill I would really love to learn is public speaking, something I have always found rather [[daunting]]. I can talk comfortably to one student at a time, but standing in front of a room full of people is a completely different story. I want to learn it because being able to speak confidently in front of others is genuinely valuable, both professionally and personally. At the moment, the thought of addressing a large audience makes me quite nervous, and I would love to overcome that. In fact, my consultancy sometimes holds information sessions for students and parents, and I usually let my colleagues do the talking. I would probably start by joining a speaking club, where I could practise regularly in a supportive environment. There are a few groups like that in Dhaka, and some even meet online, which would suit someone living outside the capital like me. I might also record myself and watch it back, which sounds painful but would show me exactly what to improve. I know it would require stepping well outside my comfort zone and a good deal of [[perseverance]]. Still, I believe the reward would be immense. Being an effective communicator could open up all sorts of opportunities in my career, and it would make me far more [[articulate]] in meetings. Honestly, I think it is one of the most [[empowering]] skills a person can develop. It would also boost my confidence in everyday situations. It is definitely near the top of my list of things to work on once I have the time to commit to it properly.

followUps.q: Have you ever had to give a speech?
followUps.answer: Yes, once at my university farewell programme. I had to say a few words on behalf of my batch, and although my hands were shaking, everyone was kind, and I felt quite proud afterwards.

followUps.q: Do you think public speaking can be taught?
followUps.answer: I think so. Some people are naturally confident, but most good speakers have simply practised a lot. With honest feedback and regular practice, even a fairly [[reserved]] person can become comfortable in front of an audience.

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

For me, that field is education, and more specifically helping students from small towns like Sirajganj get into good universities abroad. This matters to me because I believe finding your work meaningful is essential to a happy life. I see many bright young people around me who have the ability but lack the right guidance, and I would love to help fill that gap. To achieve it, I am steadily developing my skills and gaining as much relevant experience as possible at the consultancy where I work. I also hope to do a master's degree abroad myself, so that I understand the whole journey first-hand. I know it will require patience and a lot of [[persistence]], as such things rarely happen overnight. I try to set myself small, [[attainable]] targets along the way to stay motivated. Honestly, the thought of one day doing work that I find genuinely [[fulfilling]] is incredibly motivating. If I achieved it, I think I would feel an enormous sense of pride and satisfaction, especially seeing former students thrive. It is not about wealth or status for me, but about purpose. I am fully aware the road will be [[arduous]], but I am prepared to put in the effort, because I believe it will be thoroughly worth it in the end.

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say people today change jobs too often. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not entirely agree that it is a problem. Changing jobs frequently is often a sensible way to gain diverse experience, increase pay and find a better fit, especially in a fast-changing economy. The old model of [[lifelong loyalty]] is somewhat [[outdated]]. That said, changing too often can look unstable to employers and prevent one from developing deep [[expertise]], so a degree of balance is wise.

sample.answer: A healthy habit I have developed over the past couple of years is going for a brisk walk every evening. I usually head down to the embankment along the Jamuna, not far from our flat, and walk for about forty minutes as the sun goes down. I started it during a stressful period when I needed a way to clear my head, and it quickly became a daily ritual. At the time, I was working long hours and hardly moving at all, and I could feel it affecting both my energy and my mood. What I love about it is that it is so simple yet genuinely [[beneficial]], both physically and mentally. After a long day at a desk, the fresh air and movement are wonderfully [[refreshing]]. It has noticeably improved my mood and helps me sleep far better at night. Sometimes my younger sister joins me, and we end up having the kind of relaxed conversations we rarely have at home. Honestly, this small habit has had a surprisingly [[profound]] effect on my overall wellbeing. I think habits like this are important because they are sustainable; unlike intense workouts, a daily walk is something you can [[sustain]] for years. It requires no equipment or gym membership, just a bit of consistency. I would genuinely recommend it to anyone. It has become one of the most valuable parts of my daily routine, and I would find it hard to give up now, especially on calm evenings when the river looks so [[tranquil]].

followUps.answer: Not always. When it is pouring, I sometimes walk up and down the stairs of our building instead, which my neighbours find rather amusing. But I try not to let the weather become an excuse.

followUps.q: Do you prefer walking alone or with someone?
followUps.answer: Mostly alone, because it gives me time to think things through. That said, walks with my sister or a friend are lovely too; they are just more about conversation than quiet [[reflection]].

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

I can swim, as I learned in my grandparents' village pond as a boy, but I would need to build up my stamina and get used to breathing through the equipment. I imagine my first dive would be both terrifying and [[exhilarating]] in equal measure. I have watched countless videos of divers gliding past shoals of fish, and I always find myself wishing I were there. There is something about entering a completely different environment that appeals to my sense of curiosity. Honestly, I think it would be an [[unforgettable]] experience, quite unlike anything I have done before. Of course, it requires overcoming a certain amount of fear, but I think that is part of the appeal. It is firmly on my list of things to do, and I am [[resolved]] to try it one day.

followUps.q: Would you go diving alone or with friends?
followUps.answer: Definitely with friends, and of course with a qualified instructor. Sharing something that nerve-racking with people you know makes it less frightening, and it gives you a story to laugh about together afterwards.

followUps.q: Is scuba diving popular in your country?
followUps.answer: Not really, although it is slowly growing. Most people here see the sea as somewhere to walk along the beach, so diving is still a fairly [[niche]] activity, mainly for adventurous young people.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

sample.answer: A positive change I genuinely want to make is to spend less time on my phone and social media. I have noticed that I waste far too many hours [[scrolling]] mindlessly, which leaves me feeling drained rather than refreshed. It usually starts innocently, checking one message, and suddenly forty minutes have disappeared. I want to make this change because I believe that time could be far better spent on hobbies, exercise or real relationships. Even at the dinner table, which is a special time in my family, I sometimes catch myself glancing at the screen, and I don't like that about myself. To do it, I plan to set strict limits on certain apps and keep my phone out of reach during meals and before bed. I also want to replace the habit with something better, such as reading a few pages instead of reaching for my phone. I know breaking such an [[ingrained]] habit will require real [[discipline]]. Honestly, I think reducing screen time would have a hugely [[beneficial]] effect on my focus and mental wellbeing. It would allow me to be more [[fully present]] instead of constantly distracted. I have already started making small changes, such as turning off notifications for most apps, and I have noticed a difference. I seem to get through my work faster, and I actually finish the books I start. I think in our hyper-connected world, consciously stepping back from technology is one of the healthiest changes a person can make.

followUps.q: Has anyone in your family commented on your phone use?
followUps.answer: Yes, my mother, many times! She jokes that the phone is my second sister. She means it kindly, but it did make me realise how much of our time together I was wasting.

followUps.q: Do you think you will succeed in making this change?
followUps.answer: I think so, as long as I am realistic. I don't plan to give up my phone completely, since I need it for work, but cutting down gradually feels [[achievable]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: On the whole, I think they have, though not without significant drawbacks. Smartphones have put a world of information, communication and services in our pockets, which is genuinely empowering and convenient. However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of [[dependence]] that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them [[consciously]] rather than [[compulsively]].

part3Samples.q: How was life different before smartphones?
part3Samples.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.

part3Samples.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely [[impair]] both our mental and physical wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more [[anticipatory]] and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to [[blur]] further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

part3Samples.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
part3Samples.answer: There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. [[Designating]] device-free times and zones, such as during meals or in the bedroom, helps re-establish boundaries. Using apps that track and limit screen time can raise awareness of usage. Ultimately, consciously replacing [[mindless scrolling]] with more rewarding activities is the most sustainable way to [[loosen the phone's grip]].

part3Samples.q: Some say social media does more harm than good. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I am somewhat [[torn]] on this. There seems to be compelling evidence of harm, from mental health issues to the spread of misinformation, which I take seriously. However, I cannot ignore the genuine benefits, such as connecting isolated people and enabling social movements. So rather than declaring it simply harmful, I would say its impact is highly dependent on usage. The technology is not inherently [[malign]]; our habits determine its [[net effect]].

What appeals to me most is how [[applicable]] it is to everyday life; understanding human behaviour is useful in almost any profession. I think it would help me become more [[empathetic]] and a better communicator, both personally and professionally. In my line of work, being able to read people and put them at ease is half the job. Honestly, I believe it is one of those subjects that genuinely changes how you see the world. You start noticing patterns in your own behaviour, and you become a little more patient with others. It bridges science and human experience in a way I find deeply appealing. It is definitely something I hope to pursue once my circumstances allow, because I think it would enrich both my career and my understanding of the people around me.

followUps.q: Would you like to work as a psychologist?

part3Samples.q: Do you think a university degree is necessary for success?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think it is strictly necessary, though it certainly helps in many fields. A degree provides knowledge, [[credentials]] and valuable connections, and for professions like medicine it is essential. However, success can absolutely be achieved through other routes, such as vocational training or [[entrepreneurship]]. In my view, a degree is a powerful tool, but it is not the only path, and it is no [[guarantee]] of success.

part3Samples.q: Is academic education or vocational training more valuable?
part3Samples.answer: I believe both are equally valuable, just for different purposes, and society needs both. Academic education develops theoretical knowledge and critical thinking, suited to research and the professions. Vocational training provides practical, [[job-ready]] skills that are in high demand and often lead directly to employment. Unfortunately, vocational paths are often unfairly [[stigmatised]], when in reality [[skilled trades]] are absolutely essential and highly rewarding.

part3Samples.q: Why do so many young people want to attend university nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: There are several reasons. Firstly, a degree is often seen as a minimum requirement for many good jobs, so there is [[mounting pressure]] to obtain one. There is also considerable social [[prestige]] attached to a university education in many cultures. Additionally, university offers young people independence and a chance to grow. However, this rush has led to some [[devaluation]] of degrees, as they become more common.

part3Samples.q: How do you think universities will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect universities to become more flexible and accessible. Online and hybrid degrees will likely become [[mainstream]], allowing people to study while working. There may be a shift towards shorter, more [[modular]] courses focused on specific skills rather than lengthy traditional degrees. Universities will also need to work more closely with industry to ensure their qualifications remain relevant in a [[fast-changing]] economy.

part3Samples.q: University is becoming very expensive. What could be done about this?
part3Samples.answer: This is a [[pressing issue]] in many countries. Governments could increase funding and [[subsidies]] to keep public universities affordable, treating education as an investment rather than a cost. Expanding scholarships and income-based repayment schemes would help ensure that talent, not wealth, determines access. Promoting quality alternatives, like online courses and apprenticeships, would also [[relieve pressure]] on the traditional, expensive model.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

I made this decision fairly recently, after realising that international experience would greatly benefit my career. Ironically, it was helping other students with their applications every day that finally convinced me to take the step myself. To carry it out, I have been researching universities, preparing for the required exams and saving diligently, since it is quite an [[ambitious]] undertaking. At the moment, I am working on my IELTS, practising a little every evening after work. The process is genuinely demanding, but I am approaching it in a [[methodical]], step-by-step way. My younger sister has been a great help too, quizzing me on vocabulary over dinner. This plan is important to me because I believe studying in a different country would be a hugely [[enriching]] experience, both academically and personally. It would push me out of my comfort zone and expose me to new perspectives. Honestly, the thought of it is both exciting and slightly nerve-wracking, especially the idea of being so far from my family. I know there will be challenges along the way, but I am fully committed to [[seeing it through]]. It represents a significant investment in my future, and I am determined to make it a reality, so that I can come back with skills that are genuinely [[transferable]].

followUps.q: How does your family feel about your plan?

followUps.q: Would you come back to Bangladesh afterwards?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think so many students want to study abroad?
part3Samples.answer: There are several compelling reasons. Studying abroad often provides access to higher-quality education and internationally recognised qualifications, which boost career prospects. Beyond academics, it offers an invaluable chance to experience a new culture, gain independence and [[broaden one's horizons]]. For many, it is a genuinely [[transformative]] personal journey as much as an academic one, offering [[exposure]] that home study cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Is studying abroad better than studying in one's own country?
part3Samples.answer: It depends entirely on the individual and their goals. Studying abroad offers [[cultural immersion]] and independence that home study cannot, and sometimes access to better facilities. However, it is expensive, and studying at home is cheaper, closer to family, and free of the challenge of adapting to a foreign culture. So neither is universally better; it is a matter of [[weighing]] the [[enrichment]] against the cost and difficulty.

part3Samples.q: What challenges do students face when studying in another country?
part3Samples.answer: They face numerous challenges. Culture shock and homesickness are extremely common, especially at first. A language barrier can make both study and daily life difficult and [[isolating]]. There are also practical hurdles, like managing finances and navigating an unfamiliar system alone. Adapting to different academic expectations can be [[daunting]] too. However, overcoming these difficulties is precisely what makes the experience so rewarding and [[character-building]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think studying abroad will become more common in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I think physical study abroad will remain popular but may face competition from online alternatives. Increasingly, students can access foreign universities' courses remotely, offering the academic benefits without the cost of [[relocating]]. However, the cultural and personal growth of actually living abroad is [[irreplaceable]], so demand will [[persist]]. The future may see a mix of physical and virtual international education, making it more accessible and diverse.

part3Samples.q: How can universities better support international students?
part3Samples.answer: Universities can do a great deal. Providing strong orientation programmes and language support eases the initial transition. Pairing international students with local mentors or buddy schemes helps combat isolation and homesickness. Practical guidance on visas, housing and finances is also invaluable. Essentially, creating a genuinely [[inclusive]] and welcoming environment helps international students [[integrate]] and [[flourish]] rather than feeling like outsiders.

part3Samples.q: Some say there are too many university graduates today. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is some truth to this in certain fields. The rapid expansion of higher education has, in some cases, led to a [[surplus]] of graduates in particular subjects, resulting in [[underemployment]] and a [[mismatch]] with the job market. However, I would not say education itself is the problem. The real issue is the lack of alignment between what people study and what the economy actually demands.

sample.answer: A way I love to relax is by listening to music while doing absolutely nothing else. It might sound simple, but in our busy lives, giving yourself permission to just be still is something of a [[rarity]]. I usually do this in the evening, after we have had dinner as a family, lying on my bed or sitting on the rooftop of our building with a cup of tea. The rooftop is my favourite spot, because it is quiet up there and on clear nights you can feel a gentle breeze coming off the river. What makes it so relaxing is that it lets my mind completely [[unwind]] after a hectic day. Depending on my mood, I choose calming acoustic tracks or something more uplifting. I never use music as background noise at these times; I give it my full attention, which is what makes the difference. Quite often I end up listening to old Bengali songs that my parents used to play, which feel like home to me. There is something almost [[meditative]] about focusing purely on the music and letting my thoughts settle. Honestly, this small ritual has become essential for my mental wellbeing. In a world that constantly demands our attention, having a way to properly [[decompress]] is genuinely valuable. It costs nothing and asks nothing of me, which is exactly why I love it. I always feel noticeably calmer and more centred afterwards, ready to face whatever comes next, and I think everyone deserves a little [[sanctuary]] like that.

followUps.q: Do you use headphones or play the music aloud?
followUps.answer: Usually headphones, because I don't want to disturb my sister while she's studying. On the rooftop, though, I sometimes play it quietly through my phone, which feels more relaxed and natural.

followUps.q: Have your ways of relaxing changed since you were a child?
followUps.answer: Quite a lot. As a child I relaxed by running around outside with my cousins. Now I need calm rather than excitement, which I suppose is a natural part of growing older.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

sample.answer: A daily routine that has genuinely benefited me is waking up early and having a calm, [[unhurried]] start to my day. I get up around six, well before I need to, which gives me time for myself before the world wakes up. Our neighbourhood is very quiet at that hour, apart from the birds and the odd rickshaw bell, and I really value that peace. I use this quiet period to plan my day, read a little and enjoy a proper breakfast rather than rushing. My mother is usually up too, so we often share the first cup of tea together before the rest of the family is awake. What makes it so valuable is that it sets a productive, positive tone for everything that follows. I keep it up by going to bed at a reasonable hour, since [[discipline]] at night makes the mornings easier. I also leave my phone in another room, so I am not tempted to stay up late scrolling. Honestly, starting the day calmly rather than in a panic has had a [[remarkable]] effect on my mood and focus. It gives me a sense of control that lasts throughout the day, and I rarely feel that I am chasing my own schedule. When I have skipped it, perhaps after a late wedding or a long journey, I can really feel the difference. I think how you begin your morning genuinely shapes the rest of it. This routine has become one of the most [[beneficial]] habits I have ever developed, and I would recommend it to anyone who feels [[perpetually]] rushed.

followUps.q: Is it hard to keep this routine at the weekend?
followUps.answer: A little. On Fridays I sometimes allow myself an extra hour in bed, but I try not to change my sleep pattern too much, because Saturday mornings then feel much harder.

followUps.q: Were you an early riser as a child?
followUps.answer: Not at all. My mother practically had to drag me out of bed for school. It is funny how things change; now I am often the first one awake in our flat.

part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?

sample.answer: A tradition I love in my country is the celebration of Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year. It takes place in mid-April and marks the beginning of the year according to our traditional calendar. It is a public holiday, so almost everyone is free to join in, whatever their background. On this day, people dress in traditional clothes, usually red and white, and the streets come alive with colourful processions, music and fairs. In Sirajganj, there is a big fair, or mela, where you can buy clay toys, handmade crafts and sweets, and children walk around with their faces painted. Many families start the morning with panta bhat, which is soaked rice, served with fried hilsa fish. What I find so special is how it brings the entire community together in a spirit of joy and [[renewal]]. Families gather to share traditional food, and there is a wonderful sense of [[festivity]] everywhere. It is important because it celebrates our cultural identity and heritage, which I think is vital to preserve. Unlike religious festivals, it belongs to every Bengali, which makes it wonderfully [[inclusive]]. In an increasingly globalised world, traditions like this help [[keep our roots alive]]. Honestly, the atmosphere on that day is genuinely [[uplifting]], and it fills people with optimism for the year ahead. Every year I go to the fair with my younger sister, and even though we buy the same sweets and wander past the same stalls, it never loses its charm. I think it is a beautiful example of how a shared tradition can strengthen a whole community's sense of belonging.

followUps.q: Has the way people celebrate it changed?
followUps.answer: Somewhat. It has become more commercial, with shops running special offers and people posting endless photos online. But the heart of it, dressing up and spending the day together outdoors, has stayed the same.

followUps.q: Do young people still care about this tradition?
followUps.answer: Very much, in my experience. If anything, young people are the most enthusiastic, because it is colourful, joyful and a chance to [[show off]] traditional outfits with friends.

sample.answer: A festival I thoroughly enjoy celebrating is Eid, which is one of the most important occasions in my culture. There are actually two Eids each year, but the one after Ramadan is my favourite, because it follows a month of fasting and reflection. The day begins with special prayers at the Eidgah, the open prayer ground, followed by visiting relatives, exchanging gifts and, of course, an enormous feast. The atmosphere is wonderfully [[joyous]], with everyone dressed in their finest clothes and children excitedly collecting small gifts of money, which we call salami. I celebrate it with my entire extended family, which is a big part of why I love it so much. We usually spend it at my grandparents' village home, and my elder sister travels up from Dhaka with her husband and children, so the house is full of noise and laughter. My four-year-old nephew always comes straight to me for his salami. What I enjoy most is the strong sense of [[togetherness]] it creates; in our busy lives, it is one of the few times the whole family gathers. The food, prepared over several days by my mother and grandmother, is absolutely [[delectable]]. Honestly, the warmth and generosity that fill the day are genuinely heartwarming. It is far more than a religious occasion; it is a celebration of family, gratitude and community, and many people share food with neighbours and those less fortunate. I always look forward to it, and it leaves me feeling deeply [[content]] and grateful for the people in my life.

followUps.q: What is your favourite Eid dish?
followUps.answer: Definitely my mother's shemai, a sweet vermicelli dish cooked with milk and sugar. Eid morning doesn't feel complete until I have had a bowl of it, usually before we even leave for prayers.

followUps.q: Is Eid celebrated differently in cities and villages?
followUps.answer: A little. In Dhaka it can feel quieter, because so many people travel back to their home districts. In villages it is more communal, with the whole neighbourhood visiting each other's houses throughout the day.

sample.answer: A piece of advice I would give to any young person is not to be afraid of failure, but to see it as part of learning. It sounds like a cliché, but I think very few people actually live by it. I think this is genuinely important because so many young people are [[paralysed]] by the fear of getting things wrong. In my country especially, exam results are treated as a matter of family honour, so failing can feel like a disaster rather than a lesson. I would give this advice to my younger cousins, who sometimes hesitate to try new things in case they fail. I would also share it with the students I meet at work, many of whom are too scared to apply to good universities in case they are rejected. I would tell them that every successful person has failed countless times, and that setbacks are often the most [[instructive]] experiences of all. The key is to be [[resilient]] and to keep going. A rejection letter or a poor mark is simply information about what to improve next time, not a judgement on who you are. I believe this mindset could help them enormously, freeing them to take risks and pursue their dreams. Honestly, I wish someone had drilled this into me when I was younger, because I wasted opportunities out of fear. I think teaching young people to embrace failure rather than dread it is one of the most [[invaluable]] lessons we can offer them. It builds courage and confidence for life, and it makes the journey far less [[nerve-racking]].

followUps.q: Who gave you the best advice when you were younger?
followUps.answer: Probably my grandmother. She had little formal education, but she used to say that a tree that bends in the storm doesn't break. It took me years to appreciate how [[profound]] that was.

It is a bhatiali song, a traditional kind of boatman's song from our river region, slow and full of longing. I first heard it as a young boy, and it is deeply tied to memories of my grandparents. My grandfather used to hum it while we sat on the veranda of their village home, watching the boats move slowly along the river in the evening. Whenever I hear it now, it instantly transports me back to those [[carefree]] childhood days. What makes it so important is not the song itself but the powerful [[nostalgia]] it evokes. The gentle melody and heartfelt lyrics have a wonderfully [[soothing]] quality that I find comforting. It is amazing how a single piece of music can carry such emotional weight and instantly bring back a whole era of your life. Honestly, I think this is the true power of music; it becomes intertwined with our memories. My grandfather is in his eighties now, and he still hums it sometimes when we visit, which makes it feel even more precious to me. Listening to it now sometimes brings a tear to my eye, in the best possible way. It is a [[cherished]] reminder of my roots and the people I love, and I hope to pass it on one day, perhaps starting with my little nephew, so that it [[lives on]] in our family.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

sample.answer: A website I find genuinely useful is an online learning platform that offers courses on almost any subject imaginable. I use it regularly to develop new skills related to my work and personal interests. Over the past year, for instance, I have done a course on digital marketing, which helps with promoting our consultancy, and another on advanced spreadsheets. I usually log on three or four evenings a week, for about an hour, and a bit longer on Fridays. What makes it so useful is how [[accessible]] it makes education; I can learn from experts around the world without leaving my home. That matters a lot when you live in a smaller town like Sirajganj, where specialist training is hard to find. I have taken several courses on it, and the quality of instruction has been genuinely impressive, with clear videos, short quizzes and forums where you can ask questions and get answers from other learners. It fits perfectly around my busy schedule, since I can learn at my own pace whenever I have free time. Honestly, I think platforms like this are [[revolutionising]] the way people learn. They [[democratise]] knowledge that was once available only to a privileged few. I find it incredibly [[empowering]] to be able to keep learning and improving myself so easily. In a rapidly changing world where continuous learning is essential, I think tools like this are [[invaluable]]. It has genuinely helped me grow both professionally and personally, and I recommend it to everyone, especially students preparing to study abroad.

followUps.q: Have you ever paid for an online course?
followUps.answer: Yes, a couple of times, when I needed a proper certificate. Most of what I learn is free, but paying for a course actually makes me more committed, because I don't want to waste the money.

followUps.q: Is online learning as good as learning in a classroom?
followUps.answer: For practical skills, I think it is almost as good. But a classroom gives you spontaneous discussion and a teacher who notices when you are confused, which is hard to [[replicate]] online.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet makes people less intelligent. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I disagree with that as a [[blanket statement]], though it raises a fair concern. The internet does not make us less intelligent; rather, it changes how we use our intelligence. We may memorise less, relying on it as an external memory, but we have unparalleled access to knowledge. The risk is that passive consumption and short attention spans can weaken deep thinking. So it is a tool that can either [[enrich]] or [[diminish]] the mind, depending on use.

sample.answer: An interesting idea I came across recently is the concept of a four-day working week, which I find genuinely [[intriguing]]. I heard about it through an article discussing trials carried out by various companies in Europe. A colleague shared it in our office group chat, and it sparked quite a lively debate over lunch. The basic idea is that people work fewer days but remain just as productive, if not more so. What I find so fascinating is the claim that working less can actually make people more efficient, because they are better rested and more focused. It completely challenges the traditional assumption that longer hours mean more output. In Bangladesh, many people work six days a week, so for us the idea sounds almost like science fiction. Honestly, I think it is a genuinely [[revolutionary]] idea that could transform work-life balance. Of course, there are practical challenges, and it would not suit every industry. Hospitals, shops and farming, for example, simply cannot stop for three days, so it would probably need a rota system. Still, the early results suggesting improved wellbeing and unchanged productivity are quite [[compelling]]. Personally, I feel cautiously optimistic; I would love an extra day for my family and hobbies, but I think it would need to be introduced gradually. I think ideas like this are important because they force us to question [[long-held assumptions]] about how we live and work. It is definitely a concept I would love to see explored more widely, and I suspect it will gain [[momentum]] in the future.

followUps.q: What would you do with an extra day off?
followUps.answer: I would probably visit my grandparents in the village more often and spend more time reading. I might also finally start that public speaking course I keep putting off.

followUps.q: Do you think your employer would try it?
followUps.answer: Perhaps not straight away, because our busiest periods revolve around university deadlines. But a trial during quieter months could be [[feasible]], and I think my manager would at least be open to discussing it.

part3Samples.q: How do you think work will change in the next few decades?
part3Samples.answer: I believe work will become far more flexible and technology-driven. Remote and hybrid working, already common, will likely become the norm for many roles. Automation and AI will take over routine tasks, meaning humans will focus more on creative and interpersonal work. People will also need to [[reskill]] continuously, as the concept of a single lifelong career becomes increasingly [[obsolete]] and [[fluid]].

part3Samples.q: Is working from home better or worse than working in an office?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on the person and the job. Working from home offers wonderful flexibility and eliminates the commute, which many find [[liberating]] and more productive. However, the office provides valuable social interaction, easier collaboration and a clearer boundary between work and home life. Personally, I think a [[hybrid]] model captures the best of both, though it requires real [[self-discipline]] to work remotely well.

part3Samples.q: What effects will automation have on employment?
part3Samples.answer: Automation is a genuine [[double-edged sword]]. On one hand, it will [[inevitably]] [[displace]] many workers in routine and manual jobs, which is a serious concern. On the other hand, history shows that technology also creates entirely new industries and roles. The key effect is a shift in the types of jobs available, which means workforces will need to adapt and acquire new skills.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will work fewer hours in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is a real possibility, and one I would welcome. As automation boosts productivity, there is a strong argument that the gains could be shared through shorter working weeks. Trials of the four-day week seem to have shown [[promising]] results, with productivity maintained. However, this will not happen automatically; it will require [[deliberate choices]] by businesses and governments to [[prioritise]] wellbeing over pure output.

part3Samples.q: How can workers prepare for a rapidly changing job market?
part3Samples.answer: The single most important thing is to embrace lifelong learning. Workers should continually update their skills and remain [[adaptable]], rather than assuming their current expertise will last forever. Developing [[transferable skills]], like communication and problem-solving, is wise, since these remain valuable across industries. Staying curious and open to change is really the best [[safeguard]] against being left behind.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

sample.answer: A habit I would genuinely like to give up is my tendency to procrastinate, especially with tasks I find unpleasant. Paperwork is the worst example; I will happily reply to twenty student messages to avoid filling in one boring form. It started, I think, as a way of avoiding stress, but over time it has become quite [[ingrained]]. At university I often left assignments until the night before, and because I usually got away with it, I never learned to change. I want to give it up because it often leaves me rushing at the last minute, which is both stressful and [[counterproductive]]. I know that if I tackled things sooner, my life would be far calmer and more organised. It also isn't fair on my colleagues when they have to wait for my part of the work. To break the habit, I have started using to-do lists and breaking large tasks into smaller, more [[manageable]] steps. I have also tried the technique of simply starting a task for five minutes, which often removes the initial reluctance. Once I begin, I usually realise the task is not nearly as bad as I had imagined. I have also started tackling the task I dread most first thing in the morning, while my energy is high. Honestly, procrastination is a surprisingly [[stubborn]] habit to break, and I have to remain constantly [[vigilant]]. Still, I have made real progress, and I feel much better when I stay on top of things. It is a work in progress, but one I am fully committed to.

followUps.q: Do other people in your family procrastinate?
followUps.answer: Not really, which makes it more embarrassing! My younger sister is incredibly disciplined and finishes her work days early. She often teases me about it, which is actually good motivation.

followUps.q: Is procrastination always a bad thing?
followUps.answer: Mostly, yes, but occasionally a little delay helps, because ideas have time to develop. The problem is when it becomes a [[chronic]] pattern and you are always working under pressure.

part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

sample.answer: A personal quality I believe is essential for success is perseverance, the ability to keep going despite setbacks. In my view, talent alone is rarely enough; it is [[persistence]] that ultimately makes the difference. I think this is important because the path to any worthwhile goal is inevitably filled with obstacles and failures. Anyone who expects a smooth journey is likely to give up the first time things go wrong. A close friend of mine embodies this quality perfectly; he failed several times before finally building a successful business, but he never gave up. His first venture, a small clothing shop, closed within a year, and his second barely covered its costs. What I admire is his refusal to be [[discouraged]] by temporary defeats. Each time, he studied what had gone wrong and tried again, and today he runs a thriving online shop. I have seen the same quality in my father, who kept his small business going for over thirty years through floods, price rises and difficult seasons. I genuinely believe that this kind of [[resilience]] is what separates those who succeed from those who quit. Honestly, in a world that often celebrates instant success, we forget how much quiet, stubborn effort lies behind most achievements. Perseverance keeps you moving forward when motivation fades, and motivation always fades at some point, however excited you were at the start. I think it is one of the most [[underrated]] qualities a person can have, and it is something I consciously try to [[cultivate]] in myself.

followUps.q: Do you think perseverance can be learned?
followUps.answer: I think so, mostly through experience. Every time you push through a difficulty and see the result, you become a bit more confident that you can do it again next time.

followUps.q: Is there a time you showed perseverance yourself?
followUps.answer: Getting my first job was one. I had several rejections after graduating, which was disheartening, but I kept improving my CV and interview skills until the consultancy finally offered me a position.

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some people say governments should promote positive role models. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree. Governments can certainly [[showcase]] admirable citizens, such as scientists or humanitarians, to counterbalance shallow celebrity culture. However, I am slightly cautious, because state-endorsed role models can easily become [[propaganda]] if handled poorly. So while the intention is commendable, it needs to be done [[transparently]] and without any political agenda.

sample.answer: Something I make a conscious effort to do for the environment is reduce my use of single-use plastic. I started a couple of years ago, after seeing some genuinely [[alarming]] documentaries about ocean pollution. Around the same time, I noticed how much plastic was piling up along the banks of the Jamuna near my home, and it really hit me that this was not just a distant problem. Now I carry a reusable water bottle and cloth shopping bags everywhere, and I avoid plastic packaging wherever I can. Jute bags are easy to find in Bangladesh, so there is really no excuse. I have even persuaded my mother to take a basket to the market instead of coming home with a dozen polythene bags. I do it because I feel we all have a personal responsibility to protect the planet, however small our individual contribution. I am [[under no illusion]] that my efforts alone will solve the problem, but I believe change starts with individuals. Honestly, I think it is easy to feel helpless about huge issues like climate change, but taking small actions gives me [[a sense of agency]]. It also makes me more mindful of my consumption in general, and I think twice before buying things I don't really need. I feel genuinely good about doing my part, however modest. I think if enough people adopt these [[sustainable]] habits, the collective impact could be significant. It is a small change, but it lets me live with a [[clear conscience]].

followUps.q: Do your friends do the same?
followUps.answer: A few of them do, and some started after teasing me about my cloth bag. Most still use plastic without thinking, though, so I try to set an example rather than lecture anyone.

followUps.q: What else would you like to do for the environment?
followUps.answer: I would like to join a riverbank clean-up group, as some young people organise them in our area. Planting a few trees on my grandparents' land in the village would also be a [[worthwhile]] project.
