part3Samples.q: Whose responsibility is it to protect the environment?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a shared responsibility, though the [[burden falls unevenly]]. Individuals certainly have a role through their daily choices, but honestly, their impact is limited compared to that of governments and large corporations. Governments must implement effective policy and regulation, while industries must change their practices. So while everyone should do their part, I think the greatest responsibility lies with those who hold the power to [[enact]] [[systemic change]].

part3Samples.q: Are individuals or governments more effective at protecting the environment?
part3Samples.answer: While individual actions are valuable and add up, I would argue governments are far more effective due to their [[scale of influence]]. A single person recycling makes a small difference, but a government can regulate entire industries, invest in renewable energy and shape behaviour through law. That said, individual pressure and voting ultimately influence what governments do. So the two are [[interconnected]], but the [[leverage]] of government is undeniably greater.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some people do not care about the environment?
part3Samples.answer: There are several reasons. For some, environmental problems feel distant and abstract, so they do not feel a sense of urgency. Others prioritise immediate economic concerns, like putting food on the table, over long-term issues. There is also a feeling of [[helplessness]], that individual action is [[futile]]. Additionally, some are simply unaware or misinformed. So it is usually a mix of [[apathy]], immediate priorities and a sense of powerlessness.

part3Samples.q: Are you optimistic about the future of the environment?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic, though the challenges are [[daunting]]. On one hand, the scale of problems like climate change is alarming, and progress often feels too slow. On the other hand, awareness has never been higher, technology in renewable energy is advancing rapidly, and younger generations are deeply committed to the cause. So while I have real concerns, I believe human [[ingenuity]] and growing collective will give us genuine [[grounds for hope]].

part3Samples.q: What can ordinary people do to help the environment?
part3Samples.answer: There is a surprising amount individuals can do. Reducing consumption and waste, recycling, and being [[mindful]] of energy and water use all help. Choosing sustainable transport, like walking or public transit, and eating less meat can significantly cut one's [[carbon footprint]]. Beyond personal habits, supporting green businesses and, crucially, voting for environmentally responsible policies [[amplifies]] our impact. Collectively, these individual choices can drive genuine change.

part3Samples.q: Some say sustainable products are too expensive for ordinary people. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is some truth to this currently, though it is changing. It is true that some sustainable products, like organic food or electric cars, carry a higher [[price tag]], which can put them [[out of reach]] for those on tight budgets. This is a real barrier to [[widespread adoption]]. However, as demand grows and technology improves, prices are steadily falling. So while cost is a genuine obstacle today, I believe sustainability is becoming increasingly affordable and accessible.

sample.answer: A way I keep fit and healthy is by going to the gym a few times a week, which has become an important part of my lifestyle. There is a small gym about ten minutes from our flat, and I usually go on Saturday, Monday and Wednesday evenings after work, for roughly an hour each time. I started a couple of years ago, initially just to lose a little weight, but it soon became something I genuinely enjoy. At first I felt quite self-conscious, because everyone else seemed to know exactly what they were doing, but one of the trainers kindly showed me the basics. What works for me is having a set routine, which keeps me [[accountable]] and stops me making excuses. Beyond the obvious physical benefits, I find exercise incredibly [[therapeutic]] for my mental health. After a stressful day, a good workout is the perfect [[outlet]] for releasing tension. On the days I don't go, I still take a walk by the river, so I am rarely completely inactive, even during the busiest weeks. Honestly, the sense of discipline it has given me has spilled over into other areas of my life. I feel more energetic, sleep better and generally more positive. It required real commitment to make it a habit, but now I would feel restless without it. I think finding a form of exercise you actually enjoy is the key to [[sustaining]] it long term, and for me, the gym is exactly that, a routine I would find very hard to [[abandon]].

followUps.q: Do you ever go to the gym with a friend?
followUps.answer: Sometimes, with a university friend who lives nearby. Having a partner helps on days when I feel lazy, because I don't want to let him down, although we do end up chatting more than training.

followUps.q: Is going to the gym popular where you live?
followUps.answer: It is becoming more popular among young people, even in a modest town like Sirajganj. A few years ago there were hardly any gyms, but now several have opened, which shows how attitudes are changing.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

sample.answer: A course I would genuinely love to take is one in creative writing, something I have long been curious about. I have always enjoyed writing, but I feel my skills are quite [[rudimentary]] and could benefit from proper guidance. I have a notebook full of half-finished short stories, mostly about village life and my grandparents' generation, but I never quite know how to shape them. I want to take it because writing well is such a valuable and [[versatile]] skill, useful in almost any field. In my job, for example, I often help students with their personal statements, and I can see how much a well-told story can strengthen an application. I would probably take it online, so I could fit it around my work, though a face-to-face class with feedback would be ideal. There are occasional workshops in Dhaka, so I might try to attend one when I visit my elder sister. What appeals to me most is the chance to learn techniques from experienced writers and to receive [[constructive criticism]]. Honestly, I think a good course could help me express my ideas far more clearly and creatively. It would also give me a productive and [[fulfilling]] hobby outside of work. I believe learning should be a lifelong pursuit, and this is one course I am determined to take eventually. It is exactly the kind of skill that could enrich both my professional and personal life, and who knows, perhaps one day I will finally finish one of those stories and see it [[in print]].

followUps.q: Would you write in English or Bengali?
followUps.answer: Probably both. Bengali feels more natural for stories about village life, because some expressions simply don't translate. But writing in English would help my work and reach a wider audience.

followUps.q: Have you ever shown your writing to anyone?
followUps.answer: Only to my younger sister, who is a very honest critic. She once told me a story was far too long and rather [[repetitive]], which hurt a little, but she was absolutely right.

part3Samples.q: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?
part3Samples.answer: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely [[outdated]], especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn [[keeps the mind sharp]], opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a [[lifelong pursuit]], not a phase.

part3Samples.q: Is it easier to learn when you are young or when you are older?
part3Samples.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

part3Samples.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
part3Samples.answer: It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer [[subsidies]] or learning accounts. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?

The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

sample.answer: An ambition I have held for many years is to one day start my own business. I first had this dream as a teenager, watching my father run his small enterprise with such dedication. He ran that business for over thirty years before retiring recently, and I saw both the freedom and the worry it brought him. What has always appealed to me is the idea of building something of my own and being [[self-reliant]]. More specifically, I would love to open my own education consultancy in Sirajganj, so that students here would not have to travel to Dhaka for reliable advice. Towards this goal, I have been gaining relevant work experience and quietly saving whatever I can. My current job has taught me how the whole process works, from counselling students to dealing with universities and visa requirements. I am also constantly learning about how businesses operate, since I know success requires far more than just a good idea. This ambition matters to me because it represents freedom, creativity and the chance to make a real impact. Honestly, I find the idea both thrilling and slightly [[daunting]], given the risks involved. Still, I believe the potential rewards, both financial and personal, are worth it. My father always says that a business is like a child, needing constant care, and I think he is right. I know it will require enormous [[perseverance]], but it is a dream I refuse to let go of. With my father's [[hard-earned]] advice and enough preparation, I am confident that one day I will make it happen and prove myself as a genuinely [[entrepreneurial]] person.

followUps.q: Would you ask your father to help with your business?
followUps.answer: Definitely, at least as an adviser. He knows a great deal about managing money, dealing with customers and surviving difficult years, which is exactly the kind of practical wisdom no textbook can give you.

followUps.q: Do many young people in your country want to start a business?
followUps.answer: More and more, I think. Many young graduates are frustrated by limited job opportunities, so they start small online businesses. Social media has made it much easier to get started with very little [[capital]].

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say job security is more important than job satisfaction. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends heavily on a person's circumstances. For someone supporting a family, security is understandably the priority, as it provides essential [[peace of mind]]. However, I personally lean towards satisfaction, because a secure but miserable job can [[take a serious toll]] on one's mental health over time. Ideally, one should not have to sacrifice one for the other, though reality often forces a [[compromise]].

sample.answer: A sport I absolutely love is cricket, which is almost a national obsession in my country. These days I mostly watch it, but I played a great deal when I was younger. I got into it as a child, playing casual games in the street with the neighbourhood kids, using a taped tennis ball and a bat my father bought me from the local market. What I love about it is the wonderful blend of strategy, skill and teamwork. As a spectator, I find major matches genuinely [[thrilling]], especially when the national team is playing. I watch almost every international match Bangladesh plays, usually at home with my father, who analyses every shot as if he were the coach. The atmosphere during a big game is electric, and the whole country seems to come to a standstill. Honestly, there is a special sense of [[unity]] that cricket brings, uniting people across all backgrounds. I still join a friendly game with old friends now and then during the holidays, as it is a fun way to stay active. What makes it so [[captivating]] is its unpredictability; a match can turn completely in a single moment. Some of the most [[nail-biting]] evenings of my life have been spent in front of the television, waiting for the final ball. I think its enduring popularity here is thoroughly deserved. For me, cricket is far more than a game; it is a shared passion that connects millions of people and brings my family together in front of the screen.

followUps.q: Have you ever watched a match in a stadium?
followUps.answer: Only once, in Dhaka, when I was staying with my elder sister. The noise and the sea of red and green shirts were unforgettable, although honestly you see the action more clearly on television.

followUps.q: Do women in your family enjoy cricket too?
followUps.answer: Yes, my younger sister is just as passionate as I am, and even my mother keeps an eye on the score during big matches. Cricket really is a family affair in our [[household]].

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.

sample.answer: A significant way I have changed over the last few years is that I have become far more patient and self-assured. In my younger days, I was quite [[impulsive]] and would get frustrated easily when things did not go my way. At university, I would argue with friends over the smallest things and make hasty decisions I later regretted. I think this change came about through a combination of life experience and facing a few genuine challenges. Starting work played a big part, because dealing with worried students and demanding deadlines forced me to stay calm. Around the same time, my father retired, and I found myself taking on more responsibility at home. Overcoming difficulties taught me that most problems are temporary and that panicking rarely helps. As a result, I now approach setbacks far more calmly and rationally. This shift has affected me profoundly; I feel more [[grounded]] and less anxious than I used to. It has also improved my relationships, as I listen more and react less. Honestly, I am genuinely pleased with this change, because it has made me a more balanced person. I think personal growth like this is one of the quiet rewards of getting older. I no longer [[sweat the small things]] the way I once did. My mother says I have become more like my grandfather, which I take as the highest compliment. It is a change I am proud of, and it is genuinely [[liberating]] to feel this much calmer, as though a weight has been lifted from my shoulders.

followUps.q: Did anyone help you make this change?
followUps.answer: My grandfather, in a quiet way. Whenever I got worked up, he would just smile and tell me that no problem lasts forever. Seeing how calm he stays, even in his eighties, taught me a lot.

followUps.q: Is there anything about your younger self you miss?
followUps.answer: Perhaps a little of the fearlessness. When I was younger, I would try things without overthinking. Now I am more cautious, which is sensible, but occasionally I wish I were more [[spontaneous]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is more [[nuanced]] than that. In material terms, young people today certainly enjoy comforts and technology their grandparents lacked. However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, [[job insecurity]] and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the [[hardships]] have shifted in nature.

sample.answer: Something I would genuinely like to be better at is managing my time more effectively. While I am fairly organised, I often find myself struggling to fit everything in, which leaves me feeling [[stretched]]. Between work, my IELTS preparation, family commitments and trying to keep up my reading, there never seem to be enough hours in the day. I am constantly [[juggling]] different things and rarely feel I am giving any of them my full attention. I want to improve because I believe better time management would reduce my stress and make me far more productive. To improve, I have started using planning tools and trying to prioritise my tasks more [[ruthlessly]], focusing on what truly matters. Every Friday evening I sit down and plan the week ahead, which already helps, because I start Saturday knowing exactly what needs doing first. I am also learning to say no to commitments that are not worth my time, which is surprisingly hard in a culture where refusing an invitation can seem rude. Honestly, I think time is our most precious resource, and using it wisely is one of the most valuable skills a person can develop. If I mastered it, I believe I could achieve far more while feeling less [[overwhelmed]]. It would give me more time for the things I actually enjoy, like evening walks and dinner with my family, which is the whole point. It is an ongoing effort, but even small improvements have already made a noticeable and [[tangible]] difference to my daily life.

followUps.q: Who in your family manages time best?
followUps.answer: My younger sister, without question. She plans her study schedule weeks in advance and actually sticks to it. I have started borrowing some of her methods, although I would never admit that to her.

followUps.q: Do you think people were better at managing time in the past?
followUps.answer: Perhaps they had fewer distractions. My father's generation didn't have phones constantly buzzing, so it was easier to focus. Today the challenge is less about time and more about attention.

part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

sample.answer: A skill I firmly believe everyone should have is basic cooking. In my view, it is a genuinely essential life skill that far too many people [[neglect]]. In Bangladesh, many young men grow up never having to cook, because mothers usually take care of the kitchen, and I was exactly the same until a few years ago. It is important because it directly affects your health, your finances and your independence. Relying entirely on takeaways and processed food is both expensive and unhealthy, whereas cooking allows you to eat well and [[affordably]]. This is especially relevant for students going abroad, and I always tell the students I advise to learn a few dishes before they leave. People can learn it easily these days, with countless free tutorials available online, so there really is no excuse. Honestly, I think learning to cook is one of the most practical and [[empowering]] things a person can do. It gives you control over what you put into your body, and it means you are never stuck when you end up living on your own. Beyond the health benefits, I find cooking to be a surprisingly [[therapeutic]] and creative activity. I learned a few years ago, when my mother spent several weeks in the village looking after my grandparents, and she taught me the basics over the phone. Those weeks of burnt rice and oversalted dal were [[humbling]], but they transformed my daily life for the better. I genuinely believe that if everyone learned to cook a few simple meals, both public health and personal wellbeing would improve considerably.

followUps.q: What dish can you cook best?
followUps.answer: Probably chicken curry with rice. It took me many attempts to get the spices right, but now even my mother says it is quite good, which is high praise from her.

followUps.q: Should cooking be taught in schools?
followUps.answer: I think so, at least the basics. It would help both boys and girls become more independent, and it could also challenge the old idea that cooking is only a woman's [[responsibility]].

part3Samples.q: How important is food to a country's culture?
part3Samples.answer: Food is absolutely central to culture, in my view. It is far more than mere [[sustenance]]; it reflects a nation's history, geography, values and social customs. Sharing a meal is a universal expression of hospitality and community. Traditional dishes carry deep [[sentimental]] and cultural significance, passed down through generations. So I would say cuisine is one of the most [[tangible]] and beloved expressions of a country's identity.

part3Samples.q: How have people's eating habits changed over the years?
part3Samples.answer: Eating habits have changed considerably. In the past, people mostly ate home-cooked, seasonal and local food, often together as a family. Today, busy lifestyles have led to more processed food, takeaways and eating [[on the go]], often alone. [[Portion sizes]] have grown, and international cuisine is now widely available. While this offers more variety and convenience, I think it has come at some cost to health and the [[communal]] nature of dining.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fast food has become so popular?
part3Samples.answer: Its popularity comes down to a few key factors. Firstly, it is convenient and quick, which suits our increasingly busy, time-poor lifestyles. Secondly, it is relatively cheap and consistently tasty, engineered to appeal to our [[cravings]]. Aggressive marketing has also made it [[ubiquitous]] and aspirational. Unfortunately, this convenience comes at a cost, as many argue its popularity has contributed to rising rates of [[obesity]] and related health problems.

part3Samples.q: How do you think the way we eat will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant changes driven by health and sustainability concerns. Plant-based diets and [[alternative proteins]], like lab-grown meat, are likely to become far more [[mainstream]] as we address the environmental impact of food. Technology may also personalise nutrition. Hopefully, there will be a renewed appreciation for healthy, [[sustainable]] eating. So our diets may become more conscious and innovative, balancing convenience with health and the planet.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to encourage people to eat more healthily?
part3Samples.answer: A range of measures could help. Education about nutrition from a young age is fundamental, so people can make informed choices. Making healthy food more affordable and accessible, while perhaps [[taxing unhealthy options]], can shift behaviour. Clear [[food labelling]] and restrictions on junk food advertising, especially to children, would also help. Ultimately, creating an environment where the healthy choice is the easy, [[appealing]] choice is the most effective approach.

part3Samples.q: Some say too much emphasis is placed on paper qualifications. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree. Society has long [[placed excessive weight on]] formal certificates, sometimes [[overlooking]] genuinely talented individuals who lack them. This can create a [[rigid]] system where a piece of paper matters more than actual ability. Thankfully, this is slowly changing as employers recognise the value of skills and experience. A shift towards judging people on real competence would be a genuinely positive development.

data.prompt: Describe a way technology has changed the way we live
bullets: and how you feel about it

sample.answer: A way technology has profoundly changed our lives is in how we communicate with one another. The rise of smartphones and social media has made staying in touch almost [[instantaneous]], regardless of distance. This happened incredibly quickly; within about a decade, cheap smartphones and mobile internet reached almost every corner of Bangladesh, even villages like my grandparents'. In the past, keeping in contact with faraway friends and family relied on letters or expensive phone calls, which now seems almost unimaginable. My father still remembers queuing at a shop in town to make a short, crackly call to a relative in Dhaka, and letters took over a week to arrive. Today, a video call across continents is effortless and free, which is genuinely [[remarkable]]. I speak to my elder sister in Dhaka almost every day, and my nephew loves showing me his toys on the screen. On the whole, I think this change has been overwhelmingly positive, keeping relationships alive that might otherwise have faded. However, I do have some [[reservations]]; I feel it has sometimes replaced deeper, face-to-face interaction with shallower digital contact. There is a certain irony that we are more connected than ever yet arguably lonelier. At family gatherings, I sometimes notice everyone staring at their phones instead of talking to the people sitting right next to them. Honestly, like most technology, I think it is a [[double-edged sword]]. Used mindfully, it is an incredible tool, but it requires a degree of [[discipline]]. Overall, though, I am grateful for how it has shrunk the world and brought distant people closer.

followUps.q: Do your grandparents use video calls?
followUps.answer: My grandfather does, surprisingly well for someone in his eighties. My grandmother prefers ordinary calls, because she finds it strange to see her own face on the screen, which always makes us laugh.

followUps.q: Do you still write letters or cards?
followUps.answer: Almost never, sadly. I do sometimes write a card for Eid or a birthday, and people seem to [[treasure]] them far more than a message, precisely because they are so rare now.

part3Samples.q: Do you think digital communication is better than face-to-face communication?
part3Samples.answer: I would say it is not better, but rather different, with its own strengths. Digital communication offers [[unmatched]] convenience and lets us stay connected across any distance instantly. However, it lacks the richness of face-to-face interaction, where tone, body language and physical presence convey so much. For deep, emotional conversations, nothing beats being together in person. So digital tools are a wonderful [[supplement]], but not a full [[substitute]] for genuine human contact.

part3Samples.q: How is the way young people communicate different from older generations?
part3Samples.answer: The difference is quite marked. Young people have grown up as [[digital natives]], so they favour instant messaging, voice notes and social media over phone calls, which many find [[intrusive]]. Older generations often prefer calls or in-person conversation. Young people also communicate more through images, emojis and memes, a kind of [[visual shorthand]]. This can lead to occasional misunderstanding between the generations, though both are simply adapting to their era.

part3Samples.q: What effect has instant messaging had on our language?
part3Samples.answer: It has had a noticeable influence. Instant messaging has spawned a whole new informal language of abbreviations, emojis and slang, which allows for quick, expressive communication. Some worry this is [[eroding]] traditional writing skills and grammar, especially among the young. However, I take a more relaxed view; language has always [[evolved]], and people generally understand when to switch between casual and formal [[registers]]. So it is evolution, not decay.

part3Samples.q: How do you think we will communicate in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I imagine communication will become even more immersive and instantaneous. Technologies like virtual reality could allow us to feel genuinely present with distant people, and real-time translation may [[dissolve]] language barriers entirely. We may increasingly communicate through augmented reality overlays too. While exciting, I hope these advances [[enhance]] rather than replace human warmth, and that we do not lose the value of simple, [[unmediated]] face-to-face connection.

part3Samples.q: How can people avoid becoming too dependent on digital communication?
part3Samples.answer: Being intentional is key. Setting aside device-free time, particularly during meals or when with loved ones, helps enormously. Consciously choosing to call or meet someone rather than always texting preserves deeper connection. Turning off unnecessary notifications reduces the [[constant pull]] of our devices. Essentially, we need to treat technology as a tool that serves us, rather than allowing it to [[dominate]] our attention and [[displace]] real interaction.

part3Samples.q: Some say people cannot live without their phones now. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think that is an exaggeration, but it contains an [[uncomfortable truth]]. Obviously, people survived perfectly well before phones, so it is not a literal dependency. However, phones have become so [[integral]] to how we work, navigate and communicate that living without one would be genuinely inconvenient and isolating in modern society. So while we could live without them, our society has become so [[reliant]] on them that it would be a difficult adjustment.

sample.answer: A cultural event I would love to attend is the Lalon festival, a large traditional music gathering held every year in Kushtia, in the west of Bangladesh. It celebrates Lalon, a nineteenth-century mystic poet and songwriter whose songs are still sung all over the country. Although I have seen it on television, I have never experienced it in person, which I would genuinely love to change. It takes place over several days at his shrine and showcases performers from all over the region, especially Baul singers, the wandering minstrels in their saffron robes. Kushtia is not too far from Sirajganj, so it would be quite easy to get there by bus, and I could stay for a couple of nights. I want to attend because I believe experiencing such an event live would be far more [[immersive]] and moving than watching a screen. What draws me to it is the celebration of our rich cultural [[heritage]], which I think is increasingly important to preserve. Lalon's songs are about humanity and questioning divisions between people, and I find that message still feels [[timeless]]. I imagine the atmosphere would be absolutely [[electric]], surrounded by thousands of people sharing the same appreciation for the art. Honestly, I think events like this are vital for keeping traditions alive and passing them to younger generations. It would be a wonderfully [[enriching]] experience, deepening my connection to my own culture. It is definitely on my list of things to do, and I hope to attend it next year with a couple of friends.

followUps.q: Would you take your family with you?
followUps.answer: Probably not the first time, as it gets very crowded and the music goes on late into the night. I would go with friends first, and perhaps take my younger sister another year.

followUps.q: Are cultural events like this popular with young people?
followUps.answer: More than you might expect. Many young people find Baul music refreshingly [[authentic]] compared with commercial pop, and some modern bands have even recorded new versions of Lalon's songs.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
part3Samples.answer: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
part3Samples.answer: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have [[homogenised]] lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

part3Samples.q: Some say art is not as important as science. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly disagree with ranking them this way, as they serve different but equally vital purposes. Science advances our material understanding and improves our lives technologically, which is crucial. But art nourishes our emotional and spiritual lives, fosters empathy, and gives meaning to human existence. A world with science but no art would be efficient yet [[soulless]]. So rather than one being more important, I see them as [[complementary]] pillars of a [[flourishing]] civilisation.

data.prompt: Describe a challenge that young people face today

sample.answer: A significant challenge facing young people today is the immense pressure created by social media. In my view, constant exposure to carefully curated, idealised versions of other people's lives has become genuinely [[detrimental]] to mental health. Everyone seems to be on holiday, getting engaged or landing a dream job, and it is easy to forget that these are just the highlights. This exists because platforms are designed to be [[addictive]], encouraging endless comparison. The more time we spend scrolling, the more money these companies make, so they have little reason to change. It affects almost all young people, who often feel inadequate when measuring their real lives against these unrealistic highlights. I see it in my younger sister's friends, who worry about how many likes a photo gets, and in some of the students I advise, who compare themselves with classmates who have already gone abroad. I think it can lead to serious anxiety and a distorted sense of self-worth. To tackle it, I believe we need better education about using social media [[mindfully]], along with a cultural shift towards valuing authenticity over appearances. Parents and teachers also need to talk about it openly, rather than simply banning phones. Honestly, I think the platforms themselves should also [[bear some responsibility]] for their design. It is a complex issue without a simple solution. Having grown up alongside this technology, I have felt its effects personally. I think raising awareness is the crucial first step, helping young people understand that what they see online is rarely the full, honest picture, and that real life is far more [[nuanced]].

followUps.q: Do you think this problem is worse for girls or boys?
followUps.answer: It affects both, but perhaps differently. Girls often face more pressure about appearance, while boys feel pressure to look successful or wealthy. Neither is healthy, and both deserve more attention.

followUps.q: Would you ever give up social media completely?
followUps.answer: Probably not, because I use it to stay in touch with family and for work. But I have become far more [[selective]], unfollowing accounts that make me feel worse rather than better.

part3Samples.q: Do you think social media has a positive or negative effect on society?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is genuinely a [[mixed blessing]]. On the positive side, social media connects people across distances, gives a voice to the marginalised and spreads information rapidly. However, its negative effects are equally significant, from spreading misinformation to fuelling anxiety and comparison. In my view, the platforms themselves are [[neutral]]; the real issue is how we use them. Used [[mindfully]], the benefits can outweigh the drawbacks.

part3Samples.q: How has social media changed the way people communicate?
part3Samples.answer: It has transformed communication dramatically. In the past, staying in touch required letters or calls, whereas now we can share our lives instantly with hundreds of people at once. Communication has become faster and more visual, but arguably more [[superficial]]. We interact more frequently yet often less [[meaningfully]], replacing deep conversations with quick likes and comments. So it has [[widened our reach]] while sometimes shallowing our connections.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people share so much of their lives online?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems largely from a deep human desire for validation and connection. Receiving likes and comments triggers a sense of approval that can be quite [[addictive]]. Many people also enjoy documenting their lives and keeping in touch. However, this [[compulsion]] to share can tip into oversharing, where people [[curate]] an idealised image, sometimes at the expense of actually living in the moment.

part3Samples.q: How do you think social media will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate it will become even more immersive, possibly through virtual and augmented reality, blurring the line between online and offline life further. Artificial intelligence will make content ever more [[personalised]], which raises concerns about [[echo chambers]]. Hopefully, there will also be a growing backlash leading to more regulation and healthier usage habits. So it will likely become more [[sophisticated]], but not necessarily more beneficial.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce the harmful effects of social media?
part3Samples.answer: A [[multi-pronged]] approach is needed. On an individual level, promoting digital literacy and encouraging conscious limits on usage helps enormously. Platforms themselves should be [[held accountable]] for their algorithms and do more to combat misinformation and protect young users. Governments may also need to introduce sensible regulation. Ultimately, teaching people to engage [[critically]] rather than passively is the most sustainable solution.

part3Samples.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree, though it never disappears entirely. As people mature, they generally develop a firmer sense of identity and care less about others' approval, making them more [[resilient]] to pressure. However, the pressure simply takes on a more [[subtle]] form in adulthood, such as keeping up with colleagues' lifestyles. So it lessens, but it certainly does not [[vanish]].

sample.answer: An important decision I currently need to make about my future is whether to pursue further studies abroad or continue building my career at home. It is a genuinely [[pivotal]] choice that will shape the next several years of my life. I need to make it because application deadlines for next year's intake are approaching, and universities will not wait for me to make up my mind. On one hand, studying abroad would offer invaluable experience and open new doors, but it is expensive and involves leaving my family. My father has recently retired, and my mother often travels to the village to look after my grandparents, so I feel a certain responsibility to be around. On the other hand, staying would mean steady progress but perhaps fewer opportunities for growth. I have a good position at my consultancy, and my manager has hinted that more responsibility may come my way soon. I need to make this decision soon, which makes it feel quite [[pressing]]. Honestly, I keep [[going back and forth]], weighing the potential rewards against the risks and sacrifices. It is a rather [[daunting]] choice, precisely because both paths have real merit. I have been seeking advice from people I trust, including my father and my elder sister, and trying to think about what truly matters to me in the long run. Whatever I decide, I want it to be a well-considered choice rather than an [[impulsive]] one. I am confident I will eventually reach a sensible conclusion, and that I will have no regrets.

followUps.q: What does your family advise you to do?
followUps.answer: My father encourages me to go, saying that he and my sister can manage things at home. My mother is more hesitant, although she would never stop me. Their support makes the decision a little easier.

followUps.q: How do you usually make big decisions?
followUps.answer: I write down the pros and cons, talk to a few people I trust, and then give myself a few days. Rushing never works for me; I need time for things to [[sink in]].

part3Samples.q: Why do you think so many students want to study abroad?
part3Samples.answer: There are several compelling reasons. Studying abroad often provides access to higher-quality education and internationally recognised qualifications, which boost career prospects. Beyond academics, it offers an invaluable chance to experience a new culture, gain independence and [[broaden one's horizons]]. For many, it is a genuinely [[transformative]] personal journey as much as an academic one, offering [[exposure]] that home study cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Is studying abroad better than studying in one's own country?
part3Samples.answer: It depends entirely on the individual and their goals. Studying abroad offers [[cultural immersion]] and independence that home study cannot, and sometimes access to better facilities. However, it is expensive, and studying at home is cheaper, closer to family, and free of the challenge of adapting to a foreign culture. So neither is universally better; it is a matter of [[weighing]] the [[enrichment]] against the cost and difficulty.

part3Samples.q: What challenges do students face when studying in another country?
part3Samples.answer: They face numerous challenges. Culture shock and homesickness are extremely common, especially at first. A language barrier can make both study and daily life difficult and [[isolating]]. There are also practical hurdles, like managing finances and navigating an unfamiliar system alone. Adapting to different academic expectations can be [[daunting]] too. However, overcoming these difficulties is precisely what makes the experience so rewarding and [[character-building]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think studying abroad will become more common in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I think physical study abroad will remain popular but may face competition from online alternatives. Increasingly, students can access foreign universities' courses remotely, offering the academic benefits without the cost of [[relocating]]. However, the cultural and personal growth of actually living abroad is [[irreplaceable]], so demand will [[persist]]. The future may see a mix of physical and virtual international education, making it more accessible and diverse.

part3Samples.q: How can universities better support international students?
part3Samples.answer: Universities can do a great deal. Providing strong orientation programmes and language support eases the initial transition. Pairing international students with local mentors or buddy schemes helps combat isolation and homesickness. Practical guidance on visas, housing and finances is also invaluable. Essentially, creating a genuinely [[inclusive]] and welcoming environment helps international students [[integrate]] and [[flourish]] rather than feeling like outsiders.

part3Samples.q: Some say job security is more important than job satisfaction. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends heavily on a person's circumstances. For someone supporting a family, security is understandably the priority, as it provides essential [[peace of mind]]. However, I personally lean towards satisfaction, because a secure but miserable job can [[take a serious toll]] on one's mental health over time. Ideally, one should not have to sacrifice one for the other, though reality often forces a [[compromise]].

sample.answer: A useful habit I have developed for managing money is setting aside a fixed amount of savings every single month, before spending on anything else. I developed this habit a few years ago, after realising I was spending rather [[carelessly]] and never managing to save. When I got my first salary, I spent it on eating out and new gadgets, and by the end of the month there was nothing left. My father, who ran a small business for over thirty years, sat me down and explained how he had always put something aside, even in difficult years. Now, as soon as I receive my salary, I transfer a set portion into a separate savings account. What makes it so effective is that it removes the temptation to spend that money, since it is out of sight. This habit has given me a genuine sense of [[financial security]] and a safety net for emergencies. It is also how I am funding my plans to study abroad, which would be impossible otherwise. Honestly, it has been one of the most [[beneficial]] financial decisions I have ever made. I would strongly recommend it to anyone, because it makes saving automatic rather than an afterthought. The key is to treat savings as a non-negotiable expense, just like any other bill. Over time, even small, consistent amounts add up [[considerably]]. It has taught me the value of discipline and [[delayed gratification]], which are invaluable lessons in life, and I am grateful my father taught me early.

followUps.q: Do young people in your country usually save money?
followUps.answer: Many try, but it is not easy with rising prices and the pressure to keep up with friends. Mobile banking has made saving simpler, though, and I think financial awareness is gradually improving.

followUps.q: Have you taught this habit to anyone else?
followUps.answer: Yes, my younger sister. I encouraged her to save a small part of her pocket money every month, and she was delighted when she could buy her own books without asking our parents.

part3Samples.q: How important is money in life?
part3Samples.answer: Money is [[undeniably]] important, but its importance has limits. It is essential for meeting our basic needs, providing security, and giving us freedom and opportunities, so I would never dismiss it. However, beyond a certain point of comfort, its ability to improve our happiness [[diminishes sharply]]. Health, relationships and purpose matter far more. So I see money as a vital tool and [[enabler]], but a poor ultimate goal in itself.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to save money or spend it?
part3Samples.answer: A healthy balance between the two is ideal. Saving is [[prudent]], providing security, peace of mind and the means to achieve future goals or weather emergencies. However, being excessively frugal can mean missing out on valuable experiences and enjoyment in the present. Spending wisely, particularly on experiences and things that genuinely enrich life, is worthwhile. So I favour disciplined saving combined with mindful spending, avoiding both reckless [[extravagance]] and joyless [[hoarding]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does the pursuit of wealth have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The pursuit of wealth has mixed effects. Positively, it can motivate hard work, innovation and achievement, driving both personal and economic progress. However, an excessive obsession with wealth can be corrosive, leading people to become greedy, materialistic, and to neglect relationships, ethics and their own wellbeing. It can foster perpetual dissatisfaction too. So while a healthy desire to prosper is fine, an [[all-consuming]] [[fixation]] on money can genuinely [[distort]] a person's values.

part3Samples.q: Do you think the gap between rich and poor will grow in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am concerned that it might, without deliberate intervention. Trends like automation, which may concentrate wealth among those who own the technology, and globalisation could widen the gap further. However, there is also growing awareness of inequality and political pressure to address it through [[progressive taxation]] and social policy. So the outcome is not [[predetermined]]; whether the gap widens or narrows will depend on the political choices societies make to [[redistribute]] opportunity.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce poverty?
part3Samples.answer: Reducing poverty requires a comprehensive approach. Access to quality education and healthcare is fundamental, as it enables social mobility. Creating decent, well-paid jobs and ensuring fair wages tackles the [[root causes]]. Social [[safety nets]], like unemployment support, protect the most vulnerable. Progressive taxation can fund these efforts. Ultimately, empowering people with opportunities and skills, rather than mere [[handouts]], offers the most sustainable path out of poverty.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

sample.answer: A social problem I care deeply about is the lack of quality education available to children from poorer backgrounds. In my country, a child's future is too often determined by the wealth of their family, which I find genuinely [[unjust]]. Wealthier families can pay for private tutors and good schools, while poorer children often sit in overcrowded classrooms with too few teachers. This matters to me because I believe education is the most powerful tool for breaking the cycle of poverty. I also see it every day in my work, where the students who reach us are usually the lucky ones who had support from the start. It affects millions of talented children who never get the chance to [[fulfil their potential]] simply due to their circumstances. Near my hometown, for example, there are children living on the char lands, the river islands of the Jamuna, who have to cross the river by boat just to reach school, and many simply drop out. I think this is a tragic waste of human potential. To address it, I believe there needs to be far greater investment in public schools and more scholarship opportunities for the [[disadvantaged]]. Better pay for rural teachers would also help attract talented people. Honestly, I think providing equal access to good education is one of the most important things any society can do. It is an issue I feel strongly about, and I try to support relevant charities where I can. I genuinely believe that giving every child a fair start would create a more [[equitable]] and prosperous society for everyone.

followUps.q: Have you ever volunteered to help with this problem?
followUps.answer: A little. During university, I taught basic English to children in my grandparents' village during the holidays. It was only a few weeks, but seeing their enthusiasm was incredibly [[rewarding]].

followUps.q: Do you think the situation is improving?
followUps.answer: Slowly, yes. More girls are in school now than a generation ago, and mobile phones give some access to online lessons. But the gap in quality between rich and poor areas is still very wide.

part3Samples.q: Do you think society treats everyone equally?
part3Samples.answer: Unfortunately, I do not think any society treats everyone truly equally, though many have made real progress. Despite laws promoting equality, discrimination based on factors like gender, ethnicity, class or background still persists, often subtly. People's opportunities are still heavily influenced by the [[circumstances of their birth]]. So while the ideal of equality is widely embraced, in practice significant [[disparities]] and [[injustices]] remain that we must continue to address.

part3Samples.q: Has society become more or less equal over time?
part3Samples.answer: In many respects, society has become considerably more equal. Enormous progress has been made in areas like women's rights, racial equality and the rights of minorities compared to the past. Legal discrimination has been [[dismantled]] in many places. However, economic inequality has actually widened in some countries. So the picture is mixed; we have [[made great strides]] in social and legal equality, while economic disparities remain a [[persistent]] challenge.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of inequality in society?
part3Samples.answer: Inequality stems from a [[complex web]] of factors. Unequal access to quality education and healthcare is a major driver, as it limits opportunity from birth. Discrimination based on gender, race or class also plays a role. Economic systems that concentrate wealth, along with the circumstances one is born into, [[perpetuate]] the cycle. So inequality is rarely due to a single cause; it results from [[structural]], historical and social factors that reinforce one another.

part3Samples.q: Do you think full equality is achievable?
part3Samples.answer: I think complete [[equality of outcome]] is probably unrealistic, given natural differences in talent, effort and luck. However, equality of opportunity, where everyone has a genuinely fair chance to succeed, is a [[worthy]] and achievable goal to strive towards. We may never reach a perfectly equal society, but we can continually reduce unfair barriers. So while perfect equality may be an ideal rather than a destination, meaningful progress towards fairness is absolutely [[attainable]].

part3Samples.q: How can governments promote greater equality?
part3Samples.answer: Governments have powerful tools. Ensuring universal access to quality education and healthcare is perhaps the most important, as it [[levels the playing field]]. Progressive taxation and social welfare programmes can reduce economic disparities. Strong anti-discrimination laws protect marginalised groups. Investing in disadvantaged communities helps break cycles of poverty. Essentially, by actively removing barriers and [[redistributing]] opportunity, governments can foster a more [[equitable]] and inclusive society.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

sample.answer: An outdoor activity I thoroughly enjoy is hiking, particularly in the hill areas of Sylhet and Bandarban. Sirajganj itself is completely flat, so I usually go on a trip once or twice a year, often during the cooler winter months when the trails are dry. I usually go with a small group of close friends from university, which makes it even more enjoyable. We share the planning, travel overnight by bus and stay in simple guesthouses, which is all part of the adventure. What I love about it is the wonderful combination of exercise, fresh air and stunning scenery. After months of office work and busy roads, spending a few days in nature is genuinely [[rejuvenating]]. There is something deeply satisfying about reaching the top of a trail after a challenging climb and being rewarded with a [[breathtaking]] view. In Bandarban, you can sometimes stand above the clouds in the early morning, which I will never forget. Honestly, I find hiking to be both physically and mentally [[restorative]]; it clears my head like nothing else. It is also a great way to bond with friends, away from the distractions of daily life, as the phone signal is often weak anyway. I think spending time in nature is something modern life sorely lacks, and hiking is my favourite way to reconnect with it. Between trips, I make do with long walks along the river at home. I always return home feeling tired but genuinely [[content]]. It is easily one of my favourite ways to spend a holiday, and I am already counting down to our next [[excursion]].

followUps.q: Does your family worry when you go hiking?
followUps.answer: My mother certainly does. She makes me promise to call her every evening and to avoid dangerous trails in the rainy season. It is a small price to pay for her peace of mind.

followUps.q: Would you like to hike in another country?
followUps.answer: Very much. I would love to trek in Nepal one day, perhaps on one of the shorter routes in the Himalayas. The scenery there must be even more [[awe-inspiring]] than anything we have here.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].
